This analysis helps clarify why the observed genes may not be specific to a single disease but instead contribute to both conditions and the potential risks and benefits of the drugs involved.We identified 74 approved drugs targeting 30 genes that were either designated for psychiatric (as a range of psychiatric drugs can be used for treating PTSD and associated symptoms) or cardiovascular conditions (Supplementary Data DRD2, GFAP, POR and NOS1 to be targets of several CV medications that address conditions including hypo/hypertension, diabetes, cholesterol and heart failure. Only Prazosin, an alpha-1 adrenergic receptor antagonist was the only drug that is known to treat hypertension, and has off-label benefit for PTSD-associated nightmares. Among genes, DRD2 had the highest number of interactions with both psychiatric and CV drugs. While interaction type between each drug and gene target is not available, we observed that 87.5% of drugs are inhibitors, and 21.5% are agonists to DRD2.We also investigated adverse effects of these drugs, and among the 45 psychiatric drugs, most cardiovascular-system-related adverse effects included increased weight or weight fluctuations, tachycardia, and QT prolongation, which indicates a disturbance in the heart ventricle chamber signal transmission. Other CV adverse effects of psychiatric drugs include blood glucose increase, diabetes, orthostatic hypotension, and dyslipidemia.Conversely, among the 30 CVD drugs, adverse psychiatric effects were less observed, and included depression, suicide attempt, cognitive disorder, and hallucination. (Supplementary Data DiscussionTo our knowledge, this is the first work that includes a comprehensive evaluation of CV measurements from diverse sources, such as imaging, diagnoses, and risk factors. By leveraging additional GWAS data of EHR-based phecodes for CV diagnoses from the MVP, the study generates statistically well-powered GWAS results, addressing phenotypes that previously lacked sufficient power or were analyzed using data from a single source, such as the UKBB. Additionally, the study validates genetic associations between PTSD and CV conditions using observational data and dissects shared genes to explore the biological mechanisms underlying PTSD-CV comorbidity. We report causal variants for CV diagnoses and imaging traits that are shared with PTSD, while CV health behaviors, as per AHA’s LE8 show a broader genetic overlap across several loci. Among the EHR CV traits, colocalization analyses of discovery and replication cohorts indicated loci 3p21.31, 17q21.31, 7p22.3, and 7p21.3 as potential PTSD-CVD pleiotropy hotspots. Specifically, loci 3p21.31 and 17q21.31 exhibited different LD-linked causal variants, while loci 7p22.3 (MADIL1, ELFN1) and 7p21.3 (TMEM106B, VWDE, THSD7A) had the greatest number of causal variants shared between PTSD and multiple CV conditions (e.g., hypertension, diabetes, coronary artery disease, obesity/overweight, atrial fibrillation, and non-specific chest pain). Although some of these loci have been identified in the context of psychiatric disorders, we additionally observed genes at these loci also colocalize between multi-tissue molecular profiles of several cardiovascular traits, highlighting their significant role as a potential common denominator to PTSD and CV conditions. Often, genetic data is a proxy for diagnostic risk, and mirrors association, but is limited in adjusting for additional confounders without losing statistical power. We confirmed the specificity of PTSD-CV genetic relationships using epidemiological observation from EHR data of 249,906 AllofUS participants. We observed that PTSD diagnosis is associated with 13 CV diagnoses (identified using genetic data from MVP EHR data and replicated in UKBB EHRs), even after accounting for smoking, BMI, deprivation index, and depression diagnosis. Interestingly, 4 of the 13 diagnoses overlap with CV health factors from the LE8 traits – type 2 diabetes, obesity, overweight, and hypertension, which is parallel to the genetic study of ideal cardiovascular health based on LE 7.To comprehensively identify regions and genes, we recognized that LD-defined regions may not precisely align with genes based on their length or proximity. To address this, we implemented a multi-tiered analytical approach that examined both disease-related effects and quantitative trait loci effects. Specifically, we used colocalization analysis to investigate variants with disease-related effects (annotated based on their closest gene), and genes identified via PWAS, indicate a collective set of variants as protein quantitative trait loci (pQTLs) for each gene. By leveraging the cumulative effect of genetic variants on protein expression, also aids in identifying potentially actionable gene targets that overlap between PTSD and cardiovascular conditions. We identified twice as many genes using brain-based proteome expression weights than with blood. We also observed interesting relationships, such as total cholesterol demonstrating negative genetic correlation with PTSD at multiple loci, and almost half of the gene associations have opposite effect estimates between PTSD and total cholesterol. These observations may contribute to the abnormal total cholesterol reported in individuals with PTSD. Additionally, we report many shared proteomic associations of PTSD and CVD to further identify underlying common disease mechanisms and therapeutic targets. Among them, LRRC37A2 was related to the most CVD traits (N = 20), followed by MST1 (N = 18). LRRC37A2 has been associated with coronary artery disease, cardiorespiratory fitness, and thyroid function. MST1 activation has been linked to the pathogenesis of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases while its downregulation in the hippocampus appears to be protective in the context of stress-related mental health conditions (e.g., PTSD). NCAM1 showed the most statistically significant proteomic association with smoking. This is in line with previous evidence linking this locus to smoking. Other PTSD-CV shared genes with supporting evidence from previous CV studies included TMEM106B, MAD1L1, SATB1, PLCL2, FURIN, FOXP2, ESR1, and CNNM2. Pathway enrichment analyses highlighted different blood vs. brain patterns. Specifically, genes identified by the blood-based PWAS were enriched for mostly immunological and neuronal processes, while the brain-based PWAS genes were related to carbohydrate metabolism and calcium-modulating functions. The pathway enrichment of genes that are statistically causal for brain proteome expression further highlighted the role of metabolism of oxytocin, calcium signaling, adrenergic signaling in cardiomyocytes, and circadian rhythm. These findings converge with previous hypotheses related to the role of immune-metabolic signaling and calcium dysregulation in PTSD and CV pathogeneses. This tissue-specific pathway identification is likely due to the differential gene expression between blood and brain samples. Additionally, a caveat that should be considered is substantial differences in sample sizes across proteome studies: the brain-proteome reference includes only 528 samples, compared to over 7,000 and 50,000 samples in the blood-proteome studies. These sample size disparities significantly impact statistical power and our ability to detect associations, wherein the blood proteome has better power over the brain proteome as of current data available.The drug repurposing analyses contextualized the role of shared genes between PTSD and cardiovascular conditions as potential targets of both psychiatric and CV drugs, or exhibit opposing side effects, suggesting these genes may influence both conditions rather than being disease-specific. We identified DRD2, GFAP, NOS1 and POR as common gene targets of several PTSD and CV drugs. Prazosin was common to PTSD and CV conditions, although with mixed results for alleviation of PTSD and related symptoms. Altered levels of GFAP expression are associated with PTSD, and thrombotic injury to the vascular muscle leads to secretion of GFAP. Furthermore, the drugs used for PTSD treatment that we identified in our drug-gene-interaction analysis have reported adverse CV effects such as weight gain, weight changes, cardiac arrhythmia, abnormal blood pressure, and diabetes. NCAM1, which colocalizes with BMI, is on the same locus as DRD2 at 11q23.2, with both genes having molecular colocalization with insulin-like growth factor, blood pressure, and BMI. On the other hand, CVD drugs that exhibit psychiatric adverse effects such as depression and cognitive dysfunction have been associated with serotonergic, and antidepressant response respectively. These findings suggest a common role of the drugs in the two different diseases, where multiple mechanisms may be involved, either protective or detrimental.While we provide a comprehensive assessment of the biology shared between PTSD and several CV conditions, our study has some limitations. Due to the well-known disparities in genetic research, our analyses were limited to European ancestries, which do not allow generalization in all continental populations. We used MVP as the discovery cohort for EHR-based CV diagnoses due to its relatively low sample overlap with PTSD GWAS [~29%], this may have filtered out some loci that could have been identified with other cohorts as discovery. Additionally, veteran participants may not be representative of genetic profile identified from other (civilian) populations due to underlying demographic differences, such as recruitment design, varied healthcare administration patterns, type and burden of trauma exposure, higher male prevalence, and MVP being slightly older cohort (average age is 61.9 yrs) than AoU (average age is 57.3 yrs), and UKBB (average age is 56.52 yrs). Since we prioritized large and diverse measurements of CV conditions, this would lead to phenotype differences, a potential caveat to consider while interpreting results. We leveraged all the recent proteome studies to dissect molecular pathways, which led to using two different TWAS approaches, FUSION and SMR, as the weights were only available for the specific approach. While we were comprehensive in assessing all cohorts, these methodological differences could have led to capturing different sets of gene associations. Furthermore, though all the methods we implemented do account for sample overlap, there is possibility that some gene-trait associations might be cohort specific, such as those from UKBB. Therefore, these genes should be tested further when large-scale cohorts for molecular phenotypes become available in the future. While our observational analysis in the AllofUs cohort confirmed the PTSD-CV comorbidities in the civilian cohort, further studies will be needed to verify the same for PTSD-CV shared loci identified in our molecular analyses. The observational analysis was cross-sectional using the lifetime prevalence of PTSD and CV conditions. This did not permit us to investigate the temporal relationships between the two traits. The drug-gene targets and subsequent mapping to PTSD and CV conditions is explained as an example to learn about the role of gene drugs in therapeutic and adverse effects of drugs. The drugs mentioned were identified from research studies and may not reflect actual prescription practices and need further validation before we can make hypotheses regarding their impact on patients’ implications. Pharmacovigilance data for gene-drug targets was extracted from a single source and may not be updated from research data or ongoing trials.In conclusion, this study examines the shared biology of PTSD and CV health, leveraging large-scale molecular data and multi-modal information. Specifically, considering EHR diagnoses, cardiac imaging phenotypes, and cardiac health-related habits, we highlighted the local genetic correlations, proteomic and transcriptomic associations, and the potential pharmacological targets for molecular mechanisms underlying PTSD-CVD comorbidity. These findings converge on overlap in several domains across PTSD and CVD and within the context of the broader PTSD-CVD literature highlight important mechanisms relevant to potential pharmacological intervention, warranting additional research.MethodsStudy populationsWe conducted the study to explore the genetic overlap between PTSD and cardiovascular outcomes, as defined by electronic health records (EHR) and heart imaging (Fig. .Summary statistics for GWAS of PTSD utilized in this study originated from a comprehensive meta-analysis led by Nievergelt et al. that identified 76 autosomal loci (Supplementary Data N = 186,689 individuals], and 10 biobank studies incorporating EHR-derived PTSD status. In total, the study incorporated 95 GWASs, with a sample size of 1,222,882 individuals of European descent (effective sample size (Neff) = 641,533).GWAS of cardiovascular and metabolic diagnoses using EHRMillion Veteran ProgramThe CVD phenotype datasets utilized in this study were sourced from the MVP (see data availability), a nationwide initiative sponsored by the Department of Veterans Affairs Office of Research and Development. In our investigation of the genetic overlap between PTSD and cardiovascular clinical outcomes, we leveraged summary statistics from GWAS of EHR-based phecodes. Phecodes are manually curated groups of International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes-9/10, designed to capture clinically meaningful concepts for research purposes using the PheMap, which classifies diagnoses into 17 categories (available at https://phewascatalog.org/). We tested 141 diagnoses from circulatory and 105 from endocrine/metabolic categories. A detailed description of GWAS of these traits in 458,203 individuals of European genetic ancestry in MVP is available elsewhere. (Supplementary Data UK BiobankTo replicate MVP findings, we leveraged GWAS of EHR-based phecodes data available from the UK Biobank (UKBB). Specifically, we analyzed summary statistics of GWAS of phecodes in 420,531 participants of European descent performed by the Pan-UKBB initiative. Each MVP trait was matched with a corresponding UKBB phenotype based on their phecode concordance. Because MVP phecodes 278.11, 427.21, 428.3 were not available in the UK Biobank, we used the numbering to find the exact matches, some codes were unavailable, so we used the closest decimal available: Phecode 278.11 (Morbid Obesity, MVP) to Phecode 278.1 (Obesity, UKBB), Phecode 427.21 (Atrial Fibrillation, MVP) to Phecode 427.2 (Atrial Fibrillation and flutter, UKBB), and Phecode 428.3 (Heart failure with reduced EF [Systolic or combined heart failure], MVP) to Phecode 428.2 (Heart failure NOS, UKBB), and Venous thromboembolism with chronic venous insufficiency, since both conditions relate to damage in the leg veins, as that was closest proxy available. The details of the replication datasets are presented in Supplementary Data Other GWAS cohortsIn addition to the UKBB data, we replicated MVP findings also using 11 GWAS performed from major consortia that may include a combination of self-reported or clinical studies. The sample sizes of these datasets ranged from 119,715 to 1,020,441, and their diagnoses were paired with corresponding phecodes (Supplementary Data . For Type 2 Diabetes adjusted by BMI, we used summary statistics by the Diabetes Meta-Analysis of Trans-Ethnic association studies (DIAMANTE) Consortium, which are genetically correlated (rg) with Phecode 250.2 (Type 2 Diabetes: rg = 0.992, SE = 0.008; p < 1 × 10−300) and Phecode 250 (Diabetes Mellitus rg=0.991, SE = 0.008; p < 1 × 10−300).GWAS of heart imaging phenotypes from the UK BiobankTo also explore PTSD relationship with the structure and function of the heart and aorta, we incorporated summary-level data from a cardiac imaging GWAS. This study used information from UKBB participants who underwent comprehensive cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging and employed a machine learning regenerating and analyzing pipeline that resulted in 82 quantitative imaging phenotypes from 26,893 participants of European descent. These phenotypes (e.g., short-axis, long-axis, and aortic cine images) provide a detailed characterization of cardiac and aortic structure and function (Supplementary Data .GWAS of CV risk factors as defined by Life’s Essential 8To investigate the role of other factors in the genetic overlap with CV health and PTSD, we considered the LE8 checklist defined by AHA, 2022, which underscores eight key health factors and health behaviors related to CV well-being: eat better, be more active, quit tobacco, get healthy sleep, manage weight, control cholesterol, manage blood sugar, manage blood pressure. For our study, we identified 11 GWAS related to LE8 factors (N = 282,271 ~ 1,320,016), including GWAS for diet (i.e., energy intake proportion of fat, carbohydrate, protein, each adjusted by body mass index, BMI), physical activity, smoking, insomnia, BMI-adjusted waist-hip-ratio (BMI(whr)), total cholesterol, diabetes, and hypertension [MVP + UKBB]. To maximize the sample size available, we meta-analyzed hypertension GWAS (phecode 401) available from MVP and UKBB, resulting in a sample size of 433,585 cases and 421,076 controls. We used GWAS of BMI(whr), because it helps distinguish between different types of adiposity. While BMI measures overall body mass, it doesn’t differentiate between peripheral fat and central/abdominal fat, which have different metabolic implications. Central adiposity is more strongly associated with metabolic disorders and cardiovascular risk than overall adiposity. By adjusting BMI for WHR, we aim to better isolate genetic variants specifically associated with metabolic health related to central adiposity. Additionally, we do use the GWAS of BMI as part of the replication cohorts listed in other GWAS cohorts. For insomnia, we generated two GWAS datasets, one meta-analyzing GWAS of insomnia from Watanabe and colleagues with MVP GWAS of “unable to fall asleep” (SlpFall – 188,830 cases) and the other meta-analyzing Watanabe insomnia GWAS with MVP GWAS of “waking up in the night and not be able to fall back asleep” (SlpWakePM – 216,711 cases). To maximize the sample size available, when needed, GWAS datasets were meta-analyzed using a fixed-effects inverse variance-weighted model available in METAL. A detailed description of all cohorts is presented in Supplementary Data Proteomic cohortsA Proteome-Wide Association Study (PWAS) identifies whether the relationship between genetic variants and disease outcomes is mediated by changes in protein levels. It uses effect estimates (known as weights) derived from protein quantitative trait loci (pQTLs) and integrates them with disease/trait GWAS to determine if genetic variants contribute to disease risk through their effects on protein abundance. Here we describe the sources of each of the cohorts that have data available on genotypes and protein abundance from blood and brain tissues.Brain proteomic datasetsThe Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project (ROS/MAP) proteome expression weights (effect estimates of pQTLs) were generated by Wingo et al., using dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) tissues available from 376 individuals of European ancestry. Briefly, 1,475 proteins exhibited significant cis associations with genetic variation. The weights/effect estimates assigned to pQTLs were used in our PWAS. Additionally, their study utilized dlPFC genetic-proteomic data from the Banner Sun Health Research Institute (BANNER). This dataset comprises brain dlPFC samples from 152 individuals of European descent, with 8,168 proteins included in proteomic profiles following quality control. Through the integration of proteomic expression data and SNP genotypes, 1,139 proteins exhibited significant pQTLs. (See Data Availability and Links).Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) StudyTo study the plasma proteome, we utilized data from Zhang and colleagues. Proteomic data were derived from summary-level information obtained from The Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) Study, focusing on 7213 individuals of European descent. The study measures plasma proteome levels using the SOMAmer-V4 platform. After quality control, 1348 plasma proteins exhibiting associations with common variants in cis regions were investigated in our PWAS study (See Data Availability).UKBB-Plasma Proteome Project (UKB-PPP)In addition to the ARIC Study, we tested data from the UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (UKB-PPP). This project provides the plasma proteomic profiles of 54,219 participants. UKB-PPP used Olink proteomics assay for proteome assessment and reported expression weights for protein quantitative trait loci (pQTLs) for 2923 unique proteins.Risk loci from PTSD GWASTo identify genomic loci of interest in PTSD GWAS summary statistics, as per original study we used Functional Mapping and Annotation of Genome-Wide Association Studies (FUMA). Considering LD weights from the European reference populations of the 1000 Genomes Project, resulting in 76 independent genomic risk loci (P < 5 × 10⁻, r2 < 0.6, MAF ≥ 0.01, LD distance <250 kb) (Supplementary Data Shared regions and variants between PTSD and the CVD traitsLocal Analysis of [co]Variant Association (LAVA)LAVA was employed to identify loci exhibiting local genetic correlation between PTSD and a total of 328 CV traits across three categories. We applied univariate LAVA models at the 76 PTSD risk loci to estimate heritability. Loci that reached false discovery rate significance at 5% (FDR q < 0.05) for the heritability (univariate model) were selected for local genetic correlation (bivariate) between PTSD and each one of the CV/LE8 traits. Local RG results were filtered to include only those cases where both traits exhibited significant heritability on the locus, as determined by an FDR q < 0.05. Sample overlap was estimated with LD score regression (LDSC) with the European LD scores calculated from the 1000 Genomes as reference (https://github.com/bulik/ldsc). Variants that were not SNPs (e.g., indels) and SNPs that were strand-ambiguous, multi-allelic, and had a minor allele frequency (MAF) < 0.01 were excluded.Colocalization analysisColocalization is a statistical approach used to assess whether pairs of traits share a putative causal variant within the same genomic region. COLOC employs a Bayesian approach, considering various variant-level hypotheses and calculating Bayes factors from SNP effect estimates and standard errors. The variant-level hypotheses correspond to: H0 (no association to either trait), H1 (association to only trait 1), H2 (association to only trait 2), H3 (associations to both traits with different causal variants), and H4 (associations to both traits with shared causal variants). In our study, each genomic region was expanded by 500 kb on either side of the position. COLOC was applied to assess colocalization between PTSD and the significantly correlated trait. Results with H4 or H3 hypothesis probabilities ≥80% were considered as shared with default priors of 1 × 10−4. For replication, we used data from UKBB and other cohorts considering H4 or H3 hypothesis probabilities ≥70% as strong evidence of shared variants.Tissue and molecular-profile-based prioritization of genes within colocalized regionsTo identify genes within each locus (i.e., colocalized regions between PTSD and CVD traits) based on physical location, we used the UCSC Genome Browser (see Data Availability and Links). To prioritize genes based on their regulatory roles, we evaluated colocalization probabilities (H3 and H4) for molecular profiles, including gene, protein, and splicing expression across various tissues. These probabilities were obtained for the identified genes and all reported psychiatric/CV phenotypes from published GWAS studies using OpenTargets. By manually examining the traits, we labeled the traits as psychiatric and/or CVDs.Observational analysis in All of US Research ProgramStarted in 2018, the National Institutes of Health’s All of US (AoU) Research Program has enrolled over 700,000 diverse participants, emphasizing health equity in the context of precision medicine. Leveraging EHR data available for 254,700 AoU participants, phecodes were mapped from International Classification of Disease ICD9/ICD10(CM) codes using Phecode Map (see data availability and links). Logistic regression (two-sided p-value) using the PheWAS R package was employed to assess the association of PTSD (13,877 cases) with CV phecodes identified in MVP and UKBB analyses, considering three models (i) base-model (sex, age, self-reported race), (ii) socioeconomic (SES)-model (bases model covariates plus BMI, smoking, deprivation index), and (iii) depression-model (SES-model covariates plus depression diagnosis: phecode 296.2-Ncases:72,143). The self-reported demographic characteristics of AoU are as follows: females (61.8%), average age in years = 54 ± 17 (mean ± SD), 57.17% White, 19.4% (self-identified race), Black or African American, 3.54% Asian, 0.62% Middle Eastern/North African, 1.92% More than one population, 0.11% Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, and 17.1% None of the above), while 44.1% were smokers (past and current).Partitioned heritability for tissue-specific enrichmentTo identify disease-relevant tissues for PTSD and CV traits, we applied stratified LD score regression to the GWAS summary statistics of each trait. LDSC-seg leverages gene expression data from diverse tissues to quantify the heritability enrichment for specific tissues. We analyzed 205 gene expression- tissue/cell-type annotations from GTEx and Franke lab.Proteome-wide association studyProteome-wide associations of PTSD and its colocalized traits were estimated. We integrated GWAS data with tissue-specific pQTLs. For the colocalized phecodes, PWAS was conducted using the meta-analysed GWAS combining MVP and UKBB as described above, using the FUnctional Summary-based ImputatiON (FUSION) (available at http://gusevlab.org/projects/fusion/) for ROSMAP/Banner (brain), and ARIC (plasma). The subsequent genes were tested in FOCUS for prioritization of statistically causal genes. PWAS using weights from UKB-PPP plasma proteome was performed using Summary-based Mendelian Randomization (SMR). The analysis was performed using SMR. The results were adjusted for multiple testing with FDR correction (FDR q < 0.05). Significant FDR genes were prioritized using the HEIDI test to identify causality (p_HEIDI > 0.05).In-silico functional analysisPathway enrichmentTo gain insight into the shared mechanisms between PTSD and CVD traits, we conducted pathway enrichment analysis based on the genes detected in brain and blood proteome-wide analyses. Pathway enrichments for each tissue-based PWAS genes were sought using a web-based tool, g:Profiler (https://biit.cs.ut.ee/gprofiler/gost) among three libraries: Gene Ontology (GO), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG), and Reactome Pathway Database (REAC). GO Database contains three functional domains: cellular component (CC), molecular function (MF), and biological process (BP). A significance threshold of FDR q < 0.05 was used to identify significant pathways.Drug repurposing in the research contextSignificant genes from the brain and plasma PWAS and the prioritized genes from the colocalization analysis were used for identifying drugs from the drug-gene interaction database (DGidb). Secondly, we obtained information including drug ID, clinical uses, and adverse effects from stored at OpenTargets (https://www.opentargets.org/), which are originally sourced from the FDA database. The OpenTarget results were compared with current CVD and PTSD treatments to identify drugs with overlapping functions and suggest new potential therapies.Reporting summaryFurther information on research design is available in the Supplementary information
abstract_filled: Patients with post-traumatic stress disorder face increased cardiovascular risk. This study examines shared genetic regions between post-traumatic stress disorder and 246 cardiovascular conditions across electronic health records, 82 cardiac imaging, and health behaviors defined by Life's Essential 8. Post-traumatic stress disorder is genetically correlated with cardiovascular diagnoses in 33 regions, imaging traits in 4 regions, and health behaviors in 44 regions. Potentially shared causal variants between post-traumatic stress disorder and 17 cardiovascular conditions were observed in 11 regions. Subsequent observational analysis in AllofUS cohort showed post-traumatic stress disorder is associated with 13 diagnoses even after accounting for socioeconomic factors and depression. Genetically regulated proteome expression in brain and blood tissues identified 33 blood and 122 brain genes shared between the two conditions, revealing neuronal, immune, metabolic, and calcium-related mechanisms, with several genes as targets for existing drugs. These findings exhibit shared risk loci and genes are involved in tissue-specific mechanisms.

fulltext_body: Research in contextEvidence before this studyAlzheimer’s disease (AD) is a leading cause of dementia with numerous identified risk factors, including cardiovascular conditions, depression, diabetes, and hearing loss. However, most previous research has focused on individual comorbidities rather than the complex sequences of diagnoses that may precede AD onset. Recent studies using electronic health records have attempted to identify disease trajectories and predict AD risk, but these approaches often relied on disease pairs or statistical associations that oversimplify the temporal progression of conditions leading to AD.Added value of this studyBy analysing longitudinal electronic health records of 24,473 patients with AD, we investigated multi-step diagnostic trajectories culminating in AD. We identified four distinct trajectory clusters: mental health, encephalopathy, mild cognitive impairment, and vascular disease. We demonstrated that these multi-step progressions conferred a higher AD risk than single diagnoses alone. Additionally, we identified directional relationships between conditions, suggesting potential causal pathways (for example, hypertension leading to depressive episodes before AD). Our validation in All of Us confirmed the generalisability of these findings across a diverse, nationally representative cohort.Implications of all the available evidenceThese findings underscore the importance of considering sequential patterns of comorbidities when evaluating AD risk. A trajectory-based perspective offers new opportunities for earlier detection, refined risk stratification, and targeted interventions. This approach could be applied broadly to other chronic conditions to inform prevention strategies and optimise clinical care pathways. IntroductionAlzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurological disorder that primarily affects older adults, leading to memory loss, cognitive decline, and difficulty performing daily activities. In the United States alone, more than 6.7 million individuals are living with Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) and Alzheimer’s disease Related Dementia (ADRD), a number projected to reach 13 million by 2050. In 2021, AD/ADRD was the fifth-leading cause of death among individuals aged 65 and older. It imposes a significant public health burden on healthcare systems, caregivers, and families, with costs for dementia care projected to exceed $360 billion in 2024 and approach one trillion by 2050.Numerous risk factors for AD have been identified, including cardiovascular conditions, hearing loss, depression, diabetes, traumatic brain injury, and physical inactivity.Despite recent advances, current research on disease trajectories has limitations. Much of the existing work relies on disease pairs, as in Jensen et al.,To address these gaps, we developed a framework to identify common disease trajectories in longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs). We used dynamic time warping (DTW) to align patient trajectories, clustering to group similar pathways, and network methods to pinpoint dominant disease sequences, followed by rigorous causal inference. By unveiling distinct and interconnected routes to AD, this approach offers insights that may improve risk assessment, timely diagnosis, and targeted interventions.MethodsThe general study design is illustrated in Sample selection in the UC health data warehouseData source and EHR preprocessingThe University of California Health Data Warehouse is a secure, de-identified EHR repository aggregating data from six academic health centres: UC Davis, UC Irvine, UC Los Angles, UC Riverside, UC San Diego, and UC San Francisco. Since 2012, it has captured inpatient and outpatient including primary-care encounters for 8.7 million unique patients. For this study, we analysed records spanning from January 2012 to May 2024. Mortality ascertainment combines in-hospital deaths, family member reporting, and statewide death records from the California Department of Public Health. The data are de-identified to facilitate clinical research, with oversight from institutional review boards, privacy and compliance officers, and information security officers.Patients were included if they had complete demographic information (age, gender, race and ethnicity), at least two encounters on different dates (one or more encounters per year), and were aged 65 to 90 at their last visit (the dataset censors patients older than 90).We extracted all International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) codes from multiple sources within the EHR, including primary and secondary diagnosis codes, problem list entries, medical history documentation, and billing codes. At the record level, three-digit ICD-10 codes were used after truncation to achieve a granularity appropriate for phenotyping.Case definitionIn this study, we define AD as dementia due to AD based on EHR diagnostic codes. This operational definition is distinct from both clinical diagnosis of AD, which relies on comprehensive neurological examination and cognitive testing, and biological AD, which requires biomarker confirmation of amyloid and tau pathology. Patients were classified as having AD if they had at least one encounter with the ICD-10 code G30. The AD diagnoses in our cohort were made across multiple departments, including neurology, geriatrics, and primary care, following standard, real-world, clinical evaluation at health systems. These typically include cognitive assessments, neurological examination, and exclusion of alternative causes, though the specific diagnostic workup may vary by provider and department. Previous validation studies in EHR-based research have reported moderately high positive predictive values for AD codes (72–100%), suggesting that the misclassification of patients with AD is relatively limited.Pairwise ICD codes associations in a sampled populationWe used a survival analysis framework to identify risk-associated diagnoses by examining pairwise ICD codes. This step aimed to reduce noise in patients’ disease trajectories by filtering out diagnoses that were not positively associated with subsequent AD.Sample setWe combined all patients with AD (cases) with non-AD (controls) into a discovery sample. Non-AD controls required ≥5 years of follow-up, ≥2 encounters, and ≥2 encounters per year to reduce the likelihood of undiagnosed AD. We performed 1:1 propensity score matchingFine–Gray proportional subdistribution hazards modelA Fine–Gray (FG) proportional subdistribution hazards model was employed to account for competing risks such as death.Patient trajectories preprocessingDiagnoses recorded on the same date as AD were shifted one step before the AD date to preserve potentially relevant patterns. F02.8 codes overlapping with AD (often reflecting parallel mappingsFor patients with only two encounters, we applied a two-step expansion to reach three steps if the added diagnosis pairs were significant risk factors. The final trajectories ranged from three to 17 steps. To ensure alignment quality in the DTW analyses, we capped the maximum number of steps at nine, covering 99% of patients. Any patients with more than three distinct trajectories were reduced to three via clustering with DTW distances, ensuring minimal redundancy.Common AD trajectory identificationCalculate distances between trajectoriesWe used DTWTrajectory clustering and network analysesWe applied k-means,For each cluster, we constructed a “raw” network of patient trajectories and retained edges present in at least 0.5% of patients. We then applied a backbone extraction based on modularity vitality.Evaluation of common AD trajectoriesPatient characteristics across clustersAfter trajectory cleaning, each patient could have up to three unique trajectories, potentially placing them in multiple clusters. We first evaluated patient overlap across clusters via a Venn diagram.We further characterised AD features across clusters, including age at onset, time from the first AD diagnosis to the most recent visit, and time to death (when applicable). Kaplan–Meier curvesRisk trajectories testing in AD and controlsTo validate the risk of multi-step disease trajectories for AD, we redefined a new control group comprised only of individuals never diagnosed with AD or AD-exclusionary phenotypes.Causal structural learningTo investigate potential causality, we used the Greedy Equivalence Search (GES) algorithm,We applied GES to the same 1:1 matched AD-and-control sample used in FG modelling. A ten-fold cross-validation strategy was employed: in each iteration, we learned the DAG from the entire dataset excluding one-fold, repeating this for ten iterations. Only edges appearing in at least five of these iterations were deemed reliably causal. This approach offers computational efficiency while providing insights into possible causal structures underlying AD trajectories.Sensitivity analysesUsing a different case-to-control matching ratioTo assess the stability of our findings, we conducted a sensitivity analysis using different case-to-control ratio (1:3 matching) in our propensity score matching procedure. The same matched sample was also used to test the causality with GES as described above. We then compared the resulting HRs and significance patterns across the different matching ratios to evaluate the robustness of our findings.Trajectory building with one-month buffer periodTo address potential reverse causality, we implemented a one-month buffer period between each diagnosis and AD onset. This approach helps mitigate the risk that certain diagnoses might be part of the AD diagnostic workup rather than true risk factors. We repeated our trajectory construction and analysis with this buffer period and compared the results to our primary analysis. We only compared clusters that correspond by label (e.g., mental health cluster in the primary analysis vs. mental health cluster in the buffer-period analysis), ensuring a one-to-one alignment of patient-trajectory groups. To quantitatively assess differences between the original and buffer-period networks, we calculated Pearson correlation coefficients and cosine similarity metrics between standardised edge weights (divided by the total number of patients) for corresponding clusters. To maintain a consistent basis for correlation, we aligned the complete set of possible ICD-pair transitions observed in either network. Transitions present in one network but not the other were assigned a weight of zero, so the Pearson coefficient reflects both shared and differential edges.AD diagnosis stability analysisTo assess the stability of AD diagnoses in our cohort, we conducted an additional analysis examining potential changes in diagnosis after the initial AD identification. We reviewed all diagnoses recorded after the first AD onset date to identify other types of dementia (including progressive supranuclear palsy, frontotemporal dementia, vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, cerebral dementia, and substance-induced dementia).To strengthen the findings specifically for AD, we performed a sensitivity analysis focusing on diagnostic robustness. We selected patients with at least two AD diagnoses in their EHR and repeated the clustering analysis using the same methodology as our primary analysis. We then compared the consistency of clustering results with the adjusted rand index, which measures the similarity between two cluster assignments independent of permutation.Validation in the All of Us research programWe validated our findings using data from the All of Us Research Program, a diverse cohort of over 500,000 participants from across the United States.We applied the same inclusion criteria and analytical pipeline to identify patients with AD (cases) and 1:10 matched controls in this dataset. We then assessed the replicability of our risk factor associations, trajectory clusters, and causal relationships to determine the generalisability of our findings beyond our primary cohort.First, we replicated the FG modelling of all directed associations identified in the simplified networks for each trajectory cluster. For associations between specific diagnoses and AD, we utilized the full cohort of patients with AD (cases) and matched controls (n = 8512). For other pairwise ICD code associations, we restricted testing to the AD population (n = 818) to maintain consistency with our primary analysis framework. In total, 130 pairwise ICD code associations were tested, including 12 pairs of diagnoses directly linked to AD. We applied the same FDR correction methodology to adjust p-values for multiple comparisons.Second, to validate the UCHWD AD disease trajectory clusters, we developed and implemented a procedure for assigning new patients to our previously identified clusters. For each cluster, we used all paths to AD in the simplified network as reference trajectories. We then calculated cluster-specific distance thresholds by determining the mean distance (using DTW) between each patient with AD in the UC Health (discovery sample) and all reference trajectories within their assigned cluster. Cutoff values were established at Q3 + 1.5∗IQR of all patients’ mean distances within each cluster. For validation, we pre-processed the trajectories of All of Us patients with AD by extracting the first occurrence of each unique 3-digit ICD code and ordering them chronologically. We then calculated the mean distance between each patient with AD in All of US and each UCHWD cluster’s reference trajectories, assigning patients to the cluster with the minimum mean distance, provided this distance fell below the predetermined cutoff for that cluster.Third, we tested the risk trajectories identified in each cluster as potential risk factors in the All of Us cohort. Using a similar FG framework, we compared AD risk between individuals who followed a specific multi-step trajectory and those who did not, employing 1:10 propensity score matching for baseline covariates. We evaluated the same two comparative models as described above.All analyses were conducted in R (version 3.6).EthicsThis study was considered human subjects exempt. All patient data used in this research was de-identified to protect patient privacy. We confirm that all authors have read the Journal’s position on ethical publication issues and affirm that this work is consistent with those guidelines.Role of fundersThis study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, California Department of Public Health, and National Science Foundation. The Funders did not have any role in study design, data collection, data analyses, interpretation, or writing of report.ResultsPairwise ICD code temporal associations919,590 patients met our initial inclusion criteria (complete demographics, at least two encounters on different dates, and were aged 65 to 90) in the University of California Health Data Warehouse. 24,473 (2.7%) met the inclusion criteria for AD. We acknowledge there is likely an underdiagnosis of AD in this population, but we used strict inclusion criteria to ensure higher precision of cases.Using the FG subdistribution hazard model, we identified disease codes positively associated with AD incidence while accounting for the competing risk of death.In this AD-and-control cohort (n = 48,946), the FG model identified 16 ICD codes positively associated with AD incidence after false discovery rate adjustmentNext, within the AD population (n = 24,473), focusing on ICD codes with a prevalence of above 1% (n_ICD = 302), the FG model identified 32,654 significant positive temporal associations, which were used to build AD trajectories.Common AD trajectories identificationDTW alignment and clusteringTo construct AD trajectories, as described in the Methods section, we used a “cleaning” and “backward-building” approach, where we first removed diagnoses not significantly associated with AD based on the Fine–Gray model and then identified multi-step trajectories by working backward from the AD diagnosis to earlier conditions. Of the 24,473 patients with AD identified, 5762 (23.5%) patients had 6794 unique multi-step trajectories ranging from three to nine steps. This reduction in patient numbers was expected because we removed non-significant diagnosis switches, which removed patients who did not have multi-step disease trajectories with statistically significant associated pairs to ensure the robustness of our trajectory networks. Of these patients, 1571 (27%) had two-step trajectories expanded to three steps. On average, each trajectory contained six steps, and each patient had 2.3 trajectories after cleaning.We applied DTWk-means with four clusters was selected (Trajectory cluster characteristicsWe identified four distinct clusters, each with characteristic disease progressions leading to AD. Mental Health Cluster (n = 1,448, 1266 unique trajectories): Centred on depressive episode (F32). Common preceding diagnoses included essential hypertension, atrial fibrillation, disorders of lipoprotein metabolism, type 2 diabetes, anxiety disorders, dorsalgia, and other functional intestinal disorders. Representative trajectories included “lipoprotein metabolism → depressive episode → AD” and “anxiety disorders → depressive episode → AD.” Notably, 67% had unspecified depression (F32.A).Encephalopathy Cluster (n = 3,223, 764 unique trajectories): Anchored by other disorders of the brain (G93), most frequently unspecified encephalopathy (G93.40, 45%). Common precursors included essential hypertension, other cerebrovascular diseases, other urinary system diseases, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. Examples included “essential hypertension → other disorders of the brain → [other cerebrovascular diseases] → AD” and “lipoprotein metabolism → other disorders of the brain → AD.”MCI/Neurodegenerative Cluster (n = 1,502, 1658 unique trajectories): Focused on other degenerative diseases of the nervous system (G31), with 70% of patients having mild cognitive impairment (G31.84). Common precursors were transient cerebral ischaemic attacks, menopausal disorders, male erectile dysfunction, and eyelid/lacrimal system diseases. Notable sequences included “other degenerative diseases of the nervous system → vascular dementia → AD” and “transient cerebral ischaemic attacks → other degenerative diseases of the nervous system → AD.”Vascular Cluster (n = 1,446, 3106 unique trajectories): Centred on other cerebrovascular diseases (I67). Common preceding diagnoses were joint disorders, soft tissue disorders, dorsalgia, and postprocedural states. Notable trajectories included “other cerebrovascular diseases → vascular dementia → AD” and “essential hypertension → other anaemias → unspecified dementia → AD.” In this group, 44% had unspecified cerebrovascular disease (I67.9).Our methodology successfully identified both common two-step trajectories and longer multi-step pathways. Examples of longer trajectories include “essential hypertension → lipoprotein metabolism → depressive episode → AD” from the mental health cluster and “lipoprotein metabolism → essential hypertension → other joint disorder → other cerebrovascular diseases → AD” from the vascular cluster.Evaluation of common AD trajectoriesPatient characteristics across clustersA total of 4078 patients fell into only one cluster, 1511 appeared in two clusters, and 173 in three clusters (Focusing on the 4078 single-cluster patients, we observed significant demographic and EHR differences among clusters (When comparing Chapter XVIII symptoms (cognition, perception, emotional state, and behaviour) prior to AD diagnosis, vascular cluster patients were more likely to report memory loss or dizziness/giddiness, particularly within one to three years before AD onset. Across all organ systems, the vascular cluster had higher non-cognitive symptoms than other clusters (Moreover, the encephalopathy cluster exhibited the shortest interval from AD diagnosis to the last recorded visit. Survival analyses based on Kaplan–Meier curves revealed that the shortest time from a cluster’s first node to AD diagnosis occurred in the encephalopathy cluster, followed by depression, MCI, and vascular (overall log-rank p < 0.001). The shorter time from encephalopathy cluster diagnoses to AD also aligns with shorter record length in the encephalopathy cluster. Among deceased patients, encephalopathy cluster members had a shorter interval from AD diagnosis to death than those in the vascular cluster (p = 0.036), whereas other comparisons were non-significant (We investigated risk factors for mortality by comparing diagnoses between alive and deceased patients within each cluster (Single-cluster vs. multi-cluster patientsBecause the MCI/neurodegenerative cluster showed the highest overlap, we compared single-cluster MCI patients to those belonging to multiple clusters. While no significant demographic differences emerged (Risk trajectories test in controlsTo confirm that the identified trajectories confer elevated AD risk, we examined top trajectories from each cluster in a newly sampled control population devoid of AD or AD-exclusionary phenotypes. All representative trajectories (Causal structural learningWe applied the GES algorithm to infer causal directions within each cluster’s simplified network. Overall, 26.2% of edges consistently showed direct, causal relationships. While this means that approximately one-quarter of edges were deemed causal, the remaining links did not reach the consistency threshold, indicating insufficient evidence or bidirectional relationships in the data. When stratified by cluster, directed edges ranged from 24.1% in the vascular cluster to 42.9% in encephalopathy (Among the AD risk factors identified in the FG model, six ICD codes, including unspecified dementia (F03), vascular dementia (F01), depressive episode (F32), unspecified mood disorder (F39), other disorders of the brain (G93), and other cerebrovascular diseases (I67), appeared causally linked with AD. Notably, three of these codes (F32, G93, and I67) were central nodes within their respective cluster. Representative multi-step pathways included “essential hypertension → depressive episode → AD,” “acute kidney failure → other disorders of the brain → AD,” and “other cerebrovascular diseases → vascular dementia → AD,” suggesting that certain vascular, psychiatric, and systemic factors may act sequentially to increase AD susceptibility.Sensitivity analysesUsing a different case-to-control matching ratioThe sensitivity analysis using the 1:3 matched sample demonstrated consistency with our primary findings. All 16 significant associations identified in our primary 1:1 matched analysis remained significant with similar effect sizes. The correlation between effect sizes (HRs) for all ICD codes associated with AD (n = 387 association tests) was 0.992 (p < 0.001), indicating highly consistent results regardless of the control-to-case ratio employed.The causal structural learning analysis showed similar stability, with only minor differences in the identified causal links. Specifically, the F39 (Unspecified mood disorder) → AD link identified in the 1:1 matched sample was no longer classified as causal in the 1:3 matched sample, while a new causal link of F02 (Dementia in other diseases) → AD emerged. All other causal relationships remained consistent across the different matching ratios.Trajectory building with one-month buffer periodThe implementation of a 1-month buffer period resulted in 3306 patients with multi-step trajectories, compared to 5762 patients in our original analysis. The Calinski–Harabasz, Davies–Bouldin, and Silhouette analysis indicated an optimal solution of three clusters rather than the four identified in our primary analysis, with the most notable difference being the absence of a distinct “other degenerative diseases” (G31) cluster.Quantitative comparison between the buffer-period networks and corresponding components of our original networks revealed varying degrees of similarity. The mental health cluster demonstrated remarkably high consistency (Pearson correlation = 0.97, cosine similarity = 0.97), while the brain/encephalopathy networks showed moderate correlation (Pearson correlation = 0.59, cosine similarity = 0.60). The cerebrovascular disease cluster exhibited lower consistency (Pearson correlation = 0.43, cosine similarity = 0.44), indicating substantial reorganisation when the buffer period was applied.AD diagnosis stabilityOur analysis of diagnosis changes after initial AD identification revealed that among all patients with AD with follow-up data available (n = 24,473), 12.2% (n = 2979) had another dementia subtype diagnosis during follow-up. Within patients with multi-step trajectories (n = 5762), the proportion was slightly higher at 15.2% (n = 875). This finding reflects the clinical reality of mixed dementia and the evolving understanding of a patient’s condition over time.In our sensitivity analysis examining diagnostic robustness, we identified 1822 patients with at least two AD diagnoses and multi-step trajectories after cleaning (compared to 5762 patients with at least one AD diagnosis in the original analysis). With the optimum clustering number of four as in our primary analysis, the adjusted rand index comparing these results to our original clustering was 0.94, indicating high consistency and demonstrating the robustness of our findings even when using a more stringent AD case definition.Validation in the All of UsOur validation analyses in the All of Us cohort yielded several important findings that largely corroborated our primary results. Compared to patients with AD in our discovery cohort, the patients with AD from the All of Us cohort had a younger age, fewer females, different race/ethnicity distribution, longer EHR records, and fewer visits per year. The AD features for these two AD populations were also different, with the All of Us patients being younger at AD diagnosis and having a shorter time from first AD diagnosis to death (In the AD-and-control cohort (n = 8512), the Fine–Gray model validated 9 out of 12 ICD codes as being positively associated with AD after FDR adjustment (The cluster assignment validation demonstrated the robustness of our trajectory clustering approach. After minimum preprocessing, 785 patients with AD from the All of Us cohort had at least two distinct diagnoses documented before their first AD diagnosis and were therefore eligible for cluster assignment. Notably, 89.9% (706/785) of these patients were successfully assigned to at least one of our previously identified trajectory clusters using the predetermined distance cutoffs. The distribution of patients across clusters was comparable to our primary cohort, with the vascular disease (21.8%) and mental health (21.3%) clusters receiving the highest proportion of assignments. This high assignment rate confirms that the disease progression patterns we identified represent common pathways to AD that generalise beyond our initial study population.Our analysis of multi-step trajectories as risk factors revealed that most of the associations identified in our primary analysis remained significant in the All of Us cohort. Specifically, 7 out of 9 tested representative trajectories were positively associated with AD risk after controlling for demographic factors and EHR features. Importantly, in 6 of these 7 validated trajectories, the multi-step progression conferred a significantly higher risk than having any single diagnosis within the trajectory, supporting our hypothesis that sequential disease progression amplifies the likelihood of developing AD (DiscussionOur study makes several important contributions to the field. First, we developed a framework for identifying and analysing disease trajectories in EHR data, combining DTW, clustering, network analysis, and causal inference. Second, we identified four distinct trajectory clusters leading to AD, each with characteristic demographic features, comorbidity patterns, and progression rates. Third, we demonstrated that multi-step trajectories confer higher AD risk than individual diagnoses, highlighting the importance of sequential disease progression. These multi-step trajectories provide a more comprehensive view of disease progression patterns directly observed in patient records leading to AD than previous approaches focusing on isolated risk factors or disease pairs. Fourth, we validated our findings in an independent cohort, confirming the generalisability of our approach.Recent studies have applied various trajectory analysis methods to understand disease progression, including cross-sectional clustering (Alexander et al.Our study identified four distinct trajectory clusters leading to AD: mental health, encephalopathy, MCI/neurodegenerative, and vascular. These clusters exhibited significant differences in demographic characteristics, comorbidity patterns, and progression rates. The mental health cluster, centred on depression, predominantly affected women and Hispanic individuals, consistent with previous findings linking depression to AD risk.,The presence of shared diagnostic precursors across multiple clusters, particularly vascular risk factors like hypertension, suggests that common pathophysiological mechanisms may underlie seemingly distinct progression pathways. From a clinical perspective, this highlights the potential importance of managing these shared risk factors for preventing progression along multiple pathways to AD. Future research should investigate whether targeted interventions for these shared diagnoses might prevent progression to one or more AD disease trajectories.Our causal inference analyses provided additional insights into the directionality of relationships within these trajectories. The encephalopathy cluster showed the highest proportion of directed edges (42.9%), suggesting more definitive causal progressions compared to other clusters. The identification of six ICD codes causally linked to AD, including three that were central nodes in their respective clusters, further supports the validity of our trajectory-based approach.The validation of our findings in the All of Us Research Program demonstrates the generalisability of our approach across diverse populations and healthcare settings. The high assignment rate (89.9%) of All of Us patients to our previously identified clusters suggests that these trajectories represent common pathways to AD that extend beyond our initial study population. Furthermore, the confirmation that multi-step trajectories confer higher risk than individual diagnoses underscores the importance of considering sequential disease progression in AD risk assessment.Our study has several limitations. First, our dataset automatically censored patients older than 90 years, which may limit the generalisability of our findings to the oldest-old population, a group with high AD prevalence. In addition, our discovery cohort was drawn from six academic health systems in California, which may limit representativeness relative to population-based samples. Individual records within the University of California Health Data Warehouse may be incomplete, and care delivered outside the UC system is not captured. Second, the potential misclassification of patients with AD in EHR data remains a concern. While previous validation studies have reported positive predictive values ranging from 72 to 100% for AD codes,Our findings have several clinical implications. The identification of distinct trajectory clusters suggests that AD may develop through multiple pathways, each potentially requiring different prevention and treatment strategies. The recognition that certain diagnoses, such as depression or cerebrovascular disease, often precede AD by several years provides opportunities for early intervention. Furthermore, the finding that multi-step trajectories confer higher risk than individual diagnoses underscores the importance of viewing AD risk holistically rather than focusing solely on single risk factors. For example, the sequence of acute kidney failure followed by encephalopathy may contribute to increased dementia risk, suggesting that systemic organ dysfunction can hasten neurodegenerative processes. Similarly, the vascular cluster’s pathways, such as hypertension followed by other cerebrovascular disease, mirror previous work on the links between vascular insufficiency and cognitive decline.In conclusion, our study provides a comprehensive framework for identifying and analysing disease trajectories leading to AD using EHR data. By unveiling distinct and interconnected routes to AD, this approach offers insights that may improve risk assessment, timely diagnosis, and targeted interventions. Future research should focus on validating these trajectories in additional cohorts, investigating the biological mechanisms underlying these progression patterns, and developing targeted interventions for specific trajectory clusters.ContributorsMF, SS, BP, KV and TSC contributed to the conception and design of the study. MF and TSC have accessed and verified the underlying data. MF performed the statistical analysis and wrote the first draft of the manuscript. All authors contributed to manuscript revision, read, and approved the submitted version.Data sharing statementData that support the findings of this study were obtained from the University of California Data Discovery Platform (UCDDP), a HIPAA limited data set which contains patient data from all 6 UC Health academic medical centres (Davis, Irvine, Los Angeles, Riverside, San Diego, and San Francisco). Due to privacy and confidentiality restrictions, the data are not publicly available. Minimal de-identified aggregate data in the form of tables are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request and subject to corresponding author’s institutional approval. All code used for data preprocessing, modelling, and analysis in this study is available at: https://github.com/TSChang-Lab/AD-trajectory. The repository includes annotated Jupyter notebooks and scripts for reproducing the main results. No patient-level data are included to ensure compliance with data privacy regulations.Declaration of interestsThe authors have no conflicts of interest to disclose related to the content of this manuscript.
abstract_filled: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a leading cause of dementia and an escalating public health concern. Although recent research has identified multiple AD risk factors, most studies examine isolated comorbidities rather than complex, sequential progressions. In this study, we sought to identify multi-step trajectories culminating in AD by analysing longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs). We analysed data from 24,473 patients in the University of California Health Data Warehouse (UCHDW). A Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard model identified temporally associated diagnoses, from which we constructed diagnostic trajectories. We employed dynamic time warping and k-means clustering to group similar trajectories, and network analyses to characterize their common structures. Causal inferences were explored using the Greedy Equivalence Search algorithm. Validation in the UCHDW included association tests and comparison to control groups. We further validated our findings in the All of Us Research Program, a diverse, nationally representative cohort. After filtering, 5762 patients contributed 6794 unique AD progression trajectories, revealing four major trajectory clusters: mental health, encephalopathy, mild cognitive impairment, and vascular disease. These clusters differed significantly in demographic and clinical features. Approximately 26% of edges showed consistent directional ordering (e.g., hypertension → depressive episode → AD). In an independent population, these multi-step trajectories conferred greater AD risk than single diagnoses alone. Our validation in the All of Us cohort confirmed the reproducibility of these trajectory patterns in a more diverse population. Our findings demonstrate the value of examining sequential diagnostic patterns in AD pathogenesis. Multi-step progressions reveal potential latent contributors to AD, offering pathways for risk stratification, early detection, and targeted interventions. This study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Institute on Aging, the National Science Foundation, the Hillblom and Fineberg Foundations, and the California Department of Public Health.

fulltext_body: IntroductionElevated plasma cholesterol is a significant risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. In women, the risk of developing high cholesterol and atherosclerosis typically increases with age and particularly after menopause (Despite its involvement in virtually every nutrient’s metabolism, the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) remains a poorly defined nuclear factor in cholesterol homeostasis. The GR is a ligand-activated nuclear transcription factor that exerts multifaceted effects on nutrient metabolism (Previously, several genetic variants in the GR gene (NR3C1; OMIM #138040) have been described in the human population. These genetic variants can affect the transcriptional activity of the GR and its downstream target genes, potentially influencing nutrient regulation (rs6190 (c.68G>A; p.R23K) coding SNP — also known as E22R/E23K due its complete linkage to the silent p.E22E rs6189 SNP — is a genetic variant in codon 23 that results in an amino acid change from arginine (R) to lysine (K) in the N-terminus of the GR protein (In this study, we harnessed the human rs6190 SNP to identify a direct GR-mediated program governing hepatic cholesterol regulation and its association with atherogenic risk. We found that this low-frequency coding SNP correlated with increased levels of cholesterol in women from UK Biobank and All of Us (NIH) cohorts, and it promoted cholesterol and atherosclerosis in transgenic mice according to the number of SNP alleles (homo>hetero>reference). Our transcriptomic and epigenetic datasets revealed that the mutant GR perturbed cholesterol levels through transactivation of Pcsk9 and Bhlhe40, negative regulators of LDL and HDL receptors in the liver. Our study identifies rs6190 as a potential risk factor for atherosclerosis, particularly in women, and reports unanticipated mechanisms through which the hepatic GR affects cholesterol levels in the circulation.Resultsrs6190 SNP increases plasma cholesterol levels in women according to allele zygosity.To investigate the influence of the rs6190 variant on cholesterol regulation, we probed the large adult cohort from the UK Biobank, comprising 485,895 people aged 40–70 years. In this cohort, the GR rs6190 variant (NR3C1 gene, transcript ENST00000231509.3 (-strand); c.68G>A; p.R23K) exhibited a minor allele frequency of 2.75% (25,944 heterozygous, 413 homozygous individuals), categorizing it as a low-frequency variant (PCSK9, CELSR2, APOB, ABCG8, SLC22A1, HFE, MYLIP, ST3GAL4, NYNRIN, LDLR, and APOE genes (r2 < 0.001) at the genomic level. Although no associations were significant after multiple tests in men, rs6190 SNP was significantly associated with many cholesterol parameters in women, accounting for 23 out of 33 total plasma parameters with a significant rs6190 effect (adjusted P < 0.005) (We then stratified total, LDL, and HDL cholesterol values from women according to SNP zygosity. We are defining here homozygous carriers of the reference allele (control population) as GRref/ref, heterozygous SNP carriers as GRref/ALT, and homozygous SNP carriers as GRALT/ALT. We performed linear regressions with a mixed model correcting for age, BMI, diabetic status, and triacylglycerols. In parallel, we also compared median confidence intervals across rs6190 genotypes. Remarkably, total, LDL, and HDL cholesterol showed a modest but significant elevation of median levels according to the number of SNP alleles in women (https://doi.org/10.1172/JCI190180DS1). Considering the effects on cholesterol, we probed the total UK Biobank dataset for hypercholesterolemia and cardiovascular disease mortality odds ratios. In alignment with the trends in cholesterol, GRALT/ALT women displayed an increased odds ratio of 1.34 (95% CI: 1.02–1.76; P = 0.0092) for hypercholesterolemia (total cholesterol >240 mg/dL) and 2.37 (95% CI: 1.05–5.9; P = 0.01) for death due to cardiovascular diseases, compared with GRref/ref women (To probe these rs6190 correlations in a more genetically diverse human dataset, we queried the All of Us dataset, where we found the SNP at a variable minor allele frequency ranging from low frequency to rare across ancestries: African/African American, 0.49%; American Admixed/Latino, 0.84%; East Asian, 0.061%; European, 2.67%; Middle Eastern, 1.43%; and South Asian, 1.49%. In the All of Us subset of 245,385 individuals with rs6190 genotype annotation encompassing all ancestries and ages, we repeated the linear regressions corrected for age, BMI, diabetes, triacylglycerols, and the median comparisons. The analyses in the All of Us dataset confirmed a significant correlation between rs6190 zygosity and total, LDL, and HDL cholesterol levels in women (Because NR3C1 variants did not come up as top hits for cholesterol in GWAS studies so far, we counter-verified whether targeted regressions for total cholesterol could “unmask” potential correlations of NR3C1 variants not associated with cholesterol through previous GWAS studies. We extracted 38 NR3C1 locus variants with GWAS significant hits (<5 × 10−8) from the current European Bioinformatics Institute (EBI) GWAS catalog and ran linear regressions — aggregated for ancestry but disaggregated for sex — for total cholesterol in the All of Us dataset (r2 < 0.15). None of the 38 variants had a significant reported GWAS hit for cholesterol. However, our regressions showed 24 variants with correlations (adjusted P < 0.05; 20 direct; 4 inverse) with total cholesterol according to zygosity. Intriguingly, those correlations were significant only in women and not in men for all 24 variants, analogous to our findings with rs6190.Taken together, our findings highlight the association of the rs6190 SNP with modest but significant elevations of cholesterol in women from the UK Biobank and the All of Us cohorts.The rs6190 SNP is sufficient to increase plasma cholesterol and promotes GR transactivation of Pcsk9 and Bhlhe40 in mice.To elucidate the extent to which the mutant GR promotes cholesterol elevation, we introduced a genocopy of the rs6190 SNP into the endogenous Nr3c1 (GR gene) locus on the C57BL/6J background. The murine ortholog of the human GR-R23K mutation is GR-R24K due to an additional amino acid in position 10. In female littermate mice under normal chow conditions, total plasma cholesterol increased according to SNP zygosity in both fasted and fed states (ALT/ALT female mice, we found histological evidence of immature plaque formation in the aortic root (We then focused our mechanistic analyses on GRref/ref versus GRALT/ALT liver comparisons, considering the primary role of this organ in cholesterol regulation (NR3C1 expression levels in the liver, overall GR protein levels in the liver or primary hepatocytes did not change between GRref/ref versus GRALT/ALT mice (ref/ref versus GRALT/ALT liver tissues. The mutant GR showed increased nuclear/cytoplasmic signal enrichment compared with the WT GR in both control and GR-activated states (ref/ref versus GRALT/ALT hepatocytes in vitro for both Hsp90 interaction and nuclear translocation at 30 minutes after 1 μM dexamethasone or vehicle (ref/ref versus GRref/ALT versus GRALT/ALT mice, the mutant GR showed an increased epigenetic activity both at baseline and after dexamethasone stimulation, assayed through a luciferase reporter of direct GR-driven transactivation (Fkbp5 promoter, a canonical marker for GR activity (Pcsk9) was the highest hit. The increased transactivation of Pcsk9 in the liver by the mutant GR was validated at mRNA and protein levels (ALT/ALT compared with GRref/ref liver tissues (Bhlhe40 (Bhlhe40 targets in the promoters of downregulated genes in mutant versus WT livers. This analysis revealed scavenger receptor class B type I (SR-B1), encoded by Scarb1, as a unique hypothetical target of BHLHE40 from our RNA-Seq datasets.
