abstract_filled: Background: While the severity of the metabolic syndrome (MetS) is associated with type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease (CVD) in research cohorts, it is unclear if this association remains when using clinically-collected data, which is more subject to error and bias. Methods: We used a previously-validated MetS-severity z-score (MetS-Z) to compare the degree of cardiometabolic derangement between clinically-collected data from the electronic health-record (EHR) in the All-of-Us cohort (N = 101,676) with research-collected data from NHANES 2017-2020 (n = 3470). We assessed (separately) the odds of current diabetes and CVD in each cohort based on MetS z-score, adjusted for sex, race/ethnicity, education and income. Results: Mean MetS-Z-scores in All of Us (vs. NHANES) were higher overall (0.41 vs. 0.15), including being slightly higher among those without diabetes (0.03 vs. -0.09) and similar among those with diagnosed diabetes (1.42 vs. 1.50). In All of Us (vs. NHANES) MetS-Z was higher among those without CVD (0.36 vs. 0.10) but similar among those with CVD (0.72 vs. 0.66). Adjusted odds of diagnosed diabetes and CVD based on MetS-Z remained significant when using clinically-collected data in All of Us (diabetes: 3.41 [95 % confidence interval 3.34, 3.49]; CVD: 1.20 [1.18, 1.21]), though not as high as in NHANES (diabetes: 5.83 [4.52, 7.51]; CVD: 1.43 [1.27, 1.61]). Conclusion: While EHR data is limited by selection bias and data accuracy concerns (e.g. lack of fasting laboratory testing), we found overall similar relationships between MetS-severity, diabetes and CVD in EHR-based and research-based cohorts, supporting utility of these data in risk algorithms.

Purpose: Phenotype-based ascertainment of probands in studies of Mendelian disorders may exclude individuals with mild phenotypes or that lack health care access. We explore this premise in All of Us Research Program participants with pathogenic variation causal for three Mendelian conditions: autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), Marfan syndrome, and neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Methods: We identified All of Us Research Program participants with putatively pathogenic variation in NF1, FBN1, PKD1, and PKD2. Concept terms were extracted from electronic health records to assess participant diagnosis and phenotype. Variant annotation and participant surveys were evaluated to identify biological and social factors differentiating diagnosed and undiagnosed individuals. Results: Large proportions of individuals with pathogenic variation in NF1, FBN1, or PKD1/PKD2 lack the associated diagnosis of NF1 (47%), Marfan syndrome (58%), or ADPKD (52%), respectively. Pathogenic variants in diagnosed individuals have greater inferred deleteriousness for NF1 and ADPKD, and undiagnosed individuals had less severe phenotypes compared to diagnosed individuals for all three conditions. Conclusion: A genotype-first ascertainment of individuals in genomic research allows for a more comprehensive assessment of Mendelian disease and removes biases that confound our understanding of the penetrance and presentation of these conditions.

fulltext_body: IntroductionPsoriasis (PS) and Crohn's disease (CD) are mixed autoimmune and autoinflammatory diseases with local tissue and systemic effects. While the absolute incidence of comorbid PS and CD is low, they occur together more than would be expected by random chance [Due to the increasing availability of whole exome sequencing (WES) data, exome‐wide association studies (ExWAS) have helped to identify genetic associations in protein‐altering variants. Advantages of these studies, which are enriched for rare variants, are that they may demonstrate larger effect sizes compared to common variants, highlight novel susceptibility loci, and provide mechanistic insights into disease etiology given their location in the transcribed genome. A literature gap exists, however, characterizing the exonic variation associated with individuals with comorbid PS and CD.A common approach to studying the genetic overlap between two diseases employs a comparative paradigm, focusing on similarities and differences between the genetic architecture of each disease alone. An alternative and complementary strategy to investigate comorbid diseases is to study the genetic architecture via genetic association studies of patients with both diseases, but the required individual‐level genomic data is often unavailable. This may be in part due to the large number of possible comorbid disease combinations, preventing the targeted sample collection of each comorbid disease combination. To solve this challenge, however, we can take advantage of large, population‐level biobanks, such as the United Kingdom Biobank (UKB) or the All of Us Research Program (AoU), which provide phenotypic and genetic information for hundreds of thousands of participants and allow for the identification of participants with varying comorbid disease combinations. Studying the genetic architecture of comorbid diseases presents an additional benefit: in addition to the traditional case–control comparison (i.e., comorbid disease versus controls), a within‐cases study can be performed, comparing participants with comorbid disease to each of the individual diseases in separate comparisons. These latter comparisons allow us to identify differences in the genetic architecture that are specific to the presence of comorbid disease, rather than one of the individual diseases. In the present study, we utilize this approach to study comorbid PS and CD using data from the UKB and the AoU databases. We perform a focused ExWAS, followed by a phenome‐wide association study (PheWAS) for the identified variants. We then perform a risk variant‐based analysis in the two large population‐based biobanks (UKB and AoU), followed by serum proteomic analyses.MethodsStudy PopulationUnited Kingdom Biobank—Discovery StudyThe present study utilizes data from the UKB, a prospective study conducted in the United Kingdom that collected demographic, survey, and genomic data on 502,129 participants aged 40–69 who were recruited between 2006 and 2010 [All of Us Research Program Database—Validation StudyThe All of Us Research Program (AoU) is a prospective biobank with the goal of enrolling at least 1 million individuals from the United States [Exome‐Wide Association StudyExome‐wide association studies test the association between a variant of interest in the exonic genome and a phenotype of interest. Variants selected for the study were obtained from the AstraZeneca PheWAS Portal (AZP, https://azphewas.com/). WGS variants were downloaded for CD and PS (data accessed in March 2025), and variants achieving suggestive significance to p < 1 × 10−4 were included (n CD variants = 289, n PS variants = 2700), allowing the study to focus on genomic regions that are more likely to be associated with both diseases. Variant QC and the statistical framework are described in Appendix Risk Variant AnalysisIn the UKB and AoU data, the proportion of participants (controls, CD, PS, and comorbid disease) with the digenic or trigenic risk variant was calculated across each group using PLINK (UKB) and HAIL (AoU) generated allele frequency data. The digenic risk variant is defined as an individual with at least one of the identified risk variants at both HLA‐C (rs17408553) and CFB (rs4151651). For example, an individual is annotated as possessing the digenic risk variant in any of the following scenarios: one effect allele in rs17408553 and one effect allele in rs4151651, two effect alleles in rs17408553 and one effect allele in rs4151651, one effect allele in rs17408553 and two effect alleles in rs4151651, or two effect alleles in rs17408553 and two effect alleles in rs4151651. The trigenic risk variant is similarly defined as an individual with at least one of the identified risk variants at HLA‐C, CFB, and TAP2. Significance between the groups was established using the Chi‐squared test.Proteomic AnalysisThe UKB Pharma Plasma Proteome (UKB‐PPP) contains proteomic sampling of plasma samples from 54,219 individuals using the Olink Explore 3072 platform, which measures 2941 protein analytes across 2923 unique proteins [n = 594) and samples homozygous for the digenic risk variant reference alleles (n = 17,566) were kept for differentially expressed protein (DEP) analysis, and detailed methods are available in Appendix ResultsExonic Architecture of Comorbid CD/PS More Closely Resembles PS A case–control focused ExWAS was run using the allelic test for comorbid disease versus controls, in addition to two within‐cases ExWASes comparing comorbid disease versus CD and comorbid disease versus PS (Figure HLA‐C, rs17408553 (chr‐bp‐ref‐alt; 6–31,271,630‐G‐T), demonstrated the strongest association in the comorbid disease versus controls (OR = 3.01, p = 2.15 × 10−13) and comorbid disease versus CD (OR = 2.82, p = 2.61 × 10−11) comparisons but did not achieve the adjusted significance thresholds in comorbid disease versus PS (OR = 1.47, p = 0.01). The second strongest association was another exonic missense variant in HLA‐C (rs2308557, 6–31,271,640‐C‐T) for both comorbid disease versus controls (OR = 2.85, p = 7.19 × 10−13) and comorbid disease versus CD (OR = 2.70, p = 4.92 × 10−11), though this marker is in strong linkage disequilibrium with rs17408553 (R 2 = 0.99). Similarly, rs2308557 did not achieve the adjusted significance threshold in comorbid disease versus PS (OR = 1.40, p = 0.02).Dominant and recessive models (Table HLA‐C variant rs17408553 demonstrated strong associations (OR = 3.04, p = 6.86 × 10−8 and OR = 3.27, p = 2.68 × 10−7, respectively).Conditional Analysis Identifies Two Putatively Independent Variants Associated With Comorbid CD/PS The presence of strong linkage disequilibrium in the genome, especially in the MHC region of chromosome 6, may mask additional independent association signals. To solve this challenge, conditional analysis was performed by including the lead variant, rs17408553, as an additional covariate in a multivariable logistic regression with Firth's correction model. First, the multivariable model was run without conditioning, and the results largely replicated those identified from the two‐sided Fisher's exact test (Figure CFB, rs4151651 (6–31,947,837‐G‐A), appeared as the strongest remaining independent signal (p = 6.05 × 10−5) (Figure p = 4.42 × 10−5, Table TAP2, rs2228397 (6–32,832,447‐C‐A), appeared as the strongest remaining independent signal (p = 6.61 × 10−5) (Figure HLA‐C and CFB variants are putatively functional missense variants, the synonymous TAP2 variant is likely a proxy variant in linkage disequilibrium with a nearby non‐exonic variant that is driving the association. PheWAS of Identified Variants Highlights Associations With CD and PS A phenome‐wide association study (PheWAS) was performed for rs17408553 (HLA‐C), rs4151651 (CFB), and rs2228397 (TAP2) utilizing data from the AZP (Figure Risk Variant Analysis Identifies Germline Differences Among GroupsNext, we aimed to characterize the proportion of individuals with a digenic (rs17408553 and rs4151651) and trigenic (rs17408553, rs4151651, and rs2228397) risk variant across each of the four studied groups in the UKB (Figure p = 5.8 × 10−4; AoU, OR = 2.44, 95% CI = 1.07–4.81, p = 0.02). In the AoU data, however, no significant differences were observed among the proportion of individuals with the digenic risk variant. In both analyses, the proportion of individuals with comorbid disease and the digenic risk variant was greater than the proportion of individuals with comorbid disease and the trigenic risk variant.Characterizing Proteomic Associations With Identified Digenic Risk VariantFinally, we aimed to characterize proteomic associations with the digenic risk variant in the UKB data. The differentially expressed protein analysis included age, sex, and CD or PS status as covariates but did not account for treatment status, which may introduce potential confounding. Differentially expressed protein (DEP) analysis between individuals with the digenic risk variant effect alleles was compared to individuals with the digenic risk variant reference alleles (Figure DiscussionIn the present study, we leverage WGS data from the UKB and AoU to uncover a trigenic exonic risk variant in variants located in HLA‐C, CFB, and TAP2 that is associated with increased risk of comorbid CD and PS when compared to controls and PS alone. A digenic risk variant including the putatively functional HLA‐C and CFB variants is also associated with proteomic alterations in several immune‐related proteins. The exonic risk variants and/or the proteomic alterations associated with the risk variants have the potential to be evaluated as prognostic biomarkers for the development of comorbid disease in individuals diagnosed with PS. Given the low incidence of comorbid disease and relatively small sample sizes (111 individuals in the UKB and 260 in AoU with comorbid disease), it will be important to validate our exploratory findings in additional cohorts and as more data becomes available in the AoU database. Though future clinical implications from the present study will require additional validation and testing, the hypothetical implications are interesting and may be useful for designing future studies. For example, a patient presenting to the dermatology clinic with PS who receives genetic testing identifying the presence of the trigenic risk variant has an increased risk of developing comorbid PS and CD (UKB, OR = 4.52, 95% CI = 1.55–10.30, p = 5.8 × 10−4; AoU, OR = 2.44, 95% CI = 1.07–4.81, p = 0.02). This patient may be counseled to increase gastrointestinal symptom monitoring. Additionally, this patient may benefit from biologic therapy with biologics approved for both PS and CD (such as adalimumab, infliximab, ustekinumab, guselkumab, and risankizumab), in addition to avoiding anti‐IL‐17 biologics that may worsen a future potential CD [Our study identified three primary variants associated with comorbid disease, with HLA‐C variant rs17408553 and CFB variant rs4151651 demonstrating the strongest evidence for independent association with comorbid disease. HLA‐C variation, specifically the HLA‐Cw6 allele, is the strongest known genetic risk factor for psoriasis, and it is associated with both early‐onset psoriasis and more severe disease [HLA‐Cw6 allele likely contributes to psoriasis pathogenesis through autoantigen presentation, thereby activating autoreactive T cells and leading to a CD8+ T‐cell mediated autoimmune disease [HLA alleles from exonic data is challenging, especially in the present study given the focus on a smaller number of exonic variants that were already suggestively associated with either PS or CD, the association between exonic HLA‐C variation and comorbid disease is unsurprising. The within‐cases analysis also suggests that this exonic variation in HLA‐C makes comorbid disease exonically distinct from CD alone and thus may represent a potential biomarker that can identify individuals with a higher germline genetic risk of developing comorbid disease.Upon conditional analysis, CFB variant rs4151651 was identified. A recent study characterized the association of this variant with Crohn's disease, identifying that this variant was associated with perianal CD in three independent cohorts [A final variant, rs2228397, was observed in TAP2, a protein expressed on the endoplasmic reticulum that forms a heterodimer with TAP1 and is involved in loading high‐affinity peptides onto MHC‐I [HLA‐C and CFB variants themselves are associated with comorbid disease, rather than serving as proxy variants. While this study focused on exonic variation, an adequately powered GWAS might be able to identify an additional variant responsible for the identification of this TAP2 variant.Given the likelihood of the TAP2 variant signal being a result of linkage disequilibrium, the digenic risk variant, rather than the trigenic risk variant, was used to probe the serum proteome. Proteomic associations with the digenic risk variant were compared to the digenic risk variant reference alleles. This analysis was performed agnostic to treatment status, which is a potential limitation as treatment may impact serum protein levels. For example, higher serum expression of a given protein may be a result of treatment status, rather than germline genetics, which may weaken the biologic interpretation. However, the results from this analysis suggested an association between the digenic risk variant and immune dysregulation. Higher proteomic levels of IL‐10 and CCL19 were observed in carriers of the digenic risk variant. CCL19, which is a ligand for the T‐cell CCR7 receptor, is thought to be upregulated in psoriatic fibroblasts [and disease status may help to tease out additional complexities in the proteomic associations.The present study has several limitations. First, only individuals of European ancestry were included in this study, preventing generalization of the results from the study to additional populations. Given the low incidence of comorbid disease in the overall population, the restriction to individuals of European ancestry was necessary to maintain sufficient power. However, individuals of other ancestries may possess differing allele frequencies for the studied variants, variation in the prevalence of comorbid disease, and differences in overall genetic architectures, thereby decreasing the generalizability of the present results to a multi‐ancestral population. Until more diverse populations can be studied, our results have limited generalizability to non‐European descent populations. Furthermore, the Northern European and British ancestry in the UKB likely encompasses a different genetic ancestry compared to the European population studied in AoU, which may in part explain differences in the risk variant analysis results between the two biobanks. Second, the study lacked replication of the proteomic results, in addition to performing the proteomic risk variant association analysis agnostic to disease status. Third, more detailed phenotyping may also help to identify specific PS and CD subtypes that are comorbid with each other, in addition to potential exonic variants associated with the specific comorbidity, given that each disease contains a large underlying phenotypic spectrum. While population‐level biobanks are excellent hypothesis‐generating and exploratory study tools, they may lack the phenotypic precision needed for more specific disease insights, such as differentiating between the subtypes of PS, and are also prone to electronic health record biases, such as incomplete or inaccurate information. Fourth, the present study would benefit from an increased sample size, though this is challenging given that the absolute incidence of comorbid PS and CD is low. The goal of this analysis was to identify initial associations that may benefit from targeted future studies. Future studies with access to detailed phenotypic, genetic, proteomic, and treatment data may be able to address additional related questions. For example, these studies may help to determine whether individuals with a single disease and the presence of the digenic or trigenic risk variant should receive certain biologics, with the end goal of potentially improving biologic selection for patients with PS or CD.Ethics StatementOnly de‐identified data from the UKB and AoU was used; therefore this study is not considered Human Subjects Research and is exempt from IRB review.Conflicts of InterestJ.M.C. serves on a data safety monitoring board (DSMB) for Advarra and has served as a consultant for Novartis, Takeda, and GSK.Supporting information
abstract_filled: Background: Psoriasis (PS) and Crohn's disease (CD) are chronic immune-mediated inflammatory diseases with overlapping immunologic mechanisms. Although comorbidity is rare, epidemiologic and genetic studies have highlighted a significant association between PS and CD. Methods: We performed a focused exome-wide association study (ExWAS) comparing individuals with comorbid PS and CD to healthy controls (case-control design) and to individuals with PS or CD alone (within-cases design) in the UK Biobank (UKB) and performed validation analyses in the All of Us (AoU) Research Program. Results: The exonic architecture of comorbid PS and CD more closely resembles that of PS alone. Three protein-coding variants, including two putatively functional variants and one proxy variant, were significantly associated with comorbidity: a missense variant in HLA-C (Asn104Lys), a missense variant in CFB (Gly252Ser), and a synonymous variant in TAP2. A significantly greater proportion of individuals with comorbid disease harbored at least one risk variant in all three genes (trigenic risk variant) compared to controls and PS-only individuals in both the UKB (odds ratio [OR]=4.52, 95% confidence interval [CI]=1.55-10.30, p=5.8×10-4) and the AoU (2.44, 95% CI=1.07-4.81, p=0.02). Conclusions: This study identifies novel exonic, protein-coding genetic variation associated with the comorbidity of PS and CD, in addition to identifying an association between combined carriage of three risk variants with comorbid disease compared to controls and PS alone in multiple datasets. These risk variants may serve as prognostic biomarkers and guide personalized biologic treatment strategies in affected individuals.

fulltext_body: IntroductionUsing Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) to prevent HIV infection is a key strategy to end the HIV epidemic. The United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS) has set a goal for 2025, ensuring that 95% of people at risk of HIV have access to and use PrEP. However, as of 2023, only about 35% of at-risk individuals worldwide were receiving PrEP. The US Food and Drug Administration has approved two types of daily oral PrEP regimens, including emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF). Both regimens have been shown to significantly reduce the risk of HIV acquisition. Compared with TDF, TAF could achieve more sustained and higher intracellular drug levels at lower tenofovir serum concentrations, potentially enhancing effectiveness and improving bone and kidney safety. However, the DISCOVER trial (n = 5,387), which compared once-daily TAF/FTC or TDF/FTC in HIV-negative cisgender adult men or transgender women who have sex with men and had an increased risk of HIV acquisition, suggested that TAF may be associated with an increased risk of weight gain. While such evidence is derived from clinical trials, there is limited real-world evidence regarding such potential adverse effects, indicating a critical data gap.To address this gap, a comprehensive assessment of the potential negative effects of oral TAF/FTC is needed in a large, geographically diverse US population. Using multi-sourced real-world data, including electronic health records (EHRs) and survey responses, from the All of Us initiative—a national program aimed at accelerating health research and medical breakthroughs—this study aimed to investigate whether TAF use for PrEP is associated with increased risk of weight gain, adjusting for selected sociodemographic characteristics.MethodsData source and study populationThis study included cisgender male and transgender female PrEP users identified in AoU with at least two weight measures, with one being taken within 180 days before and another being taken between 90 and 365 days after initiating PrEP. No cisgender women or transgender males were included because TAF-based PrEP is currently not approved for use in individuals at risk of HIV via receptive vaginal sex. The National Institutes of Health’s AoU Research Program is a national community-engaged program designed to advance health research by partnering with one million participants, more than 80% of whom come from historically underrepresented communities in biomedical research in the United States (US). All US adults (≥ 18 years) who can provide consent to participate and are not in prison are eligible to participate in the AoU Research Program. Participants are recruited either online or through partner healthcare practitioner organizations. This study utilized data from the AoU Controlled Tier dataset, version 8, which includes participants enrolled in the program between May 6, 2018, and October 1, 2023. All analyses were conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines posted in the AoU Code of Conduct.PrEP cohort identificationThe PrEP cohort was defined based on the following criteria: (1) individuals with negative HIV laboratory test results; (2) patients with either or both of the following medication records: (a) emtricitabine + TDF (any dose; any type of dose); (b) emtricitabine + TAF (any dose; any type of dose); and (3) No other combination of drugs beyond those specified (e.g., single drugs or regimens involving more than two drugs were not considered PrEP). Specifically, to identify negative HIV laboratory test results, a concept set of HIV-specific laboratory tests was identified. Individuals whose HIV screening results were reported as anything other than “HIV-1 positive,” “reactive,” “abnormal,” “detected,” “positive,” and “high” were classified as having negative HIV laboratory test results. The PrEP cohort was further categorized into three groups based on the observed medication records: TDF only, TAF only, and individuals who switched from TDF to TAF. Due to the limited number of observations (less than 10) or short duration of follow-up for weight gain after PrEP initiation (less than 90 days), certain PrEP medication records were excluded from the analyses. These exclusions included individuals with multiple drug switches (e.g., TDF-TAF-TDF-TAF, TDF-TAF-TDF, and TDF-TAF-TDF-TAF-TDF) and those who transitioned from TAF to TDF. Cisgender male or transgender female PrEP users were identified if they responded “male” to the sex assigned at birth question in the survey, “What was your biological sex assigned at birth?”Weight gainFor the TDF- and TAF-only groups, weight gain was calculated as the difference between the first weight measurement taken between 90 and 365 days following PrEP initiation and the last weight measurement documented within 180 days before starting TDF or TAF. For individuals who switched from TDF to TAF, weight gain was calculated as the difference between the first weight measurement taken between 90 and 365 days after the TAF initiation and the last weight measurement within 180 days before starting TAF.Sociodemographic characteristicsA total of seven sociodemographic characteristics were identified, including age group (18–44, 45–54, 55–64, and 65+ years old), sexual orientation (heterosexual, gay, and other/unknown), gender identity (cisgender and transgender), race/ethnicity (non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic/Latino, and Asian/other/unknown), income level in dollar (< 25,000, 25,000–50,000, > 50,000, and unknown), employment status (employed and unemployed) and health insurance (have health insurance and have no health insurance). Except gender identity, which was determined based on both EHR data and survey data, all other characteristics were derived solely from survey responses. Participants were identified as suspected transgender if they: (1) responded “transgender”, “non-binary”, or “Additional options” to the gender identity question “What terms best express how you describe your gender identity?” (2) had inconsistent responses to the gender identity question and the sex assigned at birth question; (3) had at least one record of gender dysphoria-related diagnosis ICD-9/10 codes; or (4) had any combination of two of the following three indicators: endocrine disorder not otherwise specified (Endo NOS) diagnoses, transgender-related procedure codes, and sex-discordant hormone therapy. Detailed information on transgender identification has been described elsewhere.Statistical analysesDescriptive statistics, including counts (percentages) and mean (standard deviation [SD]), were used to describe the sociodemographic characteristics of PrEP users identified by PrEP regimens. Linear regression was conducted to explore the association between different PrEP regimens and weight gain, adjusting for key sociodemographic characteristics. All analyses were performed within a secure informatics workspace provided by the NIH that allows users to analyze a centralized version of the AoU data. A statistical significance level of p value < 0.05 was applied to all statistical tests. This study used de-identified data from the AoU Researcher Workbench and was exempt from institutional review board approval under program policy, as it did not constitute human participant research.ResultsUsing data from surveys and various domains within EHRs, we identified 385 male and transgender female PrEP users who had at least two weight measures, with one being taken within 180 days before and the other being taken between 90 and 365 days after initiating PrEP. Among the 385 included participants, 284 (73.8%) used TDF only, 52 (13.5%) had TAF records only, and 49 (12.7%) switched from TDF to TAF. Most of the included PrEP users were MSM (303, 78.7%), aged between 18 and 44 (230, 59.7%), non-Hispanic White (221, 57.4%), with household income over $50,000 (183, 47.5%), and employed (242, 62.9%). The mean weight gain after taking PrEP was largest in the TAF-only group (1.80 kg [kg]), followed by the group switched from TDF to TAF (1.74 kg) and the TDF group (− 0.68 kg). (Table DiscussionsTo the best of our knowledge, this is one of the first studies to use AoU data to explore the impact of TAF on weight gain compared with TDF. Using multi-sourced real-world data, we found that a higher risk of weight gain was observed in the TAF group compared to the TDF group. The findings of this real-world study are consistent with existing clinical trials examining the efficacy and safety of oral PrEP, which have also reported greater weight gain in those who initiated TAF-containing therapy.For patient-focused selection of PrEP medication for individuals at risk of HIV, weight gain may be a factor to consider when discussing PrEP options. A 1 kg difference in weight was observed in between TAF and TDF in a TAF PrEP registration data. The higher risk of weight gain in the TAF group could lead to a higher risk of hypertension, myocardial infarction, and type 2 diabetes. An observational study of 6,834 PrEP users in the US suggested that people taking TAF had a significantly increased risk of hypertension and a more frequent need for statin treatment than those taking TDF. The potential mechanisms of TAF-associated weight gain remain incompletely understood, and it is unclear whether the differences in weight trajectories between TAF and TDF are because TDF is mitigating weight gain. Since we used TDF as a comparator, our findings could also be due to the potentially higher risk of weight loss in the TDF group. However, a recent retrospective study found that higher doses of TAF were associated with greater weight gain than lower doses of TAF, suggesting that TAF might affect the weight trajectory directly. Future research is needed to better understand the biological processes underlying weight changes with TAF as PrEP and further explore differences based on sex at birth and genetic factors.This study has some limitations. First, medication records in the EHR data do not necessarily confirm that the medication was taken as prescribed, which may lead to an overestimation of the number of PrEP users. Second, individuals with greater health care access and financial stability may be overrepresented in AoU. This selection bias may lead to the underrepresentation of individuals taking PrEP who face greater socioeconomic challenges. Third, the relatively small number of PrEP users identified in the current study limits the statistical power and generalizability of the findings.ConclusionsUsing multi-sourced real-world data, this retrospective study described the characteristics of people who initiated TDF/FTC or TAF/FTC for daily oral PrEP. Overall, TAF use was associated with a higher risk of weight gain compared to TDF use. Given this finding, continued monitoring of weight gain in individuals using TAF as PrEP to prevent HIV is recommended.
abstract_filled: Daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), including emtricitabine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) and emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide fumarate (TAF), is a key strategy for HIV prevention. Compared to TDF-based PrEP, TAF may be associated with greater weight gain. This study aims to examine the risk of weight gain among cisgender men and transgender women who were adults and took TAF for HIV prevention using real-world data. This study used data from All of Us, a nationwide research initiative designed to accelerate health and medical discoveries. All PrEP users in All of Us with at least two weight measures, one taken within 180 days prior to and the other between 90 and 365 days after initiating PrEP, were included in analyses. Linear regression was conducted to explore the association between different PrEP regimens and weight gain, adjusting for key sociodemographic characteristics. Among 385 eligible individuals, 284 were TDF-only users, 52 were TAF-only users, and 49 individuals switched from TDF to TAF. The median follow-up time for participants was 312 days. The average weight gain (in kilograms) for TDF-only, TAF-only, and TDF-TAD groups was -0.68 (standard deviation [SD]=5.43), 1.80 (SD=11.60), and 1.74 (SD=6.35), respectively. TAF-only (β=2.532, 95%CI 0.708-4.356) and TDF-TAF (β=2.756, 95%CI 0.890-4.621) were associated with significantly increased weight gain compared to TDF-only use. Closer monitoring of weight gain is recommended for individuals using TAF to prevent HIV.

fulltext_body: Study Highlights What is the current knowledge on the topic? Current pharmacogenomics studies have relied on European populations, leaving gaps in understanding how pharmacogenomic effects apply to diverse groups. There is a need for resources that can provide PGx information for these groups. What question did this study address? This study aims to validate known and identify novel pharmacogenomic interactions involving CYP450 enzymes using the All of Us dataset, which includes a diverse cohort with genomic and drug dosage data, despite the inherent noise of real‐world clinical data. What does this study add to our knowledge? In addition to validating established pharmacogenomic interactions, such as propranolol, metoprolol, citalopram, tramadol and sertraline with CYP2D6; paroxetine, esomeprazole, venlafaxine and omeprazole with CYP2C19; warfarin with CYP2C9; and tacrolimus with CYP3A5, not all expected associations were confirmed. This suggests that pharmacogenomic analyses using the All of Us dataset may be affected by factors such as phenoconversion, limited dose adjustments by clinicians, or inherent dataset noise. How might this change clinical pharmacology or translational science? The All of Us research program integrates both genomic and clinical drug dosage data that can be leveraged for pharmacogenomic studies. As future releases expand its participants' pool, its potential impact on precision medicine will continue to grow. Introduction Pharmacogenomics (PGx) explores the relationship between genetic variation and drug metabolism. Variants in genes encoding drug‐metabolizing enzymes, such as the Cytochrome P450 family (CYP450), influence drug pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics, leading to an altered drug response. Traditionally, PGx effects are studied through in vitro and in vivo experiments [Among the most critical determinants of interindividual variability in drug response is the Cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzyme family, with five of its members–CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP3A4, and CYP1A2–being responsible for collectively metabolizing approximately 90% of all FDA‐approved drugs [Recently, we validated known pharmacogenomic interactions using the UK Biobank data, thus demonstrating the utility of large biobanks for PGx analysis [In this context, the All of Us (AoU) biobank, which contains 51% of individuals who identify as non‐European, offers a promising alternative for PGx studies in a more genetically diverse cohort [MethodsData Source and Inclusion CriteriaWe use data from the All of Us Research Program's Controlled Tier Dataset V8, with data collected between summer 2018 and October 1st 2023. The All of Us Research Program by the National Institutes of Health represents one of the most comprehensive efforts to build a diverse genomic resource. It integrates the corresponding electronic health records (EHR), including drug dosage information, allowing for a real‐world validation and exploration of PGx effects.We derive metabolizer phenotypes for the CYP450 enzymes using the predicted phenotype calls available on the All of Us V8 platform and we include CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP2B6, CYP3A5, and CYP4F2 (All‐of‐Us‐Pharmacogenomics‐Star‐Allele‐Calling). Briefly, the AoU platform determines CYP2D6 star alleles and gene copy number using Cyrius v1.1.1. Subsequently, it assigns structural variation nomenclature and phenotype annotations via the cyp2d6_parser package. For the remaining CYP enzymes, the platform analyzes short‐read whole genome sequences (srWGS) data using Stargazer 2.0.2 to call star alleles and predict enzyme phenotype.We include participants who have at least one characterized CYP450 metabolizer phenotype, along with data on sex, BMI, age, ancestral principal component analysis (PCA), drug dosage and the end time of their drug exposure. We calculate age using the participant's date of birth and the end date of their last prescription, which is directly provided within the All of Us dataset. We obtain ancestral PCA and predicted ancestry from the AoU research platform (All‐of‐Us‐Genomic‐data). Whereas we derive the patient's race and ethnicity from respectively the race or ethnicity columns from AoU (Race‐and‐Ethnicity‐Data‐Collection‐and‐Transformation).Drug List and Maintenance Dose CalculationsWe derive the list of CYP450‐interacting drugs (Table cpic_gene‐drug_pairs.xlsx), downloaded on May 4th 2025, with CPIC guideline annotation and PharmGKB clinical annotation level of evidence. A drug is included in the PGx analysis if it has CPIC guideline annotation linking it to a CYP450 family enzyme. To ensure comprehensive coverage, drugs metabolized by multiple enzymes are included in the study. This process results in a list of known drugs metabolized by CYP450 enzymes.We calculate maintenance drug dose by averaging the daily milligram dosage across the last five observations. More specifically, we calculate the daily drug quantity by dividing the total prescription quantity by the number of days supplied. Daily drug quantity is then multiplied by the dose per unit to obtain the daily drug dosage. The maintenance dose is defined as the average of the last five daily drug doses for each patient. If the 5th prescription shares the same end date with subsequent prescriptions, all tied prescriptions are included, and we calculate the maintenance dose as the average of these. For liquid formulations, we calculate dose per unit by multiplying volume times concentration. Whereas for inhalation products, we standardize the prescription quantity to account for the number of actuations per inhaler device. We exclude outliers with the interquartile range method (IQR). We calculate the first (Q1) and third (Q3) quartiles based on the 25th and 75th percentiles of the maintenance dose distribution. We calculate the IQR as the difference between Q3 and Q1 and remove maintenance drug doses which fall below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. As a complementary filtration strategy, we also apply a more lenient outlier filtration by setting Q1 and Q3 to the 15th and 85th percentiles. We exclude combinations formulations containing two active ingredients from these calculations. Furthermore, we exclude inhalation drugs without information on the number of inhalations per device and eye drop formulations as the dose per unit is not provided. CYP450 PGx ValidationAs a first step, we validate established pharmacogenomic interactions between drugs and CYP450 enzymes. The CYP450 enzyme phenotypes from the AoU dataset are in five distinct metabolizer bins: poor, intermediate, normal, rapid, and ultrarapid, which reflect increasing enzyme activity. We exclude phenotype calls labeled as “likely” (i.e., likely intermediate metabolizer), “unknown” and “indeterminate”. We aggregate phenotypes into three bins: poor/intermediate<normal<rapid/ultrarapid. However, for genes where this aggregation was not feasible due to the absence of ultrarapid and rapid phenotypes, we analyze differences in three bins: poor<intermediate<normal. We include only drugs in the statistical analysis that have at least 50 unique patients. Additionally, we exclude drugs that do not have at least 10 unique data points per aggregated metabolizer phenotype or show no variance in maintenance dose within phenotypes.For statistical testing for associations between maintenance dose and metabolizer phenotype we use the Kruskal–Wallis (KW) (Scipy.stats 1.11.4) and the Jonckheere–Terpstra (JT) test (Clinfun 1.1.5). The KW test evaluates whether there is a statistically significant difference in the median maintenance drug dose across different metabolizers. In contrast, the JT test extends this analysis by incorporating the ordered nature of the metabolizer phenotypes. To account for data ties in the Jonckheere–Terpstra, we perform 1000 permutations to obtain an accurate p‐value. We adjust all maintenance drug dosages to age, sex, BMI and ancestry PCA through linear regression. Each drug is then tested individually for dose differences across phenotypes. Multiple testing corrections are not applied, as the analyses aim to validate existing associations.Population Subset AnalysisIn a second step, we aim to assess how many pharmacogenomic interactions can be recovered using specific subsets of the entire cohort. More specifically, we investigate which PGx interactions can be recovered in participants with self‐reported race as White, African American or Black and of self‐reported ethnicity Hispanic or Latino. For the statistical analysis we apply the same methodology as described above.Drug Use Duration Across Metabolizer PhenotypeWe additionally assess whether the duration of drug use is associated with metabolizer phenotype. For this, we define drug use duration as the time interval between the end of a participant's first prescription and the end date of their last prescription. The cohorts in this analysis are the same as in Methods 2.4, ensuring consistency with the main PGx analysis. To evaluate differences in duration across metabolizer phenotypes, we apply the Kruskal–Wallis test. As the threshold for significance, we use a Bonferroni‐corrected p‐value.Novel Association DiscoveryTo identify previously unreported pharmacogenomic interactions, we test all drugs included in this study against each of the CYP450 enzymes. Here we aim to uncover potential novel pharmacogenomic interactions, not currently recognized in CPIC guidelines. Statistical analysis was conducted with the above‐mentioned methodology, and due to the discovery nature of these statistical tests, we apply a Bonferroni correction to adjust p‐values for multiple hypothesis testing.If an enzyme‐drug pair is significant, we further validate this potential novel interaction with the UK Biobank, utilizing previously published CYP450 phenotype calls [Code AvailabilityThe code describing the analysis can be accessed on our GitHub repository (https://github.com/JanMatthias1/PGx_AoU).ResultsInitial CohortDemographics of the initial study cohort, after applying our inclusion criteria (i.e., at least one CYP450 metabolizer phenotype, along with data on sex, BMI, age, ancestral principal component analysis (PCA), drug dosage and end time of their drug exposure), are summarized in Table CYP450 PhenotypesOut of all the 10 CYP450 enzymes, 6 are available on the AoU platform namely: CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP2B6, CYP3A5, and CYP4F2 (Table Drugs Utilized in the Analysis and Drug Exposed CohortIn total, our drug list comprises 129 unique drugs across 8 CYP enzymes: CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, CYP3A5, CYP3A4, CYP2B6, CYP4F2, and CYP2C8. Among these, CYP2D6 is involved in the metabolism of 78 drugs, whereas CYP2C19 has 27 drugs. A complete list of drugs and their corresponding CYP enzymes is provided in Table Known Pharmacogenomic InteractionsIn a first step we carry out statistical testing to validate known CYP450‐drug associations across the entire AoU dataset. Due to our inclusion criteria, we test 50 known drug‐gene interactions. We successfully validate propranolol and metoprolol as known interactors of the CYP2D6 enzyme (Table Population Subset AnalysisIn the subset of participants self‐identifying as White, we test 40 drug‐gene pairs and validate citalopram and metoprolol as CYP2D6 substrates, esomeprazole and paroxetine as CYP2C19 substrates, and warfarin as a CYP2C9 interactor. Among Black or African American participants, we validate sertraline, tramadol and venlafaxine out of the 33 statistical tests. For the Hispanic or Latino subset (self‐reported ethnicity), out of 14 tests, we validate omeprazole as a CYP2C19 interactor. Complete results from the analysis are available in Table Drug Use Duration and Metabolizer PhenotypeThis section examines whether the length of drug use differs across metabolizer phenotypes using a Kruskal–Wallis test. A significant difference was observed for the atorvastatin‐CYP3A5 association, with complete results provided in Table Novel Pharmacogenomic InteractionsIn this analysis, we aim to discover novel PGx drug‐gene interactions. After conducting our statistical analysis, meloxicam‐CYP2B6 and naproxen‐CYP3A5 result in a significant p‐value with the Kruskal–Wallis test after Bonferroni correction. However we were unable to validate them using the UKBB. A complete list of statistical tests is available in Table DiscussionHere we aim to validate known interactions and discover novel pharmacogenomic effects using AoU participants, focusing on CYP450 enzymes. One of the main aims of our work was to utilize a diverse cohort, which we achieved with a total of 64,924 participants, of whom 52.65% self‐reported as White and 21.48% as Black or African American. This is in stark contrast to PGx studies carried out by [Due to our drug inclusion criteria—requiring at least 5 observations per patient, a minimum of 10 patients per aggregated metabolizer phenotype, and a minimum of 50 patients per drug—the number of unique drugs tested was reduced from 129 to 61. We averaged the last five drug dosages for each patient based on the assumption that clinicians adjust drug dosages in response to non‐responsiveness or the presence of adverse side effects. These most recent prescriptions are more likely to reflect PGx influences. Moreover, metabolizers which were labeled as “likely” intermediate or poor metabolizers were removed, as limited data is available to characterize their function [p‐value for the CYP2C19–venlafaxine association within the Black or African American subset decreased, suggesting that the “likely” classification may in fact reflect a true underlying phenotype.Our statistical analysis examines differences across phenotypes, both with and without considering the ordered nature of the metabolizer phenotypes. Testing for the order is important, as an ultrarapid metabolizer will have higher enzymatic activity, leading to a faster drug metabolism and clearance [We successfully validated known interactions for both the CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, and CYP3A5 enzymes. However, not all expected interactions reached statistical significance. When observing factors such as sample size, PharmGKB level of evidence or a CPIC guideline annotation, there is a trend favoring PGx interactions that have a stronger PharmGKB level of evidence with a larger sample size. However it should be noted that not all highly validated PGx interactions are significant. One possible explanation is that the drugs showing significant associations may have had less noise in the data. This is consistent with our observation that non‐significant interactions tended not to show clear dosage trends across metabolizer groups.Another contributing factor may be the inherent difficulty of capturing therapeutic efficacy or adverse effects for some drugs [One further explanation for the non‐replication of known PGx associations is that they may not generalize to a broader population. To investigate this, we tested whether a European‐only subset, on which many PGx interactions were discovered [As a next step we sought to explore novel drug‐gene PGx interactions within the All of Us dataset. The most promising association, based on the lowest p‐value across both statistical tests, was between meloxicam‐CYP2B6 and naproxen‐CYP3A5. However, this association did not replicate with the UKBB. Meloxicam, a non‐steroidal anti‐inflammatory drug used to treat rheumatic diseases [The AoU platform provides a valuable opportunity to link genomic data to clinical data but its effectiveness is limited by the availability of the participants' medical records. Although we considered 129 drugs metabolized across 5 distinct CYP450 enzymes, many had to be excluded due to insufficient drug dosage data. abstract_filled: The All of Us research program, a national longitudinal study conducted by the US National Institutes of Health, provides robust medical history, drug dosage and genomic data from a diverse population. All of Us offers an opportunity to discover novel correlations between drug dosage and genetic variation. However, first it is necessary to evaluate the quality and quantity of the data and its ability to replicate known associations. In this paper, we investigate whether known drug-gene interactions can be recovered from the All of Us dataset, based on data from electronic health records. Focusing on the Cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzyme family, which metabolizes approximately 90% of clinically available drugs, we evaluate 61 drugs metabolized by the enzymes. We then identify significant differences in drug dosages across CYP450 metabolizer phenotypes. Our results validate some known interactors of CYP2D6, CYP2C19, CYP2C9, and CYP3A5. However, we did not recover all validated PGx interactions, potentially due to noise, lack of doctors adjusting drug dosage or phenoconversion. Nevertheless, our findings highlight the potential of the All of Us dataset, which captures some known pharmacogenomic interactions.

Unlabelled: Polygenic scores strongly predict type 1 diabetes risk, but most scores were developed in European-ancestry populations. In this study, we leveraged recent multiancestry genome-wide association studies to create a Type 1 Diabetes Multi-Ancestry Polygenic Score (T1D MAPS). We trained the score in the Mass General Brigham (MGB) Biobank (372 individuals with type 1 diabetes) and tested the score in the All of Us program (86 individuals with type 1 diabetes). We evaluated the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and we compared the AUC to two published single-ancestry scores for European (EUR) and African (AFR) populations: T1D Genetic Risk Score 2 (GRS2EUR) and T1D GRSAFR. We also developed an updated score (T1D MAPS2) that combines T1D GRS2EUR and T1D MAPS. Among individuals with non-European ancestry, the AUC of T1D MAPS was 0.90, significantly higher than T1D GRS2EUR (0.82) and T1D GRSAFR (0.82). Among individuals with European ancestry, the AUC of T1D MAPS was slightly lower than T1D GRS2EUR (0.89 vs. 0.91). However, T1D MAPS2 performed equivalently to T1D GRS2EUR in European ancestry (0.91 vs. 0.91) and performed better in non-European ancestry (0.90 vs. 0.82). Overall, these findings advance the accuracy of type 1 diabetes genetic risk prediction across diverse populations. Article Highlights: Type 1 diabetes polygenic scores are highly predictive of disease risk, but their performance varies based on genetic ancestry. Can we develop a polygenic score that accurately predicts type 1 diabetes risk across diverse populations? Our novel polygenic score performs similar to existing scores in European populations, and it demonstrates superior performance in non-European populations. This polygenic score will improve prediction of type 1 diabetes risk in genetically diverse populations.

fulltext_body: IntroductionHealth literacy, which is broadly defined as the ability to meet the demands of the healthcare system, allows patients to effectively navigate their care and receive appropriate treatment (Low health literacy is associated with various socioeconomic factors. Lower educational attainment, lower household income, unemployment, older age, male gender, and racial/ethnic minority status have all been associated with lower health literacy (These concerns are especially pertinent for those with traumatic brain injury (TBI), for which an estimated 1.1 million Americans are treated each year (This analysis explores the associations between TBI and individual health literacy and access to care using survey responses from the National Institutes of Health's (NIH) All of Us Research program. We further investigate how TBI relates to health literacy and access to care across income and racial/ethnic groups. Elucidating health literacy among patients with TBI may provide a framework for rectifying gaps in care, especially for socioeconomically disadvantaged patients.Materials and MethodsDatasetData were retrospectively analyzed from the National Institute of Health's (NIH) All of Us Research Program, which is a patient-enrolled program that collects electronic health record (EHR) data and responses to various surveys. Namely, this analysis utilized “The Basics,” “Overall Health,” and “Health Care Access and Utilization” surveys. These surveys were selected on the basis that they assess respondents’ ability to navigate health materials and potential financial barriers to healthcare. These surveys provided standardized items across participants and enabled coding into SNOMED concepts, ensuring comparability between groups. Data collected by All of Us are accessible via their Research Workbench, which requires an institutional Data Use and Registration Agreement (DURA) and a verified Login.gov ID (Cohort DefinitionThis study utilized two cohorts: one consisting of participants with a history of TBI, per the participants’ EHR data, and one of participants without a history of TBI. Demographic information, including race, ethnicity, sex, age, education level, income, marital status, employment status, and homeowner status, was collected for each participant. Only respondents who filled out both the “Overall Health” and “Health Care Access and Utilization” surveys were included. All participants in All of Us are self-enrolled. Enrollment started in May 2017, and the respondent cohort used for analysis was created in March 2024.Participants with TBI were defined as having “traumatic brain injury” listed as a condition per All of Us’ standard vocabulary code (SNOMED code 127295002), which is converted from International Classification of Diseases 9th and 10th edition codes. These participants were included in the TBI cohort. Participants without “traumatic brain injury” listed as a condition were included in the non-TBI cohort.Variable DefinitionsQuestions from the “Overall Health” survey, which is publicly available under “Surveys” within All of Us’ data browser, were used to assess respondents’ ability to navigate health material. For respondents with multiple entries, the most recent survey responses were used for analysis. The “Overall Health” survey assessed how often participants needed assistance with medical forms, how often participants experienced difficulty understanding written information about their medical condition, and participants’ confidence levels in independently completing medical forms (question IDs 1585772, 1585778, 1585766, respectively). For each of these three questions, participants can select five varying degrees of frequency or severity (e.g., “never,” “rarely,” “sometimes,” “often,” or “always”), or, as with any question in the survey, skip the question.Responses to the “Health Care Access and Utilization” survey were used to assess access to medical care. This survey queried about participants’ ability to afford medical care, including emergency care (question ID 43528663), follow-up care (question ID 43530409), a healthcare provider (question ID 43529901), dental care (question ID 43528662), and specialist care (question ID 43530412). Whether participants delayed care due to insurance copayment (question ID 43530583), a deductible (question ID 43530585), out-of-pocket payment (question ID 43530584), childcare (question ID 43529903), or inability to take time off work (question ID 43529905) was also assessed. Additionally, responses to whether participants delayed (question ID 43530415), skipped (question ID 43530416), or took less than the prescribed amount of a prescription (question ID 43530417) were analyzed. All of these were yes/no questions regarding whether they had experienced these barriers to care in the last 12 months. Finally, levels of concern about paying for medical care at the time of filling out the survey were assessed, for which participants had three options to rank their level of concern (question ID 43530557).To account for potential confounders in the relationship between TBI and health literacy, sociodemographic and economic variables identified in prior studies as determinants of health literacy were included in analysis. Accordingly, demographic information from the “The Basics” survey was collected to ensure comparability between the two cohorts. Employment status (question ID 1585952), annual income (question ID 1585375), educational attainment (question ID 1585940), marital status (question ID 1585892), and homeowner status (question ID 1585370) were assessed from this survey. Sex and race/ethnicity were determined per EHR data. Race and ethnicity were combined to create a race/ethnicity variable with three categories: Hispanic, non-Hispanic Black, or non-Hispanic White. Participants’ education level was classified into four categories: less than high school, high school (or equivalent), some college, and college degree or higher. Employment status was dichotomized as either employed for wages or unemployed/other. Informative nonresponses (e.g., “skip,” “don’t know,” “prefer not to answer”) were collapsed into a single “skip” category, while all other responses were reported as provided. Notably, though annual income was reported as provided, it was divided into four approximate quartiles for the purposes of chi-squared analysis: less than $35,000, $35,000 to $74,999, $75,000 to $99,999, and $100,000 or more per year.Statistical AnalysisAnalysis was conducted in accordance with the All of Us’ Ethical Conduct of Research Policy and Institutional Review Board (IRB). Matching among the TBI and non-TBI cohorts based on sex, age, race/ethnicity, employment, education, income, marital status, and homeowner status was performed using the MatchIt package in R (Missing data. Finally, to assess effect modification, interaction terms between TBI and race/ethnicity, and between TBI and income, were included in regression models for each survey question. All data analysis was conducted in All of Us’ Researcher Workbench, an online platform for accessing All of Us data.Missing DataMissing survey data were categorized as either noninformative nonresponses (e.g., variables recorded as missing [NA]) or informative nonresponses (e.g., participant-selected responses of “skip” or “don’t know”). Respondents with noninformative nonresponses were excluded prior to matching to ensure valid comparisons between respondents with and without TBI. After matching, informative nonresponses were excluded from multivariable regression analysis but were included and reported separately for chi-squared analysis. A summary of missingness patterns is provided in Supplemental Table 1.To assess robustness, best- and worst-case sensitivity analyses were performed to confirm the significance of positive findings. In these analyses, informative nonresponses were reclassified as the least severe response option (best-case) or the most severe response option (worst-case), and the models were re-estimated accordingly.Correction for Multiple HypothesesFor this analysis, 15 prespecified survey outcomes were evaluated. To control for multiple testing, Bonferroni correction for 15 comparisons was applied, setting the significance threshold at P < 0.0033.ResultsCohort OverviewA total of 13,892 participants were included in our analysis. Demographic characteristics of matched participants without TBI (N = 11,562) and with TBI (N = 2,330) are summarized in Association Between TBI and Self-Reported Health Literacy and Healthcare AccessMultivariate ordinal logistic regression demonstrated a significant association between TBI and reporting issues related to difficulty navigating health material, as shown in P < 0.001) and requiring assistance with health forms (OR 1.24, 95% CI 1.12–1.36, P < 0.001). Associations with difficulty understanding and requiring assistance were consistent throughout sensitivity analysis, as shown in Supplemental Table 2.Associations between TBI and healthcare access are also reported in P < 0.001), delayed care due to transportation (OR 1.48, 95% CI 1.27–1.73, P < 0.001). Additionally, TBI was associated with delaying filling medications due to cost (OR 1.22, 95% CI 1.08–1.39, P = 0.002). These associations were consistent throughout best- and worst-case sensitivity analysis, as shown in Supplemental Table 2.Impact of Race and Ethnicity on Self-Reported Health Literacy and Healthcare Access among Participants with TBIP < 0.001), never requiring assistance with medical forms (P < 0.001), and being extremely confident with medical forms (P < 0.001). In contrast, both Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black participants reported higher rates of always experiencing difficulty understanding health material (P < 0.001) and always requiring assistance with medical forms (P < 0.001). These results were consistent throughout best- and worst-case sensitivity analysis, shown in Supplemental Table 3.P < 0.001), a healthcare provider (P < 0.001), and specialist care (P < 0.001). Non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic participants also more frequently reported delaying care due to childcare (P < 0.001) and lack of transportation (P < 0.001). Non-Hispanic White participants were more likely to report being somewhat worried about paying for medical care (P = 0.001), while Hispanic patients were most likely to report being very worried (P < 0.001). These results were consistent throughout sensitivity analysis, shown in Supplemental Table 3. Additionally, Supplemental Table 4 shows a similar trend among respondents without TBI, in which fewer non-Hispanic White respondents reported issues related to health literacy and access to care, and more Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black respondents reported these issues.P < 0.001), never needing assistance with medical forms (P < 0.001), and being extremely confident with medical forms (P < 0.001). Further, the lowest income bracket, less than $35,000 per year, was more likely to report always experiencing difficulty understanding health material (P < 0.001) and always needing assistance with medical forms (P < 0.001). Notably, when informative nonresponses were reclassified as the most severe response in sensitivity analysis, the p-value comparing responses for always experiencing difficulty understanding health material became non-significant (P = 0.004), as shown in Supplemental Table 5. All other mentioned findings were consistent throughout sensitivity analysis. Additionally, Supplemental Table 6 shows a similar trend among those without TBI, in which respondents earning $100,000 per year or more were less likely to report issues related to health literacy, and those earning less than $35,000 per year were more likely to report these issues.Association Between Interaction of TBI with Race/Ethnicity and Income with Self-Reported Health Literacy and Healthcare AccessSupplemental Tables 7 and 8 show how the interaction of TBI with race/ethnicity and income, respectively, is associated with difficulty navigating health materials and financial barriers to care, as determined via multivariable ordinal and binary logistic regression. Only delaying care due to transportation was associated with TBI and earning more than $100,000 per year (OR 2.12, 95% CI 1.29–3.50, P = 0.003). There were no other statistically significant effect modifications.DiscussionComparison between matched participants with and without EHR history of TBI demonstrated those with history of TBI are significantly more likely to report survey responses associated with low health literacy and more likely to report various financial barriers to care. Further, Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black respondents and respondents in the lower income brackets were more likely to report these issues when compared to non-Hispanic White and higher income respondents, respectively. However, history of TBI did not significantly modify the effect of race/ethnicity or income regarding reporting issues related to health literacy or financial barriers to care, except for TBI and earning $100,000 or more per year being associated with increased odds of delaying care due to transportation.Patients with TBI frequently require complex specialist care, making it particularly concerning that many may fall behind in health literacy and experience financial barriers to care (Regarding racial disparities among those with TBI, Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black respondents were significantly more likely to report difficulty navigating health material compared to non-Hispanic White respondents. Further, respondents earning less than $35,000 per year were more likely to report issues pertaining to health literacy. These findings were also demonstrated among those without TBI, indicating that these disparities are reflective of a broader issue and not specific to TBI. Additionally, TBI did not consistently modify these effects of race/ethnicity or income, suggesting that TBI may represent an additional, independent burden. These findings are particularly concerning given that Black and Hispanic patients with TBI have been identified to be less likely to be placed into rehabilitative care (Financial barriers to medical care represent a substantial challenge for individuals with TBI. Our findings show that these barriers are more commonly reported among non-Hispanic Black and Hispanic respondents with TBI. These findings are consistent with prior work showing that Black and Hispanic patients are less likely to be discharged to rehabilitation following TBI (Overall, although TBI did not consistently modify the effects of race/ethnicity and income in relation to health literacy and access, those with TBI may be uniquely susceptible to issues related to low health literacy and numerous financial barriers to care, as suggested by the self-reported survey responses, with non-Hispanic White and higher income respondents, both with and without history of TBI, being less likely to report these issues. With TBI being a potentially lifelong illness, access to care and literacy surrounding healthcare can make a difference in the long-term health outcomes of patients. With millions of Americans affected by TBI and its extensive financial burden, delay in care due to the costs could be an indirect factor in mortality for patients with TBI (LimitationsThere are several important limitations to this investigation. First, many components of All of Us data are self-reported by participants and may not align with the overall demographics of the United States (Additionally, there is no available data on how long after the initial TBI diagnosis survey results were reported. Therefore, this study only looks at association, not causation. It is possible that patients with low health literacy were at higher initial risk of TBI. Moreover, since, in this analysis, TBI diagnosis is based on affiliated EHR data, there are likely undiagnosed patients with TBI included in the non-TBI cohort. Similarly, conversion of survey responses to SNOMED codes may introduce misclassification error. While such error is expected to be nondifferential between groups, it could attenuate observed associations. Longitudinal analysis comparing health literacy and access to care before and after TBI, with validated diagnosis coding, is necessary to further interrogate how health literacy and access act as predisposing factors versus the consequences of TBI.Finally, this analysis is limited by the absence of fully validated instruments for measuring health literacy in the All of Us surveys. While there is notable overlap between All of Us survey items and established domains of social determinants of health (ConclusionIn summary, our investigation of participants in the NIH's All of Us database revealed that EHR history of TBI is associated with reporting survey responses related to lower health literacy and access to care. Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black respondents, both with and without history of TBI, were more likely to report issues related to health literacy and financial barriers to care, though history of TBI did not modify these effects. Further studies exploring the relationship between TBI, health literacy, and access to healthcare are needed to understand the epidemiology and socioeconomic impact of TBI. Nonetheless, this analysis highlights the need for targeted efforts to improve health literacy and healthcare access for patients with TBI.Supplemental Material
abstract_filled: BackgroundHealth literacy, which enables patients to effectively navigate the healthcare system, is associated with improved patient outcomes. Patients with traumatic brain injury (TBI) may be uniquely susceptible to gaps in health literacy and access to care, particularly for those of vulnerable socioeconomic status.MethodsUsing the National Institutes of Health's (NIH) All of Us Research Program, we analyzed survey responses among matched participants with and without TBI (N=2,330 and N=11,562, respectively) via nearest-neighbor propensity score matching. Chi-squared tests compared responses between racial/ethnic and income groups among those with TBI. Multivariable binary and logistic regression compared responses between matched participants with and without TBI.ResultsRespondents with TBI were more likely to report issues related to health literacy and financial barriers to care. Multivariable analyses revealed participants with TBI reported increased difficulty understanding medical forms (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.18-1.45, P<0.001) and difficulty affording emergency care (OR 1.55, 95% CI 1.26-1.90, P<0.001) when compared to those without TBI.ConclusionRespondents with history of TBI, per electronic health records, are more likely to report issues pertaining to health literacy and access to care. Among those with TBI, historically underserved populations are also more likely to report issues relating to health literacy and financial barriers to care, though TBI did not consistently modify the effects of race/ethnicity or income. Multidisciplinary efforts to address these limitations are necessary.

fulltext_body: IntroductionGlycogen storage disease type IXα1 (GSD IXα1, historically referred to as GSD IXd), is an ultra-rare X-linked recessive inherited disorder of carbohydrate metabolism caused by pathogenic variants in the PHKA1 gene (OMIM: 300559, ORPHA: 715, ICD-11: 5C51.3, ICIMD: Muscle phosphorylase kinase subunit alpha 1 deficiency). GSD IXα1 is member of the GSD IX family which includes several disease subtypes affecting the liver and/or muscle based on the defective subunit (α, β, γ, or δ) of the phosphorylase kinase (PhK) heterotetramer as a result of pathogenic variant(s) in their encoding genes. The loss of a PhK subunit leads to a dysfunctional PhK complex, hindering its ability to activate glycogen phosphorylase and initiate glycogen breakdown (Fig. PHKA2 and PHKG2 and are associated with GSD IXα2 (also known as IXa) and GSD IXγ2 (also known as IXc), respectively. Alternatively, within the muscle, the α subunit is encoded by PHKA1 and the γ subunit by PHKG1. The β subunit in both muscle and liver is encoded by PHKB and associated with GSD IXβ (also known as IXb). Neither PHKG1 nor any of the genes encoding the calmodulin δ subunit (CALM1, CALM2, and CALM3) are associated with PhK deficiency in humans.As the PHKA1 isoform is expressed primarily in skeletal muscle, GSD IXα1 is associated with dysregulated muscle glycogen breakdown and manifests with exercise intolerance, muscle cramps, myalgia, and muscle weakness. There are initial reports of muscle PhK deficiency starting in the 1980s, but to our knowledge, only 18 patients with a genetically confirmed diagnosis have been previously reported in the literature; all exhibited evidence of skeletal muscle disease, with a highly variable age of onset from infancy to late adulthood (range: 0.5–72 years). Given the symptoms can overlap with other muscle-related conditions, there may be a high occurrence of misdiagnosis and likelihood of underdiagnosis.Given the limited number of cases reported, the phenotype spectrum of GSD IXα1 is incompletely described. To address this, we document the natural history and disease progression of 14 previously unreported cases that were identified clinically with deep phenotyping performed by subspecialty teams in the United States, Canada, the Netherlands, Germany, and the United Kingdom with expertise in GSD. We compare the clinical course of these cases to those previously reported in the literature, as well as analyzed the National Institutes of Health (NIH) All of Us Research Program dataset to identify additional individuals affected by the disease. Through comparison of our new cases to those previously reported in the literature and those identified through the All of Us database, we expand the number of known cases and clinical and genotypic understanding of GSD IXα1.ResultsClinically identified cohortA total of 10 patients harbored a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in PHKA1, including 9 hemizygous males and 1 heterozygous female (Table N = 6), myalgia (N = 8), and muscle cramps (N = 5). Creatine kinase (CK) levels throughout follow-up were within normal limits in half of the patients (N = 5). Muscle biopsies were conducted in 4 participants and demonstrated variable fiber size variation with increased free and membrane-bound glycogen accumulation, rare vacuoles, and mitochondrial alterations (Supplementary Table An additional 4 cases (3 males, 1 female) had a clinical picture consistent with muscle PhK deficiency and harbored a missense variant in PHKA1 which was categorized as a VUS per ACMG criteria, including c.1745T>C (p.Ile582Thr), c.849C>G (p.Ile283Met), and c.1079T>C (p.Ile360Thr). The most common chief complaints included muscle weakness (N = 3), exercise intolerance (N = 2) and myalgia (N = 2). However, they also manifested symptoms that are less likely to be explained by the harbored VUS in PHKA1 including bony pain (patient 13), as well as fatty liver and spleen, hypertriglyceridemia and angiokeratomas (patient 14). Further details on their clinical presentation and histology findings are provided in Supplementary Table Patient 1Patient 1 is a Caucasian male who reported noticeable differences in early childhood, including not being able to turn himself over properly in the crib or keep up with his peers during physical exercise as a child. His speech always has been unclear, despite speech therapy, and this progresses during the day. He has experienced increased limitations since the age of 50 years with fatigue, diffuse myalgias, and cramping in the lower extremities and shoulders. His symptoms worsened over the course of the day and were exacerbated by physical activity; he uses a mobility scooter for assistance during walks that exceed 20 min. He reported difficulty swallowing confirmed by an otolaryngologist to be the result of reduced swallowing muscle strength. Laboratory results revealed a mild CK elevation at 365 U/L (normal limits <310 U/L). At age 66 years, WES revealed a pathogenic nonsense variant in PHKA1 (c.2806C>T, p.Arg936Ter). No second diagnosis was identified. The introduction of MCT oil supplementation at the age of 69 years did not lead to noticeable improvement. Patient 1 receives physical therapy to address muscle strength concerns and uses analgesics as needed to manage severe myalgias.Patient 2Patient 2 is a Caucasian male who reported daily myalgia predominantly affecting his lower extremities that started at age 5 years. Whole genome sequencing (WGS) at age 6 years revealed a pathogenic nonsense variant in PHKA1 (c.3334G>T; p.Glu1112Ter). A muscle biopsy of the left vastus lateralis displayed minimal fiber size variation, with slightly atrophic fibers exhibiting a rounded or polygonal shape, observed on hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining. The presence of coarse intramyofibrillar basophilia suggested abnormal mitochondria, which was further confirmed on Gomori trichrome, cytochrome C oxidase (COX), and succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) stains. Acid phosphatase staining identified rare sarcoplasmic punctate foci suggestive of vacuoles. PAS/PASD staining revealed excess glycogen in the sarcoplasm in linear aggregates and punctate forms. Oil Red O staining showed excess lipid in many myofibers. There was a normal fiber type distribution based on slow and fast myosin heavy chain immunohistochemical staining. Electron microscopy (EM) images demonstrated mostly free glycogen in between sarcomeres and occasional membrane-bound glycogen linked to autophagic vacuoles. Mitochondria were closely associated with glycogen and showed minor, nonspecific abnormalities such as enlargement, a suggestion of mitophagy, and irregular cristae (Supplementary Table Patient 3Patient 3 is a Caucasian male who presented at age 9 years with myalgia, fatigue, and proximal lower extremity weakness during physical activity. Whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed a pathogenic nonsense variant in PHKA1 (c.2806C>T, p.Arg936Ter), confirmed to be maternally inherited. Physical therapy helped address the persistent myalgia and weakness. He was prescribed emulsified medium chain triglyceride (MCT) oil and controlled quantities of pre-exercise uncooked cornstarch supplementation; no symptomatic improvement was noted with these dietary interventions. Now at 15 years old, his symptoms have persisted and progressed to include exercise intolerance.Patient 4Patient 4 is a Caucasian male who was noted to have hypotonia in infancy, which resolved without intervention. Despite his early concern for hypotonia, he achieved age-appropriate developmental milestones. At age 10 years he presented to an endocrinology clinic with a 50-pound weight gain within one year in the setting of impulsive, irregular carbohydrate-rich eating behaviors.
