fulltext_body: Key Points IntroductionColorectal cancer (CRC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality in the United States, with many patients progressing to advanced or metastatic disease despite standard first- and second-line therapies [Real-world data (RWD) provide critical insights into patterns of care, outcomes, and costs that extend beyond the scope of randomized clinical trials [All of Us Research Program is one of the largest, most diverse RWD repositories, integrating electronic health records (EHRs), surveys, genomics, and social determinants of health (SDoH) across more than 800,000 participants [All of Us has demonstrated the feasibility of identifying biomarker testing and targeted therapy use in lung, colorectal, and prostate cancers, but also documented significant under-reporting of biomarker results, imaging, and molecular diagnostics across cancers [All of Us for broad population-level insights and acknowledging the limitations inherent in real-world documentation.In metastatic CRC, biomarker testing (e.g., KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status) is essential to guide the use of targeted therapies and immunotherapies [Incomplete biomarker data introduce both clinical and economic uncertainty, complicating assessments of whether ICI use aligns with precision oncology principles.This study leverages the NIH All of Us Research Program to evaluate clinical outcomes, healthcare utilization, and cost effectiveness of ICI compared with Rego/Tri in patients with advanced CRC treated in the third-line setting. We quantify time to treatment discontinuation (TTD), estimate quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), and conduct incremental cost-effectiveness analyses from the US Medicare perspective. By integrating RWD from a diverse national cohort, this work provides pragmatic insights into the value of ICI in routine clinical practice. Our findings provide real-world evidence from a nationally distributed and demographically diverse research cohort on the value of ICI in CRC, while underscoring persistent documentation gaps and highlighting policy challenges that must be addressed to enable effective implementation of precision oncology at scale.MethodsResearch Patient Data RepositoryWe conducted a retrospective cohort study using Version 8 of the Curated Data Repository from the NIH All of Us Research Program. The All of Us program integrates electronic health records (EHRs), participant surveys (including social determinants of health), genomics, physical measurements, and data from mobile and wearable devices. As of February 2025, the program included over 800,000 participants, of whom approximately 45% identified as a racial or ethnic minority. More than 440,000 participants had linked EHRs and more than 568,000 contributed biosamples. The provider network comprises regional academic medical centers, federally qualified community health centers, and US Department of Veterans Affairs facilities. The NIH All of Us Research Program is a large, nationally distributed research cohort designed to enhance demographic and geographic diversity, including the intentional oversampling of populations historically underrepresented in biomedical research [For this analysis, we extracted demographic characteristics, diagnoses, types of visits, laboratory tests, administered medications, stage at initial diagnosis, histology, biomarker testing status, and death dates. All data were de-identified and harmonized into the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) common data model. Additional methodological details, including the dataset cover sheet and supplementary tables, are provided in the Supplementary Appendix, see electronic supplementary material (ESM).Defining and Characterizing PopulationEligible patients were adults (≥ 18 years) with advanced colorectal cancer (CRC), defined as stage IV or metastatic disease, who initiated third-line systemic therapy between January 2017 and October 2023 (Supplement Fig. A1, ESM). Third-line or later (3L+) therapy was defined pragmatically as the initiation of an ICI or regorafenib/trifluridine–tipiracil (Rego/Tri) following prior documented fluorouracil exposure. Because fluorouracil doublets (with oxaliplatin or irinotecan) constitute the universal backbone of first- and second-line metastatic CRC therapy, documented fluorouracil exposure was required to ensure that subsequent ICI or Rego/Tri initiation reflected ≥ 3L therapy. Additional prior therapies (oxaliplatin, irinotecan, bevacizumab, anti-epidermal growth factor receptor [EGFR]) were captured as binary indicators using OMOP drug_concept_ids and are summarized in Table All of Us while minimizing risk of misclassification. Treatment cohorts were defined as two mutually exclusive groups:Rego/Tri cohort (control): regorafenib or trifluridine/tipiracil (TAS-102).ICI cohort: immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy with pembrolizumab or nivolumab, with or without ipilimumab.Patients were excluded if they had (a) more than one documented primary cancer, (b) treatment dates preceding the CRC diagnosis, (c) therapy or diagnosis inconsistent with CRC, or (d) < 21 days of continuous drug exposure. The final exclusion criterion was applied to reduce bias from early discontinuation unrelated to therapeutic effectiveness (e.g., intolerance, rapid clinical decline, or administrative miscoding), thereby ensuring that treatment duration more accurately reflected therapeutic effect. A 21-day minimum exposure threshold was selected as a pragmatic cutoff aligned with common systemic therapy scheduling in routine oncology practice, including the standard 21-days-on dosing period for regorafenib within a 28-day cycle and historical every-3-week administration intervals for immune checkpoint inhibitors.Biomarker testing was identified using structured EHR data from the NIH All of Us Research Program, harmonized to the OMOP Common Data Model. Testing events were captured across the procedure (CPT), measurement (LOINC), and OMOP concept ID domains to ensure standardized ascertainment across health systems. CPT Codes included both panel-based and single-gene molecular pathology codes (e.g., MSI analysis 81301; KRAS 81275–81276; NRAS 81311; BRAF 81210; EGFR 81235; targeted genomic sequencing panels 81445, 81450, 81455, 0037U; and tiered molecular pathology codes 81400–81408). Unlisted codes (81479, 81599) were also included to capture laboratory-developed tests (Supplement Table A5, ESM). LOINC Codes including laboratory test result concepts were mapped for MSI, KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, and related molecular markers. OMOP Mapping was conducted with diagnoses and procedures were standardized to OMOP condition_concept_id and procedure_concept_id fields. Measurements were captured via measurement_concept_id, with mapping to CPT/LOINC ensuring consistency across health systems. Patients were classified as having documented biomarker testing if one or more relevant CPT or LOINC code was present; however, we anticipated under-documentation given the prevalence of free-text or scanned genomic reports in All of Us, and therefore interpret findings as reflecting gaps in documentation fidelity as well as testing utilization.Time to Treatment DiscontinuationTTD was defined as the number of days from initiation of third-line systemic therapy (Rego/Tri or ICI) to treatment discontinuation. Discontinuation was defined as the earliest occurrence of either (1) the last documented administration followed by no subsequent administration within 60 days, or (2) initiation of a subsequent systemic therapy, which was treated as a discontinuation event for the index regimen. This included switches between immune checkpoint inhibitors and regorafenib or trifluridine–tipiracil, or vice versa, consistent with standard oncology real-world evidence conventions [Participants who remained on treatment within 60 days of the database cutoff (October 1, 2023) were considered censored at their last observed administration date. TTD distributions were estimated using Kaplan–Meier methods, with censoring applied at the date of last known treatment for patients still on therapy or with follow-up shorter than 60 days.Cost-Utility Analysis FrameworkHealth Economic OutcomesHealth economic outcomes were assessed using a cost–utility analysis from the US Medicare payer perspective [Non-drug healthcare utilization was captured at the patient-event level using OMOP-standardized concepts and grouped into clinically relevant categories: laboratory tests (CEA), colonoscopy, imaging (MRI, CT, PET/CT), emergency room visits, inpatient admissions, and outpatient visits. Costs were applied using 2023 Medicare national average reimbursement rates from the Physician Fee Schedule, Inpatient Prospective Payment System, and Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (Physician Fee Schedule, IPPS, CLFS) [Baseline Demographics and Clinical CharacteristicsBaseline variables included age, race, ethnicity, sex at birth, and prior exposure to oxaliplatin, irinotecan, bevacizumab, cetuximab, and panitumumab.Quality-Adjusted Life Years (QALYs) and Economic EvaluationHealth outcomes were expressed as QALYs, calculated as treatment duration (in years) multiplied by a utility weight of 0.75, derived from published estimates for patients with advanced colorectal cancer using validated preference-based instruments, consistent with prior CRC health economic literature [All of Us dataset does not systematically capture longitudinal patient-reported outcomes (e.g., EQ-5D) or health-state transitions aligned with treatment exposure. Accordingly, QALYs in this analysis represent duration-adjusted survival on treatment rather than treatment-specific quality-of-life differences.Unweighted treatment duration (years) was reported descriptively as a secondary outcome to distinguish differences in treatment persistence from utility-adjusted outcomes, but was excluded from incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) and cost-effectiveness accessibility curve (CEAC) calculations. Sensitivity analyses varied utility weights from 0.6 to 1.0.ICERs were calculated as incremental cost divided by incremental QALYs. Incremental net monetary benefit (INMB) was computed as (ΔQALY × WTP) − ΔCost across willingness-to-pay (WTP) thresholds ranging from US$0 to US$1,000,000 per QALY [Decision Uncertainty and Value FrameworksUncertainty was evaluated using nonparametric bootstrap resampling (1000 stratified replicates preserving group sizes), a widely accepted approach for handling skewed cost data and estimating uncertainty around ICERs [Statistical AnalysisBaseline demographic and clinical characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics. Group comparisons were conducted using Student’s t tests for continuous variables and chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests for categorical variables, depending on cell counts. Statistical significance was defined as two-sided p < 0.05 or non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals.Time to treatment discontinuation (TTD) was analyzed using Kaplan–Meier survival methods, with unadjusted group comparisons performed via the log-rank test. The proportional hazards assumption for Cox models was tested using Schoenfeld residuals. Given the limited sample size (N = 82), multivariable adjustment for TTD and cost outcomes was not performed, and results should be interpreted as descriptive associations rather than causal effects.Cost outcomes were summarized using means, medians, and interquartile ranges. Nonparametric methods were used because healthcare cost data are typically right-skewed, and bootstrapping avoids distributional assumptions that may bias variance estimates. Uncertainty in incremental costs and QALYs was evaluated via nonparametric bootstrap resampling (1000 replicates) using the boot package, with INMB and CEAC constructed from the bootstrap replicates.All analyses were performed in R version 4.4.0 using the survival and survminer packages for survival analyses, the boot package for resampling, the table1 package for baseline characteristics, and the tidyverse suite (dplyr, stringr, lubridate, tidyr, ggplot2) for data management and visualization.The NIH All of Us Institutional Review Board determined that access to the de-identified participant dataset qualifies as non-human subjects research and does not require additional IRB review. In accordance with All of Us policies, all counts are rounded and results representing fewer than 20 participants are suppressed to protect privacy.ResultsDemographicsAmong 82 patients included (ICI, n = 50; Rego/Tri, n = 32), median age was slightly higher in the ICI group compared with Rego/Tri (p = 0.038). Sex distribution and race/ethnicity were generally balanced between groups, with masked counts reported for categories with < 25 patients to maintain privacy. Prior systemic therapy exposure differed markedly with patients in the Rego/Tri group more likely to have received oxaliplatin, irinotecan, bevacizumab, and anti-EGFR agents compared with ICI patients (all p < 0.001). Biomarker testing was infrequently documented, and MSI testing was not observed in any patient.Time to Treatment Discontinuation (TTD)Median follow-up time, defined as time from third-line treatment initiation to treatment discontinuation, was 4.1 months (95% CI 2.8–6.4) overall. Median follow-up was 8.0 months (95% CI 4.6–17.0) in the ICI cohort and 1.4 months (95% CI 1.0–2.8) in the regorafenib/trifluridine cohort.Among the 82 patients included in the study, median TTD was significantly longer for patients receiving ICI compared with those receiving regorafenib or trifluridine/tipiracil (Rego/Tri). Median TTD was 8.0 months for the ICI group versus 1.4 months for the Rego/Tri group (p = 0.0037). The hazard ratio (HR) for treatment discontinuation in the ICI group compared with Rego/Tri was 0.49 (95% CI 0.30–0.79), indicating a 51% reduction in the risk of discontinuation for patients treated with ICI (Fig. p = 0.009). However, given the modest sample size and sparse events, this result should be interpreted cautiously, as Schoenfeld residual tests are sensitive in small real-world datasets and may detect minor departures from proportionality [Healthcare Utilization and CostsOnly patients with documented utilization were included for each category to ensure descriptive statistics reflected actual resource use. Emergency department, outpatient, and inpatient visits were higher in the ICI cohort compared with Rego/Tri, while inpatient length of stay did not differ. Descriptive statistics for utilization events are summarized in Table Healthcare costs were evaluated over the observed treatment horizon, including non-drug utilization, drug acquisition, and total costs. Non-drug utilization costs were similar between groups, whereas drug costs were substantially higher for ICI monotherapy and combination dosing. As a result, total costs were also higher for ICI. QALYs were greater in the ICI cohort, yielding an ICER of approximately US$518,000 per QALY gained. Detailed results are presented in Table Incremental Cost-Effectiveness and CEAC ResultsICER for ICI compared with Rego/Tri was US$518,000 per QALY gained (95% bootstrap CI: wide, crossing zero in some replicates), above conventional US WTP thresholds (US$50,000–US$150,000/QALY). The CEAC indicated that ICI had ~ 0% probability of being cost effective at conventional thresholds. Probability increased to ~ 50% at a WTP threshold of US$500,000/QALY, and reached ~ 80% at thresholds ≥ US$1,000,000/QALY (Fig. Consistent with these findings, the INMB (Fig. Sensitivity AnalysisA one-way sensitivity analysis varying the utility weight from 0.6 to 1.0 demonstrated that cost per QALY decreased with higher utility assumptions for both ICI and Rego/Tri. Across all utility values, ICI remained associated with higher costs and greater QALYs, and the ICER remained above conventional WTP thresholds, though the gap between groups narrowed at higher utility weights (Fig. DiscussionThis study leveraged the NIH All of Us Research Program to evaluate real-world treatment patterns, TTD, healthcare utilization, and economic outcomes among patients with advanced CRC treated with third-line or later therapies. To our knowledge, this represents one of the first exploratory pharmacoeconomic analyses of ICI versus regorafenib/trifluridine–tipiracil using a large, nationally distributed EHR-linked cohort. The analysis reflects real-world practice during a historical and transitional treatment period (2018–2023), rather than contemporary first-line treatment paradigms. In this analysis, ICI therapy was associated with substantially longer treatment duration and greater QALYs, but also markedly higher drug costs, resulting in an ICER of approximately US$518,000/QALY. CEAC and INMB analyses indicated that ICI was unlikely to be cost effective at conventional US thresholds, though cost effectiveness improved at higher WTP values.The novelty of this analysis lies in the use of All of Us, a unique dataset designed to capture diverse populations often underrepresented in oncology clinical trials [All of Us. By integrating OMOP-coded diagnoses, CPT and LOINC biomarker codes, and CMS cost benchmarks, we provide a transparent framework for real-world economic evaluations that complements, but does not replace, clinical trial evidence. Given the heterogeneity and under documentation inherent in EHR-derived RWD, findings should be interpreted as exploratory signals that generate hypotheses rather than definitive estimates.Consistent with prior oncology RWD studies, we employed TTD as a pragmatic proxy for treatment benefit, acknowledging incomplete mortality capture in All of Us [Drug acquisition and total healthcare costs were significantly higher for ICI compared with Rego/Tri, resulting in an ICER exceeding conventional WTP. These results underscore the ongoing challenge of balancing clinical value with elevated costs in oncology [Several key limitations merit discussion around our findings. Importantly, biomarker testing was incompletely documented, and MSI/dMMR status was not reliably captured, precluding restriction of the analysis to a biomarker-defined population or direct comparison within MSI-H/dMMR subgroups. Molecular testing information in clinical practice is commonly stored in non-structured formats such as scanned pathology reports or uploaded PDF files, which cannot be parsed into CPT, LOINC, or OMOP fields. Even when orders were present in structured tables, corresponding results were frequently missing or inconsistently linked. This likely led to underestimation of biomarker testing and underscores the broader informatics barrier in oncology RWD [All of Us Research Program, key clinical variables such as ECOG performance status and disease stage at treatment initiation are not systematically captured, precluding robust adjustment and reinforcing the exploratory nature of the analysis. The exclusion of patients with < 21 days of therapy may preferentially omit individuals who discontinued very early due to intolerance, rapid clinical decline, or incomplete documentation, which could bias estimates toward patients with longer treatment persistence. Healthcare utilization events were variably coded across sites, and costs reflect CMS benchmarks rather than net prices inclusive of rebates or discounts. Additionally, the small analytic cohort (N = 82) limits precision, even with bootstrap resampling. Collectively, these limitations highlight the exploratory nature of the findings and the importance of viewing results as hypothesis generating rather than confirmatory. As the All of Us dataset matures and incorporates structured genomic results, future analyses will be able to replicate this comparison within MSI-H/dMMR-defined populations to reflect current clinical guidelines.Microsimulation or Markov modeling approaches were considered; however, due to the small sample size, lack of complete biomarker stratification, and limited real-world follow-up data on progression and survival, we opted for a patient-level cost-effectiveness analysis using observed treatment duration. Future work may incorporate simulation modeling to project lifetime costs and outcomes, particularly in biomarker-defined subpopulations.ConclusionThis exploratory analysis provides novel real-world evidence on the relative effectiveness, costs, and cost effectiveness of ICI versus Rego/Tri in advanced CRC. Findings demonstrate longer treatment persistence but substantially higher costs with ICI, yielding ICERs above conventional thresholds. These results reflect real-world practice patterns during a period of evolving biomarker testing and immunotherapy adoption and should not be interpreted as guidance for contemporary first-line treatment selection. While preliminary, these results underscore both the opportunities and challenges of using All of Us for pharmacoeconomic research and highlight the need for improved data infrastructure, biomarker documentation, and value-based frameworks to guide ICI adoption in recurrent advanced CRC.Supplementary InformationBelow is the link to the electronic supplementary material.
abstract_filled: Background: Treatment options for patients with advanced colorectal cancer who progress after standard therapies remain limited, and real-world evidence on treatment durability and economic outcomes in later lines of therapy is needed to inform clinical and policy decision making. This study evaluated real-world outcomes, healthcare utilization, and cost effectiveness of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) compared with regorafenib or trifluridine/tipiracil (Rego/Tri) in third-line (3L) advanced colorectal cancer (CRC), leveraging the nationally distributed NIH All of Us Research Program. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort cost-utility analysis using All of Us Version 8 Curated Data Repository. Eligible adults (≥18 years) with advanced CRC initiated ICI (pembrolizumab, nivolumab ± ipilimumab) or Rego/Tri during 2017-2023. Outcomes included time to treatment discontinuation (TTD), healthcare utilization, costs, and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs; base-case utility = 0.75). Costs were estimated from CMS 2023 schedules (Part B ASP for infused agents, Part D unit costs for orals; inpatient/outpatient fee schedules for non-drug services), applied per cycle and proportionally for partial cycles. Analyses were conducted from the US Medicare payer perspective, with the time horizon limited to observed TTD and no discounting applied (<1 year). Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs), incremental net monetary benefit (INMB), and cost-effectiveness acceptability curves (CEACs) were estimated using nonparametric bootstrapping (1000 replicates). Sensitivity analyses varied utility weights (0.6-1.0). Results: Among 82 patients (ICI n = 50; Rego/Tri n = 32), median TTD was significantly longer with ICI (8.0 vs 1.4 months; HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.30-0.79; p = 0.0037). Non-drug utilization costs were not significantly different, but ICI drug costs were higher (US$207,558 vs US$119,805; p = 0.001). Mean total costs were US$476,729 for ICI versus US$264,225 for Rego/Tri (p = 0.018). QALYs were higher for ICI (0.84 vs 0.43; p < 0.001). The ICER was US$518,000 per QALY gained. CEAC analysis demonstrated ~0% probability of cost effectiveness at US$150,000/QALY, ~50% at US$500,000/QALY, and ~80% at ≥US$1,000,000/QALY. Sensitivity analyses yielded consistent findings. Conclusions: In this exploratory analysis using the novel NIH All of Us Research Program, ICI therapy was associated with longer treatment duration and greater QALYs but substantially higher costs compared with Rego/Tri. ICI was unlikely to be cost effective at conventional US thresholds but may be favorable at higher willingness-to-pay values. These findings highlight both the promise of leveraging the All of Us Research Program for nationally distributed, demographically diverse pharmacoeconomic research and the challenges of interpreting real-world cost effectiveness in small cohorts. As the dataset matures and sample sizes increase, broader application of All of Us may provide valuable insights to inform precision oncology policy and value-based pricing strategies.

fulltext_body: IntroductionAging is an inevitable biological process characterized by a gradual decline in physiological functions, leading to increased vulnerability to diseases and death. The concept of healthy aging has emerged as a critical focus in geriatric research and public health. [Social determinants of health (SDOH) — the conditions where people are born, grow, work, live, and age — play a crucial role in individuals’ health, influencing the aging process and the ability to age healthily. [Existing studies on the impact of SDOH on healthy aging are limited. [To fill the gap, the objective of this study is to develop a prediction model of healthy aging by leveraging a large cohort of older adults from the AoU and advanced ML techniques. Understanding the relationship between SDOH and healthy aging holds significant clinical and policy implications. Clinically, this knowledge enables healthcare providers to create more personalized care plans that address both medical and social factors influencing a patient’s health. On the policy side, identifying key SDOH linked to healthy aging can guide targeted interventions and resource allocation, fostering public health strategies that promote healthy aging across diverse populations. Additionally, we also evaluated the fairness of the ML models in predicting healthy aging, ensuring that they do not perpetuate existing disparities and can be applied equitably across different demographic groups. Lastly, we identified the top predictors for healthy aging using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values, a well-established explainable ML method, which could inform the development of targeted interventions and policies to support healthy aging by addressing the most influential SDOH.MethodsData source and study populationWe used the registered tier data from the All of Us (AoU) Research Program registered tier dataset v7. [Study outcomeThe primary outcome is a dichotomous score of healthy aging, which was measured by a composite score of the status for 1) comorbidities, 2) cognitive conditions, and 3) mobility function. Charlson comorbidity index (CCI) by Quan. et al [We also defined a secondary cohort as a composite score of 0, with age greater than 85 classified as healthy aging, otherwise as non-healthy aging. Two distinct cohorts were then created for primary outcome and the secondary outcome analysis, respectively. The secondary cohort analysis allows us to examine whether the association between SDOH and healthy aging hold consistent when applying a more stringent definition of healthy aging. Consistent results across both cohorts would reinforce the robustness of our findings across varying definitions of healthy aging.Study designWe adopted a retrospective cohort study design and illustrated the cohort selection process in Potential risk factorsPotential risk factors (i.e., input features) were SDOH information collected from multifaceted survey questions, including The Basics (demographic information), Lifestyle (smoking, alcohol use, substance use, etc.), Healthcare Access & Utilization (access to and use of health care resources), and Social Factors (neighborhood, social life, stress, etc.). Self-reported race and gender were also recorded and included in the analysis. We reported the counts (percentages) for categorical variables and median (interquartile range) for continuous variables.Statistical analysisWe aimed to use SDOH features to develop a machine learning model to predict healthy aging. Three machine learning algorithms were applied: logistic regression (LR), multi-layer perceptron (MLP), and Extreme Gradient Boosting [After hyperparameters tuning using Bayesian optimization with 5-fold cross-validation over 100 iterations to optimize the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), we reported the performance metrics of the testing set including AUROC, precision, recall, F1 score, and specificity. In addition, we obtained the 95% confidence intervals (CI) of the averaging performance metrics by bootstrap method with 50 iterations. Specifically, the bootstrap involved repeatedly sampling with replacement from the test set, applying the final trained model with chosen hyperparameters to each resampled set, and calculating the average performance metrics. The best model is selected based on average AUROC and the potential clinical application with the goal of a higher F1 score, showing the balance between precision and recall.We then assessed the fairness of the machine learning model selected by comparing the ratios of metrics such as positive predicted value (PPV), negative predicted value (NPV), false positive rate (FPR), true positive rate (TPR), false negative rate (FNR), and overall accuracy across race and gender. We consider that models with ratios of between 0.8 and 1.25 as achieving predictive parity. We designated non-Hispanic Whites and females as the privileged groups for race and gender, respectively, and identified Black and males as the protected groups for these categories. Lastly, we adopted SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values to identify and rank the most important features, with a view to providing explainability and improved clinical decision-making. [We performed all analyses in Python (version 3.10 with libraries such as Scikit-learn, Imbalanced-learn). The study followed the STROBE cohort reporting guideline [ResultsDescriptive statisticsIn the primary cohort, 99,936 eligible older adults aged 50 or older who had responded to SDOH survey questions were included, and 44,109 (44%) were identified as healthy aging (age ≥ 75 and a composite condition score of 0, In the secondary cohort, 62,475 participants were included, and 6,648 (10.6%) were identified as healthy aging (i.e., age ≥ 85 and a composite condition score of 0, Model performance and selectionPerformance metrics on the test dataset and the AUROC for the three models are presented in Model fairness assessmentFeature importance analysisDiscussionThis cohort study leverages the AoU datasets, which not only included diverse populations from historically underrepresented groups and racial/ethnic minority groups, but also provided a rich source of SDOH through standardized OMOP data infrastructure. Our findings suggest that machine learning models are capable of identifying patterns for healthy aging from SDOH information, highlighting the promise of integrating SDOH factors into clinical decision-making.It is noteworthy that our work included high-dimensional SDOH with large-scale population and an explainable ML framework. A few of previous studies were available to include SDOH across several domains, such as neighborhood environment, education access, etc.. [Our models showed fairness in predictive parity, where the ratios of both positive (PPV) and negative predictive values (NPV) are close to 1. Ensuring that ML models do not discriminate against different racial or ethnic groups is crucial, as these models must perform equitably independent on sensitive features. In our context, if healthy aging is less accurately identified in disadvantaged groups, it may lead to unnecessary and potentially harmful treatments, thereby increasing their financial burden and causing undue harm. Therefore, maintaining equal PPV and NPV across different demographic groups is imperative to prevent such disparities and ensure equitable and healthcare outcomes. [Some machine learning classifiers are notorious as a “black box” where excellent performance is often obtained at the cost of lacking interpretability. [Past research has suggested that substance use and related drug overdoses may have contributed to lower life expectancy, [This study has some limitations. First, to date, a unanimous definition of healthy aging has not yet been reached. [Secondly, while the All of Us Research Program provides a large and diverse dataset, it may not be fully representative of the U.S. population. Participants in All of Us are volunteers who agreed to share their health data, which could introduce selection bias. These individuals may be more health-conscious, have better access to healthcare, or obtained higher educational degrees than the general population, potentially leading to an overestimation of healthy aging in our sample. While the generalizability of our findings is limited to the participants in AoU, it is important to note that the cohort is wide across the nation. Furthermore, the representation of racial and ethnic minority groups has improved in AoU, which enhances the applicability of our results to a more diverse population. [Thirdly, while we attempted to account for a wide range of SDOH factors, there may still be unmeasured confounders. For instance, we did not have data on lifelong health behaviors or early-life exposures that could significantly impact aging trajectories. Therefore, residual confounding is present that could bias our study findings, and a causal relationship could not be derived. Future studies could also consider using genetic data to understand the epigenetic factors for healthy aging. Also, those SDOH factors in the AoURP which were collected through surveys could be subject to recall bias. We also acknowledge that while our selected fairness metrics provided a quantitative approach to assess bias, these metrics may mask underlying disparities that contribute to differential outcomes. For example, achieving statistical parity may not imply that both groups have an equitable health care access. Future studies could consider integrate causal analysis to contextualize these fairness metrics by uncovering the root causes of health disparity and explore the intersectionality between SDOH.ConclusionIn this cohort study utilizing the AoU database, our machine learning model effectively predicted individuals likely to achieve healthy aging, emphasizing the critical influence of health insurance on this outcome. The findings highlight that access to health insurance is not merely a facilitator of healthcare services but a pivotal determinant of long-term health outcomes in older adults. By addressing the gaps in health insurance, policymakers can contribute to the promotion of healthy aging across diverse populations, ultimately leading to improved quality of life. The integration of health insurance into public health strategies could therefore be a powerful tool in enhancing the overall well-being of aging populations.Supporting information
abstract_filled: Introduction: The increasing aging population raises significant concerns about the ability of individuals to age healthily, avoiding chronic diseases and maintaining cognitive and physical functions. However, the pathways through which SDOH factors are associated with healthy aging remain unclear. Methods: This retrospective cohort study uses the registered tier data from the All of Us Research Program (AoURP) registered tier dataset v7. Eligible study participants are those aged 50 and older who have responded to any of the SDOH survey questions with available EHR data. Three different algorithms were trained (logistic regression [LR], multi-layer perceptron [MLP], and extreme gradient boosting [XGBoost]). The outcome is healthy aging, which is measured by a composite score of the status for 1) comorbidities, 2) cognitive conditions, and 3) mobility function. We evaluate the model performance by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and assess the fairness of best-performed model through predictive parity. Feature importance is analyzed using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) values. Results: Our study included 99,935 participants aged 50 and above, and the mean (SD) age was 74 (9.3), with 55,294 (55.3%) females, 67,457 (67.5%) Whites, 11,109 (11.1%) Hispanic ethnicity, and 44,109 (44.1%) are classified as healthy aging. Most of the individuals lived in their own house (64%), were married (51%), obtained college or advanced degrees (74%), and had Medicare (56.2%). The best predictive model was XGBoost with random oversampler, with a performance of AUROC [95% CI]: 0.793 [0.788-0.796], F1 score: 0.697 [0.692-0.701], recall: 0.739 [0.732-0.748], precision: 0.659 [0.655-0.663], and accuracy: 0.716 [0.712-0.720], and the XGBoost model achieved predictive parity by similar positive and negative predictive values across race and sex groups (0.86-1.06). In feature importance analysis, health insurance type is ranked as the most predictive feature, followed by employment status, substance use, and health insurance coverage (yes/no). Conclusion: In this cohort study, XGBoost model accurately predicted individuals achieving healthy aging, outperforming LR and MLP. Our findings underscore the significant role of health insurance in contributing to healthy aging.

Sleep is increasingly recognized as a modifiable factor for cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), yet the roles of specific sleep stages, particularly rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, and the utility of wearable-derived sleep parameters for CVD prediction remain unknown. Therefore, we aimed to investigate the associations of sleep with CVD risk and to develop multimodal prediction models for incident CVD. Using data from the All of Us Research Program, 23,413 adults who consented to share both Fitbit and electronic health record data between May 2018 and October 2023 were included in the analysis. Sleep data were obtained from Fitbit wearable devices, including sleep duration and stage-specific information such as REM sleep. Incident CVD was defined as occurring at least six months after the initiation of Fitbit monitoring. Cox proportional hazards models were applied to estimate adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for sleep duration and REM sleep in association with CVD. For the prediction of CVD within six years, two modeling strategies were implemented, including a non-invasive multimodal model using demographic, self-reported, and wearable-derived data and an invasive multimodal model that additionally incorporated laboratory measures. To compare real-world model performance, we applied and compared several conventional risk prediction models, including SCORE2, the Framingham Risk Score, AutoPrognosis 2.0, and the Pooled Cohort Equations. Among 23,413 participants (mean [standard deviation] age, 56.7 [15.5] years; 70.9% female), both short (<7 h) and long (≥9 h) sleep durations were associated with higher risk of CVDs compared with 7 to 9 h of sleep (short sleep: aHR, 1.16 [95% CI, 1.07 to 1.27]; long sleep: aHR, 1.32 [95% CI, 1.10 to 1.58]), with U-shaped relationship. Individuals with less than 20% REM sleep had a greater risk of CVDs (aHR, 1.31 [95% CI, 1.18 to 1.45]) compared with those with 20% to 25% REM sleep. These associations were consistent across CVD subtypes. In prediction analyses, soft-voting ensemble models with LightGBM and XGBoost integrating wearable, clinical, and laboratory data achieved high performance (AUROC of non-invasive models, 0.748; AUROC of invasive models, 0.782), outperforming conventional risk scores (SCORE2, the Framingham Risk Score, AutoPrognosis 2.0, and the Pooled Cohort Equations: AUROC range, 0.649 to 0.685). Short and long sleep durations, as well as reduced REM sleep, were associated with increased risk of CVD. We also derived and validated a multimodal model to predict the incidence of CVD within six years. These findings support the potential value of integrating objective sleep-stage measures and multimodal digital health data into future cardiovascular prevention strategies and guideline development.

fulltext_body: SummaryThis demographically diverse study of 5,094 IBD patients identified 22 significant comorbidities across seven organ systems, discovering novel associations including delayed postmyocardial infarction pericarditis, contact dermatitis, and carotid artery aneurysms, supporting IBD conceptualization as a multisystem disorder requiring comprehensive management.BackgroundThe rising burden of inflammatory bowel diseaseInflammatory bowel disease (IBD), comprising Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), affects approximately 4.9 million people globally, with prevalence increasing from 3.3 million in 1990 [IBD Comorbidities: current understanding and limitationsIBD comorbidities—secondary health conditions beyond the primary gastrointestinal diagnosis—significantly complicate disease management and worsen clinical outcomes. Large-scale studies have documented extensive comorbidity burden, with 78% of IBD patients having at least one comorbidity, particularly rheumatologic, dermatologic, and autoimmune conditions [Despite these advances, significant knowledge gaps persist. Most studies focus on predominantly White European populations, underrepresenting racial minorities and diverse demographics. Additionally, few studies have comprehensively examined rare cardiovascular, neurological, and metabolic comorbidities, creating gaps in understanding IBD's true systemic burden [Addressing demographic limitations in IBD researchA critical limitation of existing IBD comorbidity research is the demographic homogeneity of study populations. Major European cohorts, including the Swiss IBD Cohort Study and Dutch IBD Biobank, reflect predominantly Caucasian populations [Rationale for comprehensive investigationTo address these limitations, we employed a systematic approach targeting IBD's full spectrum of potential manifestations across four theoretical frameworks: (1) shared inflammatory pathways involving IL-17/IL-23/IL-12/TNF-α networks; (2) epithelial barrier dysfunction extending beyond the intestinal tract; (3) systemic inflammation consequences affecting cardiovascular and metabolic systems; and (4) gut-organ axis dysfunction involving bidirectional microbiome-organ communication. Our initial comorbidity framework utilized broad clinical categories commonly referenced in medical literature (Supplementary Table 1), and we implemented a validated two-step case definition requiring both IBD diagnostic codes and evidence of prescription for IBD-specific medications (Supplementary Table 2).Study aimThis study utilizes the All of Us Research Program's large, diverse dataset to systematically investigate comorbidity associations with IBD. We analyzed the complete spectrum of conditions identified through Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) coding (Supplementary Table 1) to characterize associations between IBD and dermatological, cardiovascular, autoimmune, and other systemic conditions, prioritizing rare and understudied comorbidities to inform future surveillance and therapeutic strategies for diverse IBD populations.MethodsStudy design and data sourceThis case–control study utilized data from the All of Us Research Program (version 7), a nationwide precision medicine initiative led by the National Institutes of Health that emphasizes inclusion of participants from groups historically underrepresented in biomedical research [Study populationCase definitionIBD cases were identified from the All of Us EHR data using standardized OMOP concept codes in the condition_occurrence table: 4,074,815 (Inflammatory bowel disease), 64,766,004 (Crohn's disease), and 34,000,006 (Ulcerative colitis). All participants with any IBD-related diagnostic code were analyzed as a single cohort to: (1) ensure adequate statistical power for rare comorbidity detection, (2) avoid misclassification issues when clinical distinction between subtypes may be unclear, and (3) capture the full spectrum of IBD-related systemic manifestations regardless of subtype. The index date was defined as the date of the first recorded IBD diagnosis. Participants with missing demographic information were excluded, yielding a final sample of 5,094 IBD cases.Control selectionControls were participants without any IBD-related diagnostic codes, matched 1:4 to cases by age (± 1 year), gender (exact), and race (exact) using the Cohort Matcher tool integrated in the Researcher Workbench. Matching was performed without replacement; when fewer than four controls were available, all eligible controls were included. Despite matching, significant demographic differences remained between groups (Table Demographic and clinical dataDemographic characteristics, including race/ethnicity, gender, age, annual household income, educational attainment, and health insurance status, were extracted from both EHR data and participant survey responses. Self-reported survey data were prioritized when discrepancies existed. Race/ethnicity was categorized as White, Black or African American, Asian, More than one population, Other/Not specified, and None Indicated, based on standard All of Us classifications. Age was calculated at the index date for both cases and controls. Annual household income was stratified into four categories: ≥ $75,000, $35,000–$74,999, < $35,000, and Prefer not to answer/Skip. Educational attainment was classified as College graduate or advanced degree, Some college, High school graduate or GED, Less than high school, and Not specified/Missing. Health insurance status was recorded as Yes, No, or Not specified/Missing.Statistical analysis of demographic characteristicsDemographic characteristics were compared between IBD cases and matched controls using appropriate statistical tests. For categorical variables (race/ethnicity, gender, annual household income, educational attainment, and health insurance status), we employed Pearson χ2 tests when expected cell counts were ≥ 5, and Fisher's exact tests when expected cell counts were < 5. For continuous variables such as age, independent samples t-tests were used to compare means between groups. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 for all demographic comparisons. The results of these demographic comparisons are presented in Table Comorbidity identificationComorbid conditions were selected based on a predefined list compiled through systematic literature review and clinical expertise, encompassing dermatological, cardiovascular, autoimmune, renal, neuropsychiatric, gastrointestinal, and respiratory conditions (Supplementary Table 1). Conditions were identified using OMOP standard concept codes in the condition_occurrence table. The observation period extended from the earliest available EHR entry to February 2025. Comorbidity data were structured as binary indicators. Medication data for 20 IBD-related therapies were also extracted to provide treatment context (Supplementary Table 2). Detailed data extraction procedures are provided in the Supplementary Methods.Statistical AnalysisAll statistical analyses were conducted using R version 4.2.3 and Python 3.11 within the Researcher Workbench environment. For each comorbidity, unadjusted odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using univariate logistic regression. Multiple testing was corrected using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) method with a threshold of 0.05.Predefined significance thresholds were established: OR > 1.5 and FDR < 0.05 for positive associations, and OR < 0.5 and FDR < 0.05 for negative associations. A volcano plot (Fig. 10(FDR) for all investigated comorbidities. This analysis identified 22 significant comorbidities: 15 positively and 7 negatively associated with IBD (Tables Following identification of significant comorbidities, adjusted analyses were conducted using the Mantel–Haenszel method to control for age, gender, and race/ethnicity. The procedure involved creating strata based on combinations of these confounders and computing weighted average ORs. Both unadjusted and adjusted ORs are presented in Fig. We note that our analytical approach employed stratified analysis (Mantel–Haenszel method) rather than multivariate regression modeling. While the Mantel–Haenszel method effectively controls for the categorical confounders used in stratification (age, gender, and race/ethnicity), it does not simultaneously adjust for additional potential confounders such as medication exposure, disease duration, smoking status, or socioeconomic factors. Consequently, residual confounding may persist despite adjustment.Sensitivity analysis Data sparsity analyses were conducted for associations with very low case counts. Associations involving rare conditions (prevalence < 1%) were flagged for cautious interpretation. Exploratory temporal analyses were performed where possible to assess the relationship between IBD diagnosis timing and comorbidity development.Reporting guidelinesThis study was conducted and reported in accordance with the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for case–control studies (Supplementary Table 3).ResultsDemographic and clinical characteristicsWe identified 5,094 participants with IBD and 20,376 matched controls (Table Significant socioeconomic differences were observed between groups. IBD patients were more likely to report annual household incomes ≥ $75,000 (33.0% vs. 26.7%, p < 0.001). Educational attainment was lower in the IBD group (32.4% vs. 40.0% college graduates, p < 0.001). Only 65.5% of IBD cases had documented health insurance compared to 93.6% of controls (p < 0.001), with a substantially higher proportion of missing data in the IBD group (33.5% vs. 3.5%).Comorbidity associationsOur screening identified 22 statistically significant associations spanning seven organ systems: cardiovascular (4 conditions), dermatological (6), autoimmune/rheumatologic (3), renal (3), neuropsychiatric (3), gastrointestinal (2), and reproductive/metabolic (1). Among these, psoriasis (7.3% vs. 4.7%) and irritant contact dermatitis (2.2% vs. 1.2%) had the highest clinical impact by prevalence, while delayed pericarditis, eating disorders, and carotid aneurysm were rare but showed strong effect sizes. Full results are presented in Tables Novel associationsThe most striking cardiovascular finding was delayed postmyocardial infarction pericarditis, which showed a nearly five-fold increased odds in IBD patients (adjusted OR = 4.80, 95% CI: 1.47–15.73, p = 0.004), representing one of the first large-scale documentation of this association. We also identified a significant association with carotid artery aneurysm (adjusted OR = 2.21, 95% CI: 1.30–3.77, p = 0.003), a vascular complication not previously reported in IBD literature.Contact dermatitis emerged as a prominent novel dermatological association. Irritant contact dermatitis was nearly twice as prevalent in IBD patients compared to controls (2.2% vs. 1.2%; adjusted OR = 1.84, 95% CI: 1.47–2.30, p < 0.001). Allergic contact dermatitis due to adhesive also showed significant association (adjusted OR = 2.06, 95% CI: 1.28–3.32, p = 0.002). Guttate psoriasis showed a stronger association than general psoriasis (adjusted OR = 2.55 vs. 1.56), suggesting subtype-specific relationships.Neuropsychiatric manifestations included anorexia nervosa (adjusted OR = 2.29, 95% CI: 1.46–3.60, p < 0.001) and its restricting-type subtype (adjusted OR = 4.00, 95% CI: 1.63–9.83, p = 0.001), as well as idiopathic generalized epilepsy (adjusted OR = 1.81, 95% CI: 1.15–2.87, p = 0.01).Notably, several of these novel associations involved small absolute case counts — delayed postmyocardial infarction pericarditis (5 cases, 4 controls), carotid artery aneurysm (18 cases, 35 controls), restricting-type anorexia nervosa (7 cases, 7 controls). While statistically significant, these findings should be interpreted with caution given the limited sample sizes, which may yield imprecise effect estimates.Established associationsAutoimmune and inflammatory conditions clustered prominently in IBD patients. Drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus showed a strong association (adjusted OR = 4.32, 95% CI: 2.51–7.45, p < 0.001), as did autoimmune hepatitis (adjusted OR = 2.43, 95% CI: 1.72–3.44, p < 0.001). Acute vascular insufficiency of the intestine was over three times more common in IBD patients (adjusted OR = 3.47, 95% CI: 2.52–4.76, p < 0.001). Psoriasis affected 7.3% of IBD patients compared to 4.7% of controls (adjusted OR = 1.56, 95% CI: 1.38–1.76, p < 0.001). The associations with drug-induced lupus and autoimmune hepatitis may partly reflect medication-related adverse effects, as several IBD therapies (particularly anti-TNF agents, thiopurines, and methotrexate) are known to cause these conditions.Negatively associated comorbiditiesSeven comorbidities showed significantly reduced prevalence in IBD patients (OR < 0.5, FDR < 0.05), predominantly involving pregnancy complications and obesity-related disorders. Maternal obesity syndrome demonstrated the strongest negative association (adjusted OR = 0.36, 95% CI: 0.20–0.63, p < 0.001), with consistent inverse relationships observed across multiple obesity-related conditions including obesity complicating childbirth (adjusted OR = 0.43), maternal obesity complicating pregnancy (adjusted OR = 0.48), and extreme obesity with alveolar hypoventilation (adjusted OR = 0.48).Sensitivity analysisThe calcium oxalate calculus of kidney association (unadjusted OR = 12.0, 95% CI: 0.96–627.9, p = 0.03) exhibited extreme data sparsity (3 cases, 1 control), preventing reliable adjusted analysis. Despite biological plausibility through established enteric hyperoxaluria pathways, this finding requires confirmation in larger cohorts.Several other significant associations involved rare conditions (prevalence < 1%): delayed postmyocardial infarction pericarditis (5 cases, 4 controls), restricting-type anorexia nervosa (7 cases, 7 controls), and carotid artery aneurysm (18 cases, 35 controls). While these met our statistical thresholds, the small absolute numbers warrant confirmation in larger, condition-specific studies.DiscussionThis study identified 22 significant comorbidity associations across seven organ systems in 5,094 IBD patients from the All of Us Research Program. Our analysis revealed several previously unreported associations—including delayed postmyocardial infarction pericarditis, contact dermatitis, and carotid artery aneurysms—that demonstrate IBD's extensive systemic manifestations. The demographic diversity achieved (29.2% non-White participants versus 10–15% in traditional cohorts) enabled discovery of associations with enhanced generalizability.Novel comorbidity associationsThe strong association between IBD and delayed postmyocardial infarction pericarditis (Dressler's syndrome) represents a clinically significant novel finding. While cardiovascular complications in IBD are increasingly recognized [The association with carotid artery aneurysm reveals specific patterns of vascular vulnerability extending beyond general cardiovascular risk, complementing work by Prijić et al. [The associations between IBD and contact dermatitis represent important novel findings. Both irritant and allergic forms showed consistent relationships, with irritant contact dermatitis affecting 2.2% of the IBD cohort, making it one of the most prevalent novel comorbidities identified. While psoriasis associations are well-established [Established associations in diverse populationsOur study validates established associations across enhanced demographic diversity. The strong association with autoimmune hepatitis aligns with recent Mendelian randomization studies demonstrating causal relationships [Demographic diversity and generalizabilityThe consistency of our findings across racial groups suggests these comorbidities reflect fundamental IBD pathophysiology rather than population-specific phenomena. Our diverse cohort also revealed important socioeconomic disparities: IBD patients reported lower educational attainment despite higher incomes, and concerning insurance gaps, highlighting health equity considerations in IBD management.Clinical practice implicationsThese findings support specific practice modifications beyond routine IBD care. The dermatological findings reinforce the need for systematic skin assessment during routine visits. The neuropsychiatric associations support structured mental health evaluation using validated tools, especially especially for anorexia nervosa and restrictive eating behaviors. Our results support multidisciplinary care models integrating dermatologic and mental health evaluations, with patient education addressing skin care strategies and early eating disorder warning signs.Limitations and future directionsSeveral limitations warrant consideration. First, our cross-sectional design limits causal inference; the temporal relationships between IBD diagnosis and comorbidity development cannot be definitively established. Second, reliance on diagnostic codes may introduce misclassification bias, though this limitation affects most large-scale EHR-based studies. Third, unmeasured confounding factors including medication exposure, disease duration, and disease severity could influence associations. Fourth, despite our 1:4 matching approach, significant demographic differences remained between cases and controls, necessitating statistical adjustment. Fifth, our study employed Mantel–Haenszel stratified analysis rather than multivariate regression modeling. While this method effectively adjusts for age, gender, and race/ethnicity, it does not account for additional potential confounders such as body mass index or smoking status, and residual confounding may persist. Future studies incorporating multivariate logistic regression with a broader set of covariates are needed to further clarify the independence of these associations. Sixth, some rare outcomes have very small case counts that limit the precision of effect estimates, including delayed pericarditis (5 cases, 4 controls), carotid aneurysm (18 cases, 35 controls), and restricting-type anorexia nervosa (7 cases, 7 controls). These associations, while biologically plausible and statistically significant, require replication in larger, condition-specific cohorts before definitive clinical conclusions can be drawn. The calcium oxalate kidney stone association in particular (unadjusted OR = 12.0, 3 cases and 1 control) requires confirmation in larger cohorts, though the high point estimate aligns with established pathophysiology involving enteric hyperoxaluria [Future research should prioritize: (1) replication studies in independent cohorts for low-prevalence associations; (2) longitudinal analyses to establish temporal relationships; (3) mechanistic studies investigating shared pathways for autoimmune clustering; (4) pharmacovigilance research examining whether certain associations reflect IBD pathophysiology versus treatment effects; and (5) integration of genetic and microbiome data to identify high-risk patients for personalized prevention strategies.ConclusionThis analysis identified several novel IBD comorbidities, including delayed postmyocardial infarction pericarditis, contact dermatitis, and carotid artery aneurysms, alongside significant associations with anorexia nervosa, autoimmune hepatitis, and other systemic conditions. Based on a large and demographically diverse IBD cohort, these findings demonstrate IBD's extensive systemic manifestations and support conceptualizing IBD as a multisystem disorder requiring comprehensive management approaches. The novel associations discovered underscore the importance of demographic diversity in biomedical research and necessitate updated IBD surveillance protocols validated across diverse populations.Supplementary Information AcknowledgementsThe All of Us Research Program is supported by the National Institutes of Health, Office of the Di-rector: Regional Medical Centers: 1 OT2 OD026549; 1 OT2 OD026554; 1 OT2 OD026557; 1 OT2 OD026556; 1 OT2 OD026550; 1 OT2 OD 026552; 1 OT2 OD026553; 1 OT2 OD026548; 1 OT2 OD026551; 1 OT2 OD026555; IAA #: AOD 16037; Federally Qualified Health Centers: HHSN 263201600085 U; Data and Research Center: 5 U2C OD023196; Biobank: 1 U24 OD023121; The Participant Center: U24 OD023176; Participant Technology Systems Center: 1 U24 OD023163; Communications and Engagement: 3 OT2 OD023205; 3 OT2 OD023206; and Community Partners: 1 OT2 OD025277; 3 OT2 OD025315; 1 OT2 OD025337; 1 OT2 OD025276. abstract_filled: BackgroundInflammatory bowel disease (IBD) manifests systemically, yet most comorbidity studies rely on predominantly European populations. The All of Us Research Program enables investigation across demographically diverse groups.MethodsWe matched 5,094 IBD patients 1:4 with controls by age, gender, and race, analyzing comorbidities using logistic regression with Mantel–Haenszel adjustment. Multiple testing correction used false discovery rate (FDR) with significance thresholds of OR > 1.5 or < 0.5 and FDR < 0.05.ResultsOur cohort included 29.2% non-White participants versus 10–15% in traditional studies. We identified 22 significant associations across seven organ systems. Three novel discoveries included delayed postmyocardial infarction pericarditis (adjusted OR = 4.80), contact dermatitis (adjusted OR = 1.84), and carotid artery aneurysm (adjusted OR = 2.21). Other significant associations included drug-induced lupus (adjusted OR = 4.32), autoimmune hepatitis (adjusted OR = 2.43), and anorexia nervosa (adjusted OR = 2.29). IBD patients showed decreased obesity-related conditions.ConclusionThis demographically diverse study discovered novel IBD comorbidities and confirmed established associations across racial groups. Findings support conceptualizing IBD as a multisystem disorder requiring comprehensive management and demonstrate the importance of diverse research populations.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12876-026-04732-6.Keywords: Inflammatory bowel disease, Comorbidities, All of Us Research Program, Health disparities, Demographic diversity Key messages• What is already known? IBD patients have increased risk of autoimmune, dermatologic, and cardiovascular comorbidities, but most studies focus on predominantly White European populations with limited demographic diversity.• What is new here? This large, demographically diverse IBD study (29.2% non-White participants) identified three novel associations: delayed postmyocardial infarction pericarditis, contact dermatitis, and carotid artery aneurysms across 22 significant comorbidities spanning seven organ systems.• How can this study help patient care? These findings support implementing multidisciplinary IBD care with enhanced cardiovascular monitoring post-myocardial infarction, systematic dermatologic screening, and updated surveillance protocols addressing newly identified systemic manifestations.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12876-026-04732-6.

Racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic disparities in pain severity and treatment persist across healthcare settings, reflecting inequities shaped by patients' experiences of discrimination and bias. Perceived healthcare discrimination (PHCD), feeling dismissed, disrespected, or treated unfairly by healthcare providers, may contribute to persistent pain disparities among socially disadvantaged populations, yet its independent role relative to everyday discrimination remains underexplored. Using cross-sectional data from the All of Us Research Program, we examined associations between PHCD and pain severity among 89,069 participants from the Registered Tier Dataset (v7, R2022Q4R9), excluding individuals with missing data or non-categorized racial identities. Multinomial logistic regression models adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, income, and education were used to estimate odds ratios (ORs) for pain severity. Both occasional and frequent PHCD were significantly associated with higher odds of mild, moderate, and severe pain (all p <.001). Participants reporting frequent PHCD had nearly eightfold higher odds of severe pain compared with those reporting no discrimination (OR = 7.98, 95% CI: 6.85-9.30). These associations persisted after full covariate adjustment, demonstrating a clear dose-response relationship between discrimination frequency and pain severity. PHCD emerged as a robust and independent predictor of pain severity in a large, diverse national sample, highlighting discrimination as a modifiable social determinant of pain and underscoring the need for equity-focused clinical communication and systemic interventions to improve pain management. PERSPECTIVE: This study, the largest to date examining perceived healthcare discrimination, demonstrates a significant association with greater pain severity across diverse populations. Highlighting a critical social determinant of health, these findings underscore the importance of addressing discrimination within clinical care. Integrating equity-focused strategies into pain assessment and management is essential to reduce disparities and improve outcomes among marginalized communities.

fulltext_body: Research in contextEvidence before this studySleep traits, including sleep apnoea, insomnia, daytime sleepiness, and snoring and cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs) show high comorbidity and considerable heritablility. Previous studies have identified genetic loci for individual traits or diseases and suggested some causal associations, but the underlying genetic architecture across multiple traits have not been comprehensively understood.Added value of this studyThis study applied pleiotropic analyses, colocalisation, enrichment analysis and Mendelian randomisation to examine shared genetic variants, pleiotropic genes, pathways and causal correlation between four sleep traits and CMDs. Several pleiotropic SNPs were identified, some of which were further validated to be significantly associated with both sleep and CMD traits in large cohorts. Key pleiotropic loci shared across traits included 16q12.2 (FTO), 4p12 (GNPDA2), and 3q27.1 (ECE2). Shared genes were enriched in phenotypes related to mortality, growth, and liver system. Pathway analysis highlighted Cushing syndrome, hormone secretion, and signalling pathways including cGMP-PKG, Ras and calcium signalling. After adjusting for relevant physiological traits, genetically predicted type 2 diabetes increased risk of sleep apnoea, sleepiness, and snoring. Conversely, sleep apnoea was positively associated with heart failure and type 2 diabetes independently.Implications of all the available evidenceThese findings reveal shared genetic determinants between sleep traits and CMDs, potentially explaining in part their frequent co-occurrence. They highlight hormone-related biological pathways that may serve as targets for prevention and treatment, and underscore the value of integrated management of cardiometabolic and sleep disorders. IntroductionCardiometabolic diseases (CMDs), including cardiovascular disorders such as coronary heart disease, stroke, and heart failure, as well as metabolic disorders like type 2 diabetes, constitute a major global health challenge.,,The most prevalent subtype of SA is obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA),,Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNP) associated with sleep traits and CMDs.,,,,In this study, using genome-wide association summary data, we employed integrative approaches aiming to detect pleiotropic variants, shared loci and genes, enriched phenotype, and pathways characteristics between sleep traits and CMDs. In addition, those pleiotropic variants were further validated in individuals from large cohorts. Finally, we performed multiple MR analyses to identify causal and independent associations accounting for several disease-relevant physiological traits.MethodsA detailed flowchart outlining the study design is presented in GWAS data sets and quality control of summary statisticsWe acquired GWAS summary statistics of individuals of European ancestry from publicly accessible data sources for four sleep traits (SA, daytime sleepiness, insomnia and snoring) and seven CMDs (atrial fibrillation (AF), coronary artery disease (CAD), heart failure (HF), hypertension (HTN), ischaemic stroke, type 2 diabetes (T2D) and venous thromboembolism (VTE)). In addition, to detect the contributions from other potential factors, we also included 15 disease-relevant physiological traits encompassing glucose metabolism, lipid metabolism, cardiac function, vascular circulation, and obesity. GWAS with sample sizes exceeding 50000 were chosen to ensure statistical power. For SA, we obtained GWAS summary statistics from FinnGen (the Finnish Genomics Initiative), which provides clinically diagnosed cases with high-quality electronic health records-based ascertainment. Other three sleep traits, including insomnia, snoring, and daytime sleepiness, were acquired from UK Biobank, where self-reported questionnaires data capture broader symptom variation and allow sufficient statistical power for analysis. All GWAS had ethics approval and informed consent, and details are provided in We conducted additional quality control on GWAS summary data. SNPs were aligned to hg19 human reference genomes. Variants without rsIDs or located in the MHC region (chr6: 28477797–33448354, GRCh37) were excluded. Biallelic SNPs with a minor allele frequency (MAF) over 0.01 were retained. Further data processing procedures were tailored to the requirements of each downstream analysis.Genetic correlation analysisWe calculated genome-wide genetic correlations between four sleep traits (SA, daytime sleepiness, insomnia, and snoring) and seven CMDs, resulting in 28 unique trait-pairs, using two distinct methods: Linkage Disequilibrium Score Regression (LDSC)P < 1.8 × 10−3, 0.05/28) were retained for downstream analysis.Cross-trait pleiotropy analysisWe applied PLACO+, a general method for pleiotropic analysis under composite null hypothesis to identify pleiotropic variants between genetically correlated trait pairs using GWAS summary statistics.PPLACO+ < 5 × 10−8) were considered pleiotropic within a given trait pair. Independent pleiotropic variants were identified using clumping implemented in PLINK (r2 = 0.001, window = 10000 kb).Individual-level data cohort informationIndividual-level data from the All of Us Research Program (AoU) and summary statistics from the Million Veteran Program (MVP) were used for validation analyses. To align with the GWAS datasets included and minimise population heterogeneity, validation analyses are based on participants of European ancestry. Parallel analyses were additionally conducted in multi-ancestry populations.Data from the AoU cohort was used to validate single variant associations for six CMDs (except stroke, due to limited number of cases) and the three sleep traits, including insomnia, SA, and snoring without sleepiness as it is not available in AoU. These phenotypes were derived from linked electronic health records (EHR) using standardised SNOMED and OMOP Concept IDs, as detailed in Single variant associations of sleep traits and stroke were also extracted from summary statistics from a few separate recently published GWAS from the MVP.The characteristics of the samples used in the validation analysis in AoU study is summarised in Validation of pleiotropic SNPsTo validate the pleiotropic associations identified from the PLACO+ analysis, single–variant association analyses were performed in the AoU study and MVP participants of European ancestry and multi-ancestry. abstract_filled: Background: Sleep traits, including sleep apnoea (SA), insomnia, daytime sleepiness, and snoring, frequently co-occur with cardiometabolic diseases (CMDs), with shared genetic factors suspected to underlie these associations. However, the contribution of shared genetic determinants to these associations is not fully understood. Methods: We conducted a genome-wide pleiotropic association study applying sequential genetic methods to identify shared genetic variants, genes, pathways and causal associations between the four sleep traits and seven CMDs, including LDSC, high-definition likelihood analysis, colocalisation, gene-based tests, enrichment analysis and Mendelian randomisation. Next, validation of those pleiotropic variants was performed in individuals from the All of Us and MVP studies. Findings: Among 28 pairs of sleep traits and CMDs, 25 showed significant genetic correlations. Pleiotropic analysis identified 754 independent SNPs (691 unique) and 102 colocalized loci (85 unique). Among these, 47 SNPs (44 unique) were validated as significantly associated with both traits in the pairs, and notably, rs429358 (19q13.32, APOE) demonstrated pleiotropic effects across SA, insomnia and type 2 diabetes (T2D). Forty-eight annotated genes were validated by gene-based tests. Shared genes were enriched in phenotypes related to mortality and growth. Pathway analysis highlighted Cushing syndrome, hormone secretion, and cGMP-PKG, Ras and calcium signalling pathways. After adjusting for glycaemic traits and blood pressure, genetically predicted T2D increased risk of SA, sleepiness, and snoring. Conversely, SA was positively associated with heart failure and T2D independently. Interpretation: This study of sleep traits and CMDs reveals shared genetic determinants that may partially explain their epidemiologic association and suggests potential treatment targets. Multiple sclerosis is a chronic disease with a great burden not only in healthcare costs but to a person's quality of life. The All of Us Research Program's large, diverse and broadly accessible data resource could be extremely useful to multiple sclerosis researchers, allowing them to consider individual differences in lifestyle, socioeconomic factors, environmental, genetic and other biological characteristics to advance precision prevention, diagnosis and treatment. The objective of this analysis was to demonstrate the richness of the All of Us data in prevalence, demographic and geographic distribution of participants reporting a history of multiple sclerosis either by electronic health record data, survey data or both. The prevalence of multiple sclerosis within the All of Us population was higher than most previous reports, overall and within demographic and geographic categories. Differences were also seen in prevalence by the type of data provided, with lowest prevalence in those who had both medical record and self-reported multiple sclerosis. These findings, along with the diversity of data types available in this cohort, may make it an ideal place for MS researchers to conduct studies, particularly etiologic and translational research. The ability to link participant reported survey data with electronic health record data, genetic and biospecimen data could allow for new studies that could not only improve our understanding of the disease, but present opportunities to develop personalized multiple sclerosis preventive interventions and treatments in the future.

Background: NPs (natriuretic peptides) are bioactive hormones crucial for regulating blood pressure, glucose homeostasis, and lipid metabolism. Despite the high heritability of circulating NP levels, the genetic determinants of NP regulation, particularly across ancestries and sexes, remain poorly understood. The objective of the current study was to identify genetic variants associated with NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-B-type NP) levels in a multiancestry study population. Methods: Whole genome sequencing and array-based data from 81213 individuals without heart failure were analyzed from the Trans-Omics for Precision Medicine cohorts, UK Biobank, All of Us Research Program, and REGARDS (Reasons for Geographic and Racial Differences in Stroke) study to identify common, rare, and structural variants associated with NT-proBNP levels. The main outcome of the study was log-transformed and standardized NT-proBNP levels. Genetic associations with NT-proBNP were examined, followed by gene prioritization, transcriptome-wide association studies, colocalization, and rare variant analyses. Results: Nine novel loci and 3 previously reported loci were identified to be associated with NT-proBNP levels. Novel structural variants were detected across 12 loci. Similar effect sizes were observed for both common and rare variants. Key genes such as BAG3 (10q26.11) and SLC39A8 (4q24) were identified through gene prioritization, with prior animal models supporting their therapeutic relevance. Rare variant analysis identified 6 masks with significant associations, specifically noncoding masks, suggesting regulatory modulation of NT-proBNP. Conclusions: This study identifies novel common, rare, and structural variants associated with NT-proBNP levels, highlighting the contribution of both coding and regulatory noncoding variation. These findings advance our understanding of the genetic architecture of NT-proBNP and may inform future cardiometabolic therapeutic strategies.
