abstract_filled: Objectives The current study evaluated the association between glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and substance use disorders (SUD) in type 2 diabetes and obesity. Methods We conducted a retrospective nested case-control study using the All of Us Research Program data. Cases were defined as diabetes/obese individuals with a new diagnosis of alcohol use disorder (AUD), opioid use disorder (OUD), nicotine use disorder (NUD), or cocaine use disorder (CUD). Control participants were drawn from individuals with diabetes or obesity who had no documented history of SUD. Conditional logistic regression was performed to estimate the association between SUD and GLP-1 RA exposure. Results The study included a total of 22,652 participants in the AUD group, 13,226 in the OUD group, 42,320 in the NUD group, and 9,296 in the CUD group; each group comprised both cases and matched control participants. GLP-1 RA use was associated with a 74% reduction in the odds of AUD (odds ratio [OR] = 0.26; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.20–0.34), a 69% reduction in the odds of OUD ( OR = 0.31; 95% CI: 0.23–0.42), a 68% reduction in the odds of NUD ( OR = 0.32; 95% CI: 0.27–0.39), a 75% reduction in the odds of CUD ( OR = 0.25; 95% CI: 0.16–0.40), and 75% lower odds of any SUD compared with non-users participants (OR = 0.25, 95% CI 0.22–0.30). Conclusions GLP-1 RA use was consistently associated with lower odds of developing SUDs among individuals with type 2 diabetes or obesity. These findings suggest potential for GLP-1 RAs to help mitigate SUD in these populations.

fulltext_body: BackgroundLung cancer has emerged as the leading cause of cancer-related death in females [Evidence regarding the interplay between sociodemographic factors, reproductive factors, and metabolic disorders in female lung cancer risk remains limited and inconsistent. Most existing studies have focused on generalized risk factors or selected individual genetic variants within predominantly European-descent populations, which limits the generalizability of their findings. More comprehensive and diverse research is needed to develop better prevention and treatment strategies for female with lung cancer. This study aims to fill this gap by employing a case-control design within the All of Us Research Program cohort to investigate the relationship between sociodemographic characteristics, reproductive factors, metabolic disorders, and lung cancer risk among a diverse female adult.MethodsData sourceTo conduct our analysis, we used data from the All of Us Research Program, specifically the Controlled Tier Dataset v8 (CT v8), version C2024Q3R4, released on February 3, 2025. The quality and collection procedures for these data have been described previously [All of Us Researcher Workbench, a cloud-based platform that allows authorized researchers to build datasets from cohort data and conduct analysis in Jupyter Notebooks. The cohorts, concept sets, and analysis notebooks used for this project are available to authorized Workbench users in the Researcher Workbench Version 8 Workspace Rafiq Projects (https://workbench.researchallofus.org/workspaces/version8rafiqprojects/ or from the corresponding author upon reasonable request. We used the Workbench Dataset Builder to create datasets of female participants categorized into two groups: those with lung cancer and those without lung cancer, determined through observation of Systemized Nomenclature of Medicine–Clinical Terminology (SNOMED-CT), ICD-09, and ICD-10 codes. Included participants were aged 19–95 with a recorded sex at birth of female and electronic health record data linked to their All of Us record. Participants were excluded if they were pregnant at the time of All of Us enrollment.The All of Us database is a comprehensive nationwide resource that prioritizes inclusivity and the representation of diverse populations. All participants provided written informed consent at the time of enrollment. The collected data undergoes rigorous de-identification procedures before being made accessible to researchers. As this study involved secondary analyses of de-identified data, it is classified as research not involving human subjects under current regulatory guidelines.Age and race/ethnicity were derived from participant-provided information at enrollment. Age was recorded in complete years and categorized into four groups (19–35, 36–50, 51–60, and 66–95 years), which were used for matching controls. Self-reported race and ethnicity were recoded as non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic, Asian, other race, and no response. Educational attainment, alcohol use, smoking status, and family history of lung, breast, and ovarian cancer were obtained from the Basics, Lifestyle, and Personal and Family Health History surveys. Education was categorized into four groups: less than high school, high school, some college, and finished college. Smoking status was categorized by lifetime exposure: <100 cigarettes as never smokers, ≥ 100 cigarettes as ever smokers. Body mass index (BMI) at enrollment was calculated and categorized as underweight (< 18.5), normal weight (18.5–24.9), overweight (25-29.9), and obese (≥ 30) [Study designWe conducted a case-control study to assess sociodemographic, reproductive, and metabolic factors associated with primary lung cancer among female participants of the All of Us Research Program. The total cohort included 633,540 participants, of whom 4,878 had a diagnosis of lung cancer. Focusing on female participants with primary lung cancer yielded 2,750 cases. To ensure adequate statistical power (80%) at a 95% confidence level, we selected a 1:1 age-matched control group of females without lung cancer, resulting in a total study sample of 5,500 participants.Statistical analysisWe utilized the Python Jupyter notebook (v.3.10.2) for conducting descriptive and inferential statistics on the study participants. Descriptive statistics were generated including mean and standard deviation for continuous variables and frequencies and percentages for categorical variables. Bivariate analyses were performed to compare characteristics between lung cancer cases and non-lung cancer controls, utilizing Chi-square tests for categorical variables and unpaired t-tests for continuous variables. Multivariable binary logistic regression models were constructed to evaluate the association between various risk factors and lung cancer occurrence among female participants in the All of Us cohort. Separate models were developed for different categories of variables, with specific adjustment strategies employed for each model type. Sociodemographic models were adjusted for body mass index (BMI), race/ethnicity, area deprivation index, smoking status, and alcohol use. Reproductive factor models were adjusted for estrogen use, postmenopausal bleeding, menopausal status, history of abortion, infertility, and polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). Metabolic disorder models were adjusted for hypothyroidism, BMI, postmenopausal bleeding, menopausal status, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and PCOS. Family history models were adjusted for family histories of lung cancer, breast cancer, and ovarian cancer. All models compared lung cancer cases to female controls without lung cancer from the All of Us cohort. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 for all analyses.ResultsOf the 633,540 participants in the All of Us cohort, 4,878 (0.77%) had a lung cancer diagnosis, and of these, 2,750 female participants were included in this analysis. The characteristics of the cohort are summarized in Table p < 0.001). Regarding neighborhood deprivation, the largest proportion of lung cancer patients (44.9%) belonged to the moderately deprived group (Q3: 0.31–0.40). Notably, both the least deprived (Q1) and most deprived (Q4) groups had higher proportions of lung cancer patients compared to controls (4.65% vs. 2.36% for Q1 and 10.72% vs. 9.67% for Q4, respectively < 001). Most female lung cancer cases were among non-Hispanic Whites (63.4%), followed by non-Hispanic Blacks (14.5%), Hispanics (12.2%), Asians (2.4%), and other races (1.1%) (Fig. Table p = 0.06). Females in the least deprived group (Q1) had a 63% higher lung cancer risk compared to the most deprived (Q4) (AOR 1.63, 95% CI: 1.37, 2.71), whereas Q2 and Q3 groups had lower risks. Female smokers had a 32% higher risk than non-smokers (AOR 1.32, 95% CI: 1.13, 1.55). Among reproductive factors, postmenopausal status and postmenopausal bleeding were associated with 47% and 59% increases in lung cancer risk (95% CI: 1.25–1.72 and 1.31–1.92, respectively) after adjustment. Other factors, such as a history of estrogen use, abortion, and infertility, showed increased risks, but these associations were not statistically significant (p = 0.60, 0.40, and 0.32, respectively). There was also an interaction between menopausal status, smoking, and race. Postmenopausal smokers had a 2.65 times higher risk of lung cancer (95% CI: 1.75–4.01) compared to non-smokers. Additionally, being Asian was associated with a 2.67 times higher risk (95% CI: 1.01–7.13) compared to women of other racial groups. Among metabolic disorders, females with hyperlipidemia and hypothyroidism had an increased risk of lung cancer compared to the control group (AOR: 1.57, 95% CI: 1.40–1.77, and AOR: 1.63, 95% CI: 1.45–1.85, respectively). In contrast, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and PCOS were not associated with a higher risk of lung cancer. Interestingly, even non-smoking females with hyperlipidemia had a higher risk of lung cancer, with their risk increasing from 57% to 71% compared to females without hyperlipidemia. A family history of lung cancer was also associated with an increased risk (AOR: 1.17; 95% CI: 0.98–1.40), although this finding was not statistically significant. However, females who smoked and had a family history of lung cancer had a 94% higher risk (AOR: 1.94; 95% CI: 1.03–3.64) compared to non-smokers. Additionally, Females with postmenopausal bleeding and a family history of breast cancer had a higher risk of lung cancer (AOR: 1.82; 95% CI: 1.11–2.99). Similarly, those with both hypothyroidism and a family history of breast cancer also had an increased risk (AOR: 1.64; 95% CI: 1.17–2.30) compared to having either condition alone.DiscussionTo our knowledge, this is the first analysis to explore female lung cancer risk factors using the All of Us Research data. Among sociodemographic factors, we observed a notable shift in the mean age of female lung cancer patients in the U.S. While existing studies report an average age of about 70 years, our All of Us cohort analysis found a slightly lower average of 67.9 years [Although BMI does not have a direct association with increased lung cancer risk in females [ Then, the index was normalized to range from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater socioeconomic deprivation [ Participants in the lowest deprivation quartile (Q1) had a 63% higher risk of lung cancer compared to those in the highest quartile. This may be due to individuals in low-indexed areas typically having better healthcare access, greater health awareness, and improved insurance coverage, leading to higher detection rates and better access than those in deprived areas who remain undiagnosed [Smoking is a well-established risk factor for lung cancer [ We examined various reproductive factors, including estrogen used for contraceptive or hormone replacement therapy, menopause status, history of postmenopausal bleeding, abortion, infertility, and PCOS. We found that their relationships with lung cancer risk exhibited different patterns. Among them, a history of estrogen use was initially associated with a modest increase (18%) in risk. However, after adjustment, this association was no longer statistically significant, suggesting that other reproductive factors may influence the effect. This suggests that the combined effect of hormonal decline and tobacco exposure may amplify carcinogenic risk. Similarly, Female participants with hypothyroidism had a higher risk of lung cancer compared to those without hypothyroidism. However, the existing literature presents conflicting evidence, suggesting that hypothyroidism may have a protective role against lung cancer [ Having a positive family history of cancer is a well-established risk factor for various cancers, including lung cancer in females [p = 0.03). This suggests a possible synergistic effect between genetic predisposition and environmental exposure, such as prolonged smoking or hormone replacement therapy. Leveraging the diverse All of Us Research Program database allowed us to include a broadly representative sample of American female lung cancer patients, enhancing the generalizability of our findings. The case-control design provided a cost-effective and time-efficient approach to simultaneously investigate multiple risk factors, including reproductive history, metabolic disorders, family history, and lifestyle behaviors. Importantly, this study focuses on non-traditional risk factors among females, moving beyond well-established smoking risks to explore gender-specific vulnerabilities. This addresses a critical gap in the literature, as many prior studies primarily compared males and females, potentially underestimating risk associations within specific subgroups of American women. Nevertheless, several limitations should be acknowledged. Some variables, such as race, reproductive history, and medical history, were self-reported, which may introduce recall bias. Additionally, there is temporal ambiguity regarding the measurement of exposure variables relative to lung cancer diagnosis. The All of Us dataset records both historical and current diagnoses, and age reflects the participant’s age at the time of survey completion rather than age at lung cancer diagnosis. Similarly, variables such as menopausal status, BMI, and comorbidities were measured at survey enrollment and may not reflect the participant’s status prior to lung cancer onset. abstract_filled: IntroductionLung cancer is the leading cause of cancer deaths in females, with slower declines in incidence compared to males. While smoking is the leading risk factor, it doesn’t fully explain the increasing lung cancer burden in females. Reproductive factors, metabolic disorders, family history, and their interactions may also influence risk; however, these remain poorly understood, particularly across diverse groups. To explore this, we conducted a case-control study using All of Us Research Program data to examine these factors and their association with lung cancer risk in adult females.MethodsUsing de-identified data from the All of Us Research Program, we conducted an age-matched case-control study to investigate the relationship between sociodemographic factors, reproductive history, metabolic disorders, and family history and lung cancer risk in adult females. Cases and controls (n = 5,500) were identified using SNOMED-CT codes with 1:1 matching. We used descriptive statistics, as well as chi-square and t-tests for group comparisons, followed by multivariable logistic regression to adjust for confounders and estimate the odds of lung cancer.ResultsLung cancer patients had a mean age of 67.9 years (SD ± 11.9) and BMI of 28.9 (SD ± 7.1). Most were non-Hispanic Whites (63.4%), followed by non-Hispanic Blacks (14.5%) and Hispanics (12.2%). Overweight females had lower odds (adjusted OR = 0.78, p = 0.0003), while smoking increased the risk (adjusted OR = 1.28, p = 0.0023). Postmenopausal bleeding (adjusted OR = 1.59, p < 0.001) and menopause (adjusted OR = 1.47, p < 0.001) increased the risk, especially in smokers (adjusted OR = 2.65, p < 0.001) and Asian menopausal females (adjusted OR = 2.67, p = 0.04). Hyperlipidemia (adjusted OR = 1.57, p < 0.001) and hypothyroidism (adjusted OR = 1.63, p < 0.001) were significant, with smoking amplifying hyperlipidemia risk (adjusted OR = 1.71, p < 0.001). Risk was also higher in smokers with lung cancer family history (adjusted OR = 1.94, p = 0.03), postmenopausal females with such a history (adjusted OR = 2.10, p = 0.03), and females with breast cancer family history combined with hypothyroidism (adjusted OR = 1.64, p = 0.0038) or postmenopausal bleeding (adjusted OR = 1.82, p = 0.017).ConclusionBeyond smoking, sociodemographic, reproductive, metabolic, and family history factors, along with their interactions, also influence lung cancer risk in females. Identifying these can aid early detection and prevention.

Topic: We evaluated the malignancy risk following herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) and ophthalmic herpes simplex virus (HSV) in a large, diverse U.S. Clinical Relevance: There has been a longstanding contention as to whether HZO serves as a clinical marker of cancer risk, with discordant findings observed across epidemiologic studies worldwide. In contrast, the relationship between ophthalmic HSV infection and malignancy remains unknown. Methods: This matched, retrospective cohort study analyzed electronic health record data from adults enrolled in the National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program. Participants with incident diagnoses of HZO or ophthalmic HSV were propensity score-matched (1:3) to controls based on sociodemographic characteristics and pre-existing immune dysregulation (i.e., autoimmune disease or immunodeficient states). Stratified Cox proportional hazards models were applied to estimate relative hazards of incident malignancy within 1-, 2-, and 3-year intervals and over the entire follow-up period. Effect modification was investigated based on age, sex, and baseline immune dysregulation. Results: The HZO cohort comprised 327 cases matched to 981 controls (mean follow-up=7.48 ± 5.33 years), and the ophthalmic HSV cohort included 292 cases matched to 876 controls (mean follow-up=8.66 ± 5.89 years). For HZO, incident malignancy risk did not differ from controls within ≤1 year (p=1.00), ≤2 years (p=0.36), ≤3 years (p=0.27), or across the full follow-up period (HR=1.01, 95% CI=[0.76, 1.36], p=0.93). However, significant effect modification by immune dysregulation was observed, with HZO associated with an increased risk of malignancy among participants with autoimmune disease (HR=2.91, 95% CI=[1.48, 5.74], p<0.01) or immunodeficient status (HR=5.75, 95% CI=[2.16, 15.35], p<0.01). For ophthalmic HSV, no increased malignancy risk was observed within ≤1 year (p=0.86), ≤2 years (p=0.18), ≤3 years (p=0.10), or across the full follow-up period (HR=0.97, 95% CI=[0.72, 1.32], p=0.87), with no evidence of effect modification. Conclusions: In this large, diverse U.S. cohort, ophthalmic herpes infections were not associated with an increased risk of malignancy in the overall cohort. However, HZO was associated with a higher subsequent risk of cancer among individuals with preexisting immune dysregulation, potentially warranting heightened oncologic vigilance in this patient demographic, thus refining the interpretation of a longstanding epidemiologic debate.

abstract_filled: AbstractBackgroundRecent genome-wide association studies for Alzheimer’s Disease and related dementias (ADRD) have increased statistical power via larger analysis datasets from biobanks by (1) including non-age-matched controls and prevalent cases, and/or (2) including individuals who report a family history of ADRD as proxy cases. However, these methods have the potential to increase noise and distort genetic associations which are important for genomic-informed prevention and treatment of ADRD. Here, we sought to understand how the effect sizes of genetic associations in ADRD could be sensitive to these methodological choices, using APOE genotypes as an example.MethodsParticipants in the All of Us Research Program over the age of 49 at enrollment (n = 229,722) were assigned one of four categories: incident ADRD (developed after enrollment in All of Us), prevalent ADRD (present on enrollment), proxy ADRD (participant noted a family history of ADRD), and control (no history or diagnosis of ADRD). ADRD diagnoses were determined using available electronic health records and APOE genotype was determined using whole-genome sequencing. Effect sizes for the associations between APOE risk alleles and ADRD diagnoses were compared using polychotomous logistic regression and presented as adjusted generalized ratios (AGR).ResultsThe mean age of the cohort was 64 ± 9 years, and it was 57% female; 65% clustered predominantly with European genetic reference populations. Among the participants, 733 (0.3%) had prevalent ADRD, 684 (0.3%) had incident ADRD, and 19,186 (8.4%) reported a family history of ADRD (proxy ADRD). The effect size for APOE ε4 heterozygote was similar for proxy ADRD (AGR [95% CI]: 2.10 [1.96–2.24]) but attenuated for prevalent ADRD (1.38 [1.17–1.63]) compared to incident ADRD (2.13 [1.81–2.50]). For APOE ε4 homozygotes, the effect sizes were significantly attenuated in both proxy (3.53 [2.93–4.26]) and prevalent (3.12 [2.20–4.45]) ADRD. Furthermore, APOE and ADRD association effect sizes increased when restricting the control (no ADRD) group to older age brackets.ConclusionsOur study highlights how genetic associations with ADRD can be sensitive to how cases are defined in biobanks like All of Us, with effect sizes downwardly biased when using prevalent or by-proxy cases compared to incident cases.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12920-026-02362-1.Keywords: Alzheimer’s Disease, Proxy case, APOE, Incidence, Prevalence, Biobank

fulltext_body: IntroductionIn real-world data, such as that found in electronic health records (EHRs), a level of apparent inconsistency or “noise” in the data appears to be inevitable [All these variations, which we will refer to as noise, stemming from measurement errors, missing information, subjective assessments, and population variability, are often difficult to detect. Completely clean datasets are rare. As a result, the level of noise is frequently unknown and overlooked. This situation introduces fundamental limits to the accuracy and reliability of models used to determine disease causes or make clinical predictions, even when advanced analytical methods are applied. To address the limitations of coded data, many research projects use natural language processing (NLP) methods to identify diagnoses, signs, and symptoms from accompanying text [When working with large amounts of EHR data in clinical research, we often perform extensive data preprocessing to assemble a relatively “clean” dataset for a given project. In such endeavors, the focus is typically placed on the main observables and an outcome, while relying on existing coded data for the identification of any important covariates. One underlying belief or hope is that a small amount of irregularity will not affect the overall study outcome and that the law of large numbers will outweigh many concerns with the data.Without a gold standard “clean” dataset, it is impossible to confirm this belief or assess the likelihood that this hope will prevail. Indeed, we have little evidence of the effect of noise in the predictors on the accuracy and utility of the findings. In observational research, we do not know how much variability will affect our results.As part of a larger project to improve EHR data quality, we investigated the effect of noise on predictive modeling performance and findings derived from the predictive models. To measure the effect, we carried out a simulation by adding varying amount of noise to a real-world dataset postulated to be accurate. To increase the generalizability of our machine learning results, we employed three algorithms (logistic regression, support vector machine classifier, and gradient boosting). To the best of our knowledge, such experiments have not been previously carried out, despite the increasing concern regarding replicability of biomedical research [BackgroundThe Shannon Channel Capacity Theorem, introduced by Claude Shannon in 1948 [A review of the literature reveals several studies that examine the impact of random noise on the performance of machine learning algorithms [ Their findings emphasize the importance of accounting for covariate inaccuracies when modeling the relationship between predictors and outcomes. Kolmar et al. studied the effects of experimental error, modeled as Gaussian noise, on RMSE and R-squared metrics across several machine learning models. They found that both metrics worsened as the level of random variation increased. None of these studies were conducted within the biomedical domain, nor did they compare different types of noise mechanisms. Moreover, they primarily focused on prediction accuracy rather than feature contributions (such as risk factors), which are often of greater importance in biomedical research.MethodsWe extracted a real-world dataset from the US NIH All of Us project [ADRD Condition DefinitionWe used a broad definition of ADRD to include different related mental conditions, including dementia, cerebral degeneration, and senile dementia and subtypes [Code BlocksCode blocks are binary variables that represent conditions with a common component as designated by their ICD 10 codes. (01= presence of condition; 0 = absence of condition) For example, conditions associated with ICD 10 codes A00 through A09 are collectively described as intestinal infectious diseases and grouped into Code Block 1, and conditions in the ICD 10 code range A15 through A19 are grouped into Code Block 2 associated with tuberculosis. DataFrom the All of Us database (with Controlled Tier access), a cohort of patients with age 55 years and older were selected. Data before January 1, 2000, were removed due to sparsity and inconsistency. In the cohort, cases are patients with an ADRD diagnosis. The control group was randomly sampled from those without ADRD diagnosis at 1:1 ratio (total n = 6,794). Data on predictors were collected before the first ADRD diagnosis for the cases and before the last visit for the controls. We converted ICD9 to ICD10 codes using the General Equivalence Mapping Tables provided by the Centers for Disease Control, and then mapped the ICD10 codes to their appropriate code blocks.Simulated NoiseIn addition to the actual data retrieved from All of Us, we simulated 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, and 30% of noisy data of the code blocks (i.e., the features) to study the effect of noise on the prediction of ADRD. In simulation studies investigating the effect of noise on machine learning algorithm performance, noise can be added as perturbation either to the features (attribute noise) or the outcome (class noise), or both. In our study, we chose to inject noise into the features and keep the outcome unmodified.Our noise generation process was modelled on three different types of missing values mechanisms from missing value research literature as described by Rubin [In NCAR generation, we generated random noises by randomly switching a variable’s value from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0. In the NAR scheme, we simulated noise in a subset of the data that was constrained by an observed variable. Specifically, we randomly separated features into “changeable” and “unchangeable’ subsets. We then randomly flipped the values of the changeable features for the instances with the highest sum of the “unchangeable’ values. In the NNAR scheme, we generated noise by randomly changing the 0s into 1s. Because in the changed data the original 0s are hidden, this is considered to be not at random. We varied the amounts of noises as different proportions of the data: 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25%, and 30%. Overall, we generated 18 simulated datasets using 3 random noise generation mechanisms with 6 proportions.AnalysisWe next applied three machine learning methods to the data for prediction of the binary outcome (ADRD). The effect of random noise on model performance was measured by noting the potential changes in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and accuracy and feature weights or impact scores across the 18 simulation experiments.In each experiment, we used logistic regression, gradient boosting (XGBoost), and linear support vector machine (SVM) models in Python to predict ADRD as a function of code blocks. We then compared the model performances to evaluate how the noise mechanisms affected the AUC and impact scores.The impact score is a measure of the contribution of a variable to the model. It quantifies the impact of an individual feature on the target outcome and is intended to quantify the explanatory power of features in linear and nonlinear machine learning models [ResultsModel Performance MetricsEffect on Coefficients and Impact ScoresAs shown in In the examination of impact scores, the results of RM-ANOVA showed that the difference between various proportions of noise is not statistically significant (for all experiments, F < 2.6, p > 0.05). A closer examination of the 10 variables with the largest impact scores from logistic regression (which are the same values as the coefficients) reveals that the changes on the individual variable level are very concerning (DiscussionIn this study, our goal was to investigate the effect of noise in clinical data, such as data from EHR databases, on the prediction performance of different predictive machine learning models, including logistic regression, SVM, and gradient boosting. We mimicked variation of data quality at different levels by adding different proportions of random and non-random binary noise to existing data curated from the All of Us database. Since it is often impossible to determine the noise level in real world clinical data, we simulated noise in a postulated gold standard in order to measure our outcomes and used three different noise generation mechanism to mimic the variability of data in EHRs.The results of these analyses tell a consistent story. In every case, increasing amounts of noise lead to lower accuracy and a diminished AUC. This result is not surprising. With more noise it is increasingly difficult to detect the signal. Whether the “noise” is simply from a random occurrence or represents another variable not included in the analysis, the resultant uncertainty has a deleterious effect on our ability to detect a signal. Of note is that the diminished signal can come from any variable, not just those of particular significance. This finding suggests that ignoring the noise in covariates is not a good strategy.The most remarkable finding is that the variance of the impact scores (see Our study was limited by the necessity of developing a reliable gold standard, leading to the requirement for simulating data and its variability. We chose ADRD as our outcome arbitrarily; we believe that the same would be true for other predictions for other outcomes as well. In addition to the effects of variability on observational studies, it is worthwhile to consider the possibility of similar effects on clinical trials. While most clinical trials using a randomized control design are tightly controlled in hopes of reducing the amount of variability involved, the hope is that any uncontrolled variable will be randomly assigned to either trial or control. Diagnosis is an uncertain process [ConclusionWhile some data may be collected from well-controlled settings, there will inevitably be variations. As a result, the data used to make predictions about biological processes will always be variable. The findings of this study suggest that the predictions may be underestimating the effect of certain variables, and that ignoring uncertainties in the known covariates may lead to misleading conclusions. The little foxes of variability in data may indeed spoil the vineyard of reproducible results.Supplementary MaterialPlease find the supplementary file here https://www.fortunejournals.com/supply/fjhs13435.finalsupplement.pdf AcknowledgmentsThis work was supported by the United States Veterans Administration Health Services Research Department grant 1I21HX003278-01A1; and by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality grant R01 HS28450-01A1.FootnotesReferencesAssociated DataSupplementary Materials
abstract_filled: It is well known that Electronic Health Records (EHR) data contain inconsistent and inaccurate data, the effect of which on predictive model performance and risk/benefit factor identification are often neglected. This study investigates how varying levels of random and non-random binary differences, often referred to as “noise”, affect modeling tools, such as logistic regression, support vector machines, and gradient boosting models. Using curated data from the All of Us database, we simulated different noise levels to mimic real-world variability. Across all models and noise types, increased noise consistently reduced classification accuracy. More importantly, noise diminished the variance of variable impact scores while leaving their means unchanged, suggesting a muted ability to identify key predictors. These findings imply that even modest noise levels can obscure meaningful signals. Measures like accuracy and hazard ratios may thus be misleading in noisy data contexts. The consistency of effects across models and noise mechanisms suggests this issue stems from inherent data variability rather than model brittleness, with broad implications for EHR data analyses.

Background And Objective: Racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic disparities in healthcare outcomes are well documented; however, their influence on health literacy, patient-reported health status, and access to care among intracranial tumor (ICT) patients remains underexplored. This study aimed to characterize these disparities within a national cohort to inform equity-focused neurosurgical care strategies. Methods: Using the National Institutes of Health All of Us Research Program (NIH AoURP) dataset, this cross-sectional analysis included 2,295 ICT patients identified via OMOP code 4116092, encompassing both primary and secondary tumors. Participants were categorized into non-Hispanic White (NHW), non-Hispanic Black (NHB), and Hispanic/Latino (HLA) groups. Data were derived from the All of Us Basics Survey, Healthcare Access and Utilization Survey, and Overall Health Survey, which include standardized patient-reported measures of sociodemographics, health literacy, and health status (including pain and emotional distress). Group comparisons were performed using chi-squared and Fisher's exact tests. Results: HLA and NHB participants demonstrated significantly higher rates of Medicaid enrollment compared to NHW participants (p < 0.001). Both HLA and NHB groups reported greater difficulty understanding medical information and completing health-related forms (p < 0.001) than NHW. Patient-reported pain severity and emotional distress were also more frequently reported among HLA and NHB participants (p < 0.05) compared to NHW. Financial and transportation-related barriers to care were disproportionately reported in HLA and NHB cohorts (p < 0.05) compared to NHW. Conclusion: Significant disparities in health literacy, patient-reported health status, and healthcare access exist among ICT patients across racial and socioeconomic groups. These findings underscore the need for literacy-sensitive communication, financial navigation support, and targeted equity-focused interventions within neurosurgical care pathways.

fulltext_body: INTRODUCTIONLimited data exist on the care experiences and health outcomes of transgender, gender‐nonconforming, and nonbinary (TGNCNB) cancer survivors.Studies have shown that lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and more (LGBTQ+) cancer survivors experience worse health‐related quality of life, greater distress, and are underserved in supportive services compared to cisgender and heterosexual survivors.Within health care, TGNCNB patients often face discrimination, and there is a lack of accurate, complete gender documentation and coordination with gender‐affirming care.Compounded with hesitations of TGNCNB individuals to approach health care environments, many oncologists feel ill‐equipped and unprepared to care for LGBTQ+ survivors.Structural social determinants of health, including area‐level socioeconomic deprivation, may further exacerbate disparities experienced by TGNCNB individuals in cancer care.This study sought to quantify the gaps in perceived health care discrimination among cancer survivors, hypothesizing that TGNCNB individuals would report higher rates of discrimination, which would contribute to poorer self‐reported health outcomes. Drawing on intersectionality theory, which proposes that social identities such as gender identity, race/ethnicity, and socioeconomic status interact to create unique experiences of discrimination and health outcomes, we controlled multiple factors that may compound disadvantages in health care settings.MATERIALS AND METHODSData source and research platformOur cross‐sectional analysis used data from the All of Us Research Program, a nationwide initiative that aims to enroll a diverse group of at least 1 million individuals in the United States to help accelerate biomedical research and improve health outcomes.All of Us Researcher Workbench with a data cutoff date of October 1, 2023. The program protocol follows the Declaration of Helsinki and is approved by the NIH institutional review board. Informed consent is received from all participants, and their data are coded for de‐identification.ParticipantsThe All of Us Research Program enrolls individuals residing in the United States who can provide informed consent. We included data on All of Us participants who reported a cancer diagnosis in the Personal and Family History questionnaire and completed the Basics and Overall Health Survey questionnaire; individuals missing data on their self‐reported health, discrimination in medical settings, and marital status were excluded (Figure Demographic measuresDemographic information was collected from the All of Us The Basics and Overall Health surveys. Variables included age at the time of the survey, gender identity, sexual orientation, race/ethnicity, marital status, annual income level, level of education, and health insurance status.Gender identity was assessed using the question “What is your current gender identity?” with options including Man, Woman, Nonbinary, Transgender, and additional gender‐diverse identities. Participants selecting Nonbinary, Transgender, or any nonbinary gender option were classified as TGNCNB; those selecting only Man or Woman were classified as cisgender. Sexual orientation was categorized as heterosexual (selecting Straight only) or nonheterosexual (all other responses). Race/ethnicity was dichotomized as White or Black, Indigenous, and People of Color (BIPOC), which included all participants who did not identify as White only. Marital status was categorized as married or not married. Complete survey questions, response options, and variable derivation procedures are provided in Table Household annual income was self‐reported and grouped into four categories: <$25,000, $25,000–$50,000, $50,000–$100,000, and >$100,000. Level of education was categorized into advanced degree, high school degree, and less than high school, based on participants' responses.Participants' health insurance was self‐reported and classified into three categories: private (employer‐based or directly purchased insurance), public (Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, VA, or Indian Health Service), or uninsured.To incorporate participants’ social adversity, we included their area deprivation index (ADI). This index is derived from a principal components analysis of six census tract‐level socioeconomic measures from the 2023 American Community Survey 5‐year estimates, including median household income, poverty level, educational attainment, health insurance coverage, public assistance receipt, and housing vacancy.Cohort matchingFor this study, the gender minority cohort was defined as TGNCNB individuals. To ensure comparable groups and minimize potential confounding factors, we performed propensity score matching using logistic regression to balance TGNCNB and cisgender individuals. This matching process incorporated covariates including age, education, income, race, insurance, and cancer site. We applied K‐nearest neighbor (KNN) matching at a 1:5 ratio to match each TGNCNB individual with five cisgender individuals based on the calculated propensity scores. All subsequent analyses to assess group differences were conducted using this matched data set.Exposure—health care discriminationHealth care discrimination was assessed using the Discrimination in Medical Settings Scale (DMS) from the All of Us Social Determinants of Health survey.Participants could respond to these questions with: “Never,” “Rarely,” “Sometimes,” “Most of the time,” and “Always.” For each of the seven questions, respondents who answered “Sometimes,” “Most of the time,” or “Always” were considered to have experienced health care discrimination for that specific question. A binary variable was also created for experiencing health care discrimination called “Overall Discriminated.” Participants who reported experiencing discrimination (responding “Sometimes,” “Most of the time,” or “Always”) on at least one item of the DMS were classified as having experienced overall discrimination (Table Outcome—self‐reported health statusSelf‐reported health status was gauged using the Overall Health survey. The survey included three questions asking participants to rate their physical, mental, and general health (Table Responses were on a 5‐point scale ranging from “Poor” (1) to “Excellent” (5). Participants who reported their physical, mental, or general health as “Fair” or “Poor” to any of the categories were categorized into an encompassing Overall Health category as “poor health.” As a sensitivity analysis, we also examined mental health and general health outcomes separately using the same hierarchical regression approach (Tables Statistical analysisDescriptive statistics were calculated for participant demographic, socioeconomic, discrimination, and health status characteristics. For the descriptive statistics (Table 2 tests were conducted to assess differences in median age (used due to non‐normal distribution) and in categorical variables across gender identity groups. For all multivariable regression models, cisgender men and women were combined into a single reference group for binary comparisons with TGNCNB individuals. After controlling for demographic and socioeconomic factors, multivariable logistic regression models were used to explore the association between health care discrimination and self‐reported poor health. We also reported point estimates as odds ratios (ORs) and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All the statistical tests were two‐sided, at the significance level p < .05. All analyses were performed using Python version 3.8.1 in Jupyter Notebook environment within the All of Us Researcher Workbench.RESULTSDemographic characteristicsThe cohort totaled 1476 patients, of which 246 (17%) identified as TGNCNB. Among the 246 TGNCNB cancer survivors, 63 (25.6%) identified as transgender and 183 (74.4%) identified gender nonconforming and nonbinary. The median (interquartile range [IQR]) age for TGNCNB participants was 55 (38–67) years. Overall, 73% identified as White, and 27% identified as BIPOC. Among our cohort, health insurance coverage was distributed as follows: 48% private, 48% public, and 4% uninsured. Over two‐fifths (42%) were married. Twenty‐one percent reported an annual income below $25,000, and 54% resided in areas of high socioeconomic deprivation. Close to 30% of TGNCNB individuals had cancers of reproductive organs and breast tissue, and 28% identified as heterosexual (Table Health care discriminationTGNCNB participants had a higher prevalence of self‐reported overall health care discrimination (63.8%), compared to cisgender women (48.5%) and cisgender men (29.8%) (χ2: p < .001). Across the specific types of discrimination, “not being listened to by a provider” was reported by 55.0% of TGNCNB participants, more than double the rate among cisgender men (21.2%). The proportion of TGNCNB participants who reported that “providers acted superior” (40.3%), “treated them with less respect” (35.9%), and “assumed they were not smart” (34.5%) was higher compared to their cisgender counterparts (Figure In separate multivariable models adjusted for ADI and marital status for each discrimination question, TGNCNB individuals reported consistently elevated odds of experiencing health care discrimination. Compared to cisgender individuals, TGNCNB participants had greater odds of being treated with less courtesy (OR, 2.46; 95% CI, 1.79–3.37), treated with less respect (OR, 2.61; 95% CI, 1.91–3.57), perceiving a provider acted afraid (OR, 2.32; 95% CI, 1.37–3.93), or acted superior (OR, 2.51; 95% CI, 1.85–3.40). TGNCNB participants also had greater odds of being perceived as not smart (OR, 2.24; 95% CI, 1.64–3.06), receiving poorer service (OR, 2.40; 95% CI, 1.74–3.30), and not being listened to by providers (OR, 2.38; 95% CI, 1.79–3.17) compared to cisgender individuals (Figure Predictors of health care discriminationTable p < .01). Participants who lived in a high‐ADI region had 41% higher odds of reporting overall health care discrimination (OR, 1.41; 95% CI, 1.13–1.75, p < .01) compared to those in a low‐ADI region. Being married was protective against discrimination (OR, 0.56; 95% CI, 0.48–0.74, p < .01).Predictors of self‐reported poor healthTable p < .01). The association remained significant in the fully adjusted model. Any health care discrimination (OR, 1.73; 95% CI, 1.29–2.33, p < .01), living in areas with high deprivation (OR, 1.72; 95% CI, 1.28–2.33, p < .01), and being married (OR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.27–2.32, p < .01) were all associated with TGNCNB having increased odds of reporting poor health in the hierarchical model. We also performed a multivariable model for poor health, adjusted for health care discrimination, ADI, and marital status (Table p < .01). TGNCNB identity was linked to higher odds of poor health (OR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.27–2.32, p < .01). Living in high‐ADI areas was also associated with higher odds of poor health (OR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.03–1.63, p < .01). Being married was associated with lower odds of reporting poor health (OR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.41‐0.64, p < .01). In the sensitivity analysis that matched on sex assigned at birth, in addition to the other covariates, results were consistent with the primary analysis. TGNCNB identity remained significantly associated with poor health outcomes in the fully adjusted model (OR, 2.08; 95% CI, 1.54–2.80, p < .01), and health care discrimination remained the strongest predictor of poor health (OR, 3.21; 95% CI, 2.57–4.02, p < .01) (Tables DISCUSSIONOur study identifies experiences of health care discrimination among cancer survivors, with TGNCNB survivors reporting notably higher rates than their cisgender peers. These findings underscore the higher levels of overall health care discrimination reported by TGNCNB cancer survivors, including specific experiences such as being ignored, receiving poorer service, provider acting afraid, and perceiving provider superiority. We found a strong association between health care discrimination and poor health outcomes, with TGNCNB identity independently linked to worse self‐reported health. This persistence suggests that disparities in health among TGNCNB cancer survivors are not fully explained by health care discrimination alone and reflect additional structural or social factors. Overall, our findings indicate that health care discrimination is a significant and independent predictor of poor self‐reported health among TGNCNB cancer survivors.These findings align with prior research, highlighting the systemic barriers faced by TGNCNB individuals during their cancer care continuum. In our study, 63.8% of TGNCNB cancer survivors experienced any form of health care discrimination. This is particularly critical, given that previous literature has shown that 23% of transgender individuals avoid health care due to the fear of discrimination and stigma from the medical staff.p < .01). TGNCNB individuals also had higher odds of poor health (OR, 1.71; 95% CI, 1.27–2.32, p < .01), which could be attributed to other clinical factors or other stressors/comorbidities, as stated in the gender minority stress theory.The health care discrimination and poor health outcomes documented in our study are compounded by several systemic barriers in cancer care delivery for TGNCNB individuals. Because of the limited cancer screening guidelines for the TGNCNB individuals, they are frequently diagnosed at later cancer stages, and are less likely to receive timely treatments, consequently leading to worse survival outcomes.Additionally, limited collection of gender identity and the underrepresentation of TGNCNB individuals in clinical trials and national cancer databases, contribute to gaps in representation and evidence generation.Furthermore, stressors and comorbidities that disproportionately affect minoritized communities, outlined by the gender minority stress theory, such as high rates of HIV infection, substance use, and psychological distress, further complicate cancer care and survivorship among TGNCNB individuals.There are several limitations to consider. The cross‐sectional nature of the data limits our ability to establish causal relationships between health care discrimination and self‐reported health. This exploratory study aimed to characterize health care experiences among TGNCNB cancer survivors; formal causal mediation analysis would require stronger assumptions and, ideally, longitudinal data with treatment and adherence information. In the All of Us database, health care discrimination and health status were self‐reported, which may be subject to social desirability bias and recall bias, as participants over‐ or underreport their experiences during their cancer care continuum. Additionally, the study data were drawn only from the All of Us Research Program and may not represent the TGNCNB population in the United States. Despite these limitations, our findings provide critical insights into the health care experiences of TGNCNB cancer survivors in a large database, showing the urgency of addressing discrimination to improve health equity and quality of life for this underserved population.Building on these findings, policy and clinical practice changes must focus on structural inclusion and clinician preparedness to reduce the disproportionate amount of health care discrimination experienced by TGNCNB cancer survivors.AUTHOR CONTRIBUTIONS Daniel Sabater Minarim: Conceptualization; investigation; funding acquisition; methodology; writing—original draft; writing—review and editing; formal analysis; and data curation. Morgan: Methodology; formal analysis; and data curation. Sakshith Reddy Chintala: Methodology; formal analysis; and data curation. Jennifer T. Anger: Conceptualization; writing—review and editing; and supervision. Carol Y. Ochoa‐Dominguez: Writing—review and editing and supervision. Matthew P. Banegas: Conceptualization; writing—original draft; writing—review and editing; and supervision. Brent S. Rose: Conceptualization; writing—review and editing; and supervision. Paul Riviere: Conceptualization; investigation; writing—original draft; writing—review and editing; project administration; supervision.CONFLICT OF INTEREST STATEMENTJennifer T.
